title: Unauthenticated remote code execution in Nginx
body_text: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 | Wiz Blog Wiz Platform Solutions Pricing Resources Customers Company Sign in Under attack? Get a demo Blog Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in NGINX: CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 Two critical HTTP/2 flaws can allow attackers to compromise NGINX servers, putting the websites, APIs, and sensitive data they handle at risk. Watch the Threat Briefing Webinar Nir Ohfeld , Tomer Schwartz November 18, 2026 | Executive Summary Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, software used to receive and route traffic to production applications and APIs. NGINX is a common default for the front door of modern web architectures, where it handles HTTPS and routes incoming traffic to the right application or API. As the world's most widely used open-source web server , it powers more than 225 million websites . Successful exploitation could let attackers take control of affected NGINX servers, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. The vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, are both rated Critical, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Websites and APIs can be exposed even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Additional conditions are described below. CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. We reported our findings to F5, the company behind NGINX, and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates when released. We recommend updating affected NGINX deployments to the latest release which includes multiple security fixes. Responsible disclosure timeline October 21, 2026: Wiz reports the HTTP/2 use-after-free vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123633, to F5, including confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass and a proposed fix. F5 confirms that another research team had previously reported the same vulnerability. November 10, 2026: F5 supplies a patch for CVE-2026-123633 for review. November 16, 2026 : Wiz reports the second HTTP/2 vulnerability, later assigned CVE-2026-123007, to F5. November 17, 2026 : F5 confirms that the second report matches CVE-2026-123007 and is included in the planned November 18 security release. November 18, 2026: F5 security release and coordinated public disclosure. Overview Wiz Research, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint independently uncovered CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, two critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in NGINX, and reported them to F5, the company behind NGINX. Successful exploitation can compromise the server running NGINX, allowing attackers to execute code, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. NGINX often handles traffic for several applications, so a single affected deployment can put multiple services at risk. The flaws are in NGINX itself and can affect websites even when their own application code is secure. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server. Our testing of CVE-2026-123007 demonstrated code execution on NGINX serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party modules. Wiz Research used Wiz Atlas , the harness powering Wiz’s AI Code scanning solution , to discover both vulnerabilities. Our researchers used Gemini 4 Carbon and ChatGPT 5.6 Sol to validate the impact of both vulnerabilities, confirming that each could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the server. We reported our findings to F5 and worked with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. The integer underflow vulnerability dates back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015, meaning it had been hiding in the code for more than a decade. The use-after-free vulnerability had been there for nearly six years. Like the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities we reported last month and Java4Shell , disclosed yesterday by Calif, these are memory-safety flaws that have historically been extremely difficult to discover and exploit. Finding them often requires tracing subtle interactions between memory operations and multiple code paths. For years, that complexity itself created a practical barrier. AI is fundamentally dissolving that barrier. As AI models get better at following those interactions, both researchers and attackers can uncover longstanding flaws in software that powers the internet and modern applications. The fact that multiple independent research teams uncovered the same vulnerabilities in both PHP and NGINX, after they had remained in the code for years, makes this shift particularly striking. And as AI capabilities advance, each new generation of models may uncover even more complex vulnerabilities that were previously beyond practical reach. Complexity can no longer be relied upon as a barrier to discovery or exploitation. This changes not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats. Over time, finding and fixing these flaws can harden the software we all depend on. In the near term, faster discovery and a shorter window between disclosure and exploitation add to an already demanding workload for security teams. Turning a published fix into protection in production still takes substantial manual work, from validating patches to coordinating rollouts with service owners. We recommend focusing on how quickly you can reduce exposure in production. Identify deployments running the affected version and configuration, prioritize those an attacker can reach, and apply mitigations while patches are tested and rolled out. In this post, we explain the vulnerabilities and their impact, and provide mitigation and detection guidance. Organizations should identify affected deployments and apply the security updates as soon as they are available. If upgrading is not immediately possible, temporarily disable HTTP/2. What is NGINX? NGINX is the world's most widely used open-source web server , powering more than 225 million websites . It is commonly used as a reverse proxy in front of websites and APIs. In this role, NGINX accepts incoming requests, forwards them to the appropriate application server based on its configuration, and returns the response to the user. NGINX can also serve web content directly and act as a load balancer , distributing traffic across multiple servers. A single NGINX deployment can serve several applications, making it a shared entry point for the websites and APIs behind it. The Vulnerabilities Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety issues in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic. In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy. Each can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. Tracking ID The bug What an attacker can achieve CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2 connection use-after-free Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Execute arbitrary code on the NGINX server without authentication. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled, but their additional requirements differ. CVE-2026-123633 affects reverse-proxy processing when available connection slots run low. CVE-2026-123007 can also affect NGINX serving content directly, as demonstrated in our testing over HTTPS on 64-bit systems. Typical memory safety mitigations such as ASLR do not protect against these issues, as attackers can use either vulnerabilities for memory read access prior to code execution. Impact On affected NGINX versions with HTTP/2 enabled, these vulnerabilities can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server. The flaws are in NGINX itself. Exploitation does not depend on a bug in the website or API behind it, so applications with secure code can still be exposed. For CVE-2026-123007, we demonstrated remote code execution on a server serving ordinary static files, without a backend application or third-party module. An attacker could use this access to run commands, steal sensitive data, tamper with websites, or disrupt services. Because one NGINX deployment can serve several applications, the impact could extend across multiple websites and APIs. Illustrative deployment: an attacker exploits NGINX to run code on the server, putting the applications and data it serves at risk. Coordinated disclosure We reported both vulnerabilities to F5 and collaborated with its security team on remediation and coordinated disclosure. We also shared proposed fixes. Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint also independently discovered and reported these issues to F5. We thank the F5 and NGINX teams for their work on the fixes. Vulnerabilities Addressed in the Release F5's security release addresses several other vulnerabilities in NGINX. Below is a summary of these additional CVEs, as well as the two critical HTTP/2 remote code execution flaws detailed in this post (captured in the first two rows of the table): CVE Description Impact CVSS Affected Versions CVE-2026-123007 Memory corruption in HTTP/2 flow control Exploitable in default configurations with HTTP/2 enabled 9.2 1.9.5-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123633 UAF in HTTP/2 Exploitable configured with HTTP/2 as a proxy server 9.2 1.19.7-1.31.8 CVE-2026-121810 UAF in HTTP/3 Exploitable configured with HTTP/3 as a proxy server 9.2 1.25.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123634 UAF during response processing in DNS resolver RCE when attacker controls upstream host name 9.2 0.6.18-1.31.8 CVE-2026-113425 UAF in mail proxy module RCE when configured as a mail server proxy with auth_http 9.2 0.5.33-1.31.8 CVE-2026-118899 Infinite loop while reading client request body Potential denial-of-service when server supports TLS 1.3 8.7 1.13.0-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120993 NULL pointer dereference Denial-of-service when configured with proxy_protocol v2 6.9 1.31.4-1.31.8 CVE-2026-125283 Buffer overflow when using alias with try_files Theoretical RCE in uncommon nginx.conf configuration 6.9 0.9.6-1.31.8 CVE-2026-123640 Insufficient validation in stream ssl_preread SSRF-like access when configured with ssl_preread 6.9 1.15.2-1.31.8 CVE-2026-120967 Client certificate bypass Client certificate bypass in specific SNI configurations 6.3 1.25.5-1.31.8 Mitigation and detection Identify affected NGINX deployments with HTTP/2 enabled and upgrade to a release that fixes both vulnerabilities as soon as it is available. Product CVE and first affected version or branch Fixed releases NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123633: 1.19.7 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123633: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.7.1; 37.2.0.1 NGINX OSS CVE-2026-123007: 1.9.5 1.30.7 stable; 1.31.9 mainline NGINX Plus CVE-2026-123007: R33; 37.0.0 37.0.8.1; 37.3.0.1 If you cannot upgrade immediately, temporarily disable HTTP/2 on affected NGINX instances: Set http2 off; in affected server blocks on NGINX 1.25.1 or later, and remove the http2 parameter from any listen directives . Test application compatibility, reload NGINX , and confirm the old workers have exited. Re-enable HTTP/2 after upgrading. Investigate unexpected NGINX worker crashes or commands launched by NGINX; these are general warning signs, not confirmed indicators of these vulnerabilities. Technical deep dive CVE-2026-123633: An active connection marked as reusable NGINX keeps a list of connections that it can close when it needs room for new ones. An HTTP/2 connection can join this list when it has no active requests, but must leave it when a request starts. We start by sending only part of a HEADERS frame, which carries an HTTP/2 request's headers. With no active request streams, ngx_http_v2_handle_connection() marks the connection as reusable while waiting for the rest: ngx_reusable_connection(c, 1); if (h2c->state.incomplete) { return; } When we send the rest of the frame, ngx_http_v2_create_stream() creates a request stream and increments h2c->processing . However, it does not remove the connection from the reusable list. We now have a request being processed on a connection that NGINX still considers safe to close. Triggering the use-after-free Next, we need NGINX to close this connection while the request is still running. Forwarding the request to an application server can trigger this. Opening an upstream connection calls ngx_get_connection() . When free connection slots run low, ngx_drain_connections() selects reusable connections to close. Our HTTP/2 connection is still on that list, so NGINX can select it while processing its own request. Before closing it, NGINX tries to send a GOAWAY frame to notify the client. Even creating this frame can fail, for example, if NGINX has reached its internal frame limit for the connection and has no frame available for reuse. In that case, the error path closes the connection and frees the memory associated with it. Processing then resumes in the original request, which still uses that memory. We have reached the use-after-free. From use-after-free to remote code execution The freed memory can now be reused for other data. The request-processing code still follows its old pointers, treating the new contents as the original request or connection. This use-after-free can lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. CVE-2026-123007: HTTP/2 send_window integer underflow Returning credit for unsent data HTTP/2 allows several requests, called streams, to share one connection. Flow control limits how much response data NGINX can send before the client is ready to receive more. NGINX tracks the connection's remaining allowance in a counter called h2c->send_window . When NGINX queues response data, it subtracts that data's size from the counter before sending it. If a stream is canceled while its data is still queued, ngx_http_v2_filter_cleanup() removes the unsent data and returns the unused allowance: h2c->send_window += window; This refund does not check HTTP/2's maximum allowed window. If the client has already increased the allowance while data was waiting to be sent, the refund can push the counter above that maximum. NGINX is now tracking a value the rest of its HTTP/2 code assumes cannot occur. A bounds check that no longer works The next problem is in ngx_http_v2_state_window_update() , which checks whether an increase would exceed the limit: if (window > NGX_HTTP_V2_MAX_WINDOW - h2c->send_window) The check subtracts the current allowance from the maximum to calculate how much room remains. But the refund has already pushed the allowance past that maximum. Because the calculation uses an unsigned integer, which cannot represent a negative number, the subtraction wraps around and underflows to a very large positive value. The check now treats an invalid counter as though it has plenty of room left and allows further increases. From an invalid length to remote code execution The invalid counter eventually reaches ngx_http_v2_send_chain() , where it is converted to the signed integer type off_t to calculate how much data to send. A sufficiently large value becomes negative. That negative length then reaches the code that describes a portion of a response buffer, leaving its end pointer before its start pointer. When the TLS send path in ngx_ssl_send_chain() processes this malformed buffer, further signed and unsigned conversions turn the invalid length into an out-of-bounds memory copy. An attacker can use this to disclose memory, corrupt the heap, and lead to unauthenticated remote code execution on the NGINX server. We confirmed remote code execution with an ASLR bypass on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds. The tested path used HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems serving response data from memory. Ordinary static files can reach this path through standard TLS processing, without a backend application or third-party module. Exploitation To confirm these vulnerabilities, Wiz Research built proof-of-concept exploits and managed to run them in multiple lab settings against servers running common NGINX configurations we’ve seen in customer environments. In the interest of customer protection, we will not be releasing these exploits at this time. Like other memory-safety issues, such vulnerabilities are difficult to exploit remotely and require the attacker to disclose memory addresses, groom and shape the heap correctly, and handle different NGINX versions, builds, and configurations. In reality, attackers may not need to target every single configuration, and we have seen in PHP2Shell that widespread attacks initially start against packaged products where many customers use the exact same build and configuration. Motivated attackers may tailor exploits for specific targets. Any exploit assumes the attacker is able to communicate directly with the affected NGINX server. CDNs and WAFs that terminate HTTP/2 may mitigate parts of the exploit by not reflecting the exact payload back to the underlying NGINX server. This depends on implementation. Specifically, CVE-2026-123007 requires the attacker to send a large number of WINDOW_UPDATE records to increase it to an arbitrary value. Detection rules covering long standing HTTP/2 connections sending large amounts of data may hint at an attack associated with this vulnerability. CVE-2026-123633 has different exploitation constraints and is more likely to be exploited when NGINX is configured in proxy configuration. How Can Wiz Help? Wiz customers can use the pre-built query and advisory in the Wiz Threat Center to search for vulnerable instances in their environment. Conclusion With NGINX handling traffic for critical websites and applications, the impact of flaws in its core extends far beyond a single service. This research is another example of AI uncovering critical vulnerabilities in widely deployed infrastructure. The flaws were already there; AI helped us find them. As we saw with PHP2Shell , AI is changing the economics of vulnerability research. The same capabilities that help defenders uncover flaws can also help attackers investigate them. Software that has been used and reviewed for years still needs to be examined as these tools improve. The opportunity is to make this work routine: finding vulnerabilities in the software organizations depend on and working with maintainers to fix them. Our collaboration with F5 brings that approach to NGINX, helping protect the applications and services behind it. Stay in touch Hi there! We are Nir Ohfeld and Tomer Schwartz from the Wiz Research Team ( @wiz_io ). We are a group of veteran white-hat hackers with a single goal: to make the cloud a safer place for everyone. We focus on finding new attack vectors in cloud software and uncovering isolation issues in the systems organizations depend on. We would love to hear from you on X or at research@wiz.io . Generative AI is experimental Voice Speed Voice Speed 0.75X 1X 1.5X 2X In this article Gemini 4 Neon is available Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Built for production-ready code Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense Designed for safe, dependable execution Built for deeper analysis Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Delivers across enterprise, analytical, and scientific work Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. Finally, it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena's new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions. On scientific and mathematical reasoning, spanning quantitative analysis, mathematics, and technical research problems, Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%). Built for production-ready code Engineered for long-running agent workflows, Neon sustains performance through complex, tool-heavy tasks end-to-end — whether running standalone or acting as a fast, high-judgment Orchestrator directing parallel Hydrogen subagents in Google Antigravity. It cuts down on redundant file reads, shares progress as it works, and handles context compaction reliably in long sessions. Across core developer and researcher workflows, Neon achieves frontier performance and is competitive with the leading models in its class, ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6), with a score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0 . For production-ready code, Neon handles multi-file debugging and refactoring across repositories with targeted, surgical edits. On SWE-sweep, it already leads on the mini-SWE harness (12.8%) and more than triples to a state-of-the-art 39.0% in Google Antigravity showing what the Antigravity harness unlocks. Driving Blender MCP in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon used /swarm to build a photorealistic 3D lab bench visualizing the model names with elemental accuracy pairing Bunsen flames for Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Hydrogen with high-voltage gas discharge tubes for Gemini 4 Argon and Neon. In Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon wrote a first-person WebGL2 freeride ski simulator from scratch on real Mont Blanc and Chamonix elevation terrain — combining 10,200 lines of custom shaders, 120 Hz ski physics across six alpine lines, dynamic carved tracks, slab avalanches, and spatial Web Audio with zero pre-made assets. Using /swarm in Google Antigravity, Gemini 4 Neon pulled archival photos to recreate Alan Turing’s 1936 study at King’s College, Cambridge in interactive 3D — from King’s Chapel outside to Room X.8 inside, complete with a working Universal Turing Machine running on his desk. In Google Antigravity, a Gemini 4 Neon agent swarm turned a single image into a 100,000-cell Google Sheet with zero embedded images and zero Apps Script — using over 500,000 live spreadsheet formulas to run edge detection, map 3D depth, and relight the scene across six interactive modes. Brings efficiency and control to production-grade workflows We’re refining thinking levels with each new model release to give teams finer control and a smoother progression from one tier to the next. Neon’s four levels scale steadily, letting teams dial intelligence and token spend to what each workload needs. Neon delivers high performance at a lower cost per task across third-party benchmarks. At its default high thinking level, it pairs a high Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index score with a 32% lower cost per task than Carbon. It also sits on the Pareto frontier on both the Vals index and Agent Arena at high, with roughly 50% to 80% lower cost per task than top competing frontier models. xhigh thinking adds deeper, multi-step reasoning for the hardest engineering, analytical, and scientific workloads. Neon shows its highest intelligence score here, while still costing 36%+ less per task than competing models at their highest setting. Built for fast, efficient, frontier-level cyber defense As agentic coding scales, generating secure code from the start is critical. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber produces more secure code than Carbon across all easy, medium, and hard challenges on AutoBaxBench , achieving state-of-the-art on the hard tier (76%). Securing systems also means proactively finding flaws before attackers do. Penetration testing has served as a cornerstone of enterprise cybersecurity. On WebExploitBench v1.2 , Neon is state-of-the-art (51.26%) at half the cost of competing large models. To fortify existing code, Neon for cyber delivers frontier-level performance across the code hardening lifecycle — vulnerability finding, validating, and patching — all while being faster and more cost efficient than large frontier models. Finding code vulnerabilities: Neon achieves state-of-the-art performance on SEC-bench Pro (90.5%), while costing roughly half as much per challenge. Validating risk through exploitation: To prioritize which vulnerabilities to remediate, defenders rely on models to check which vulnerabilities are exploitable. On ExploitGym, it achieves frontier-level performance using half the tokens of Carbon. Patching vulnerabilities: Fixing the root cause of vulnerabilities is a critical step in the cybersecurity defense lifecycle. Neon reaches 70.7% on Collinear’s CWE-bench v2 , driving a 3.4% uplift over Carbon. Gemini 4 Neon for cyber is rolling out to trusted defenders in the coming days as part of the Fairwind Program . Designed for safe, dependable execution Gemini 4 Neon builds on improvements from our Gemini 4 safety and security stack — maintaining Gemini 4 Carbon-level protections against severe misuse and prompt injection while advancing further on model alignment and agentic behavior. For a model meant to carry demanding, long-running work in production, we concentrated on: Mitigating frontier misuse safety risks: Because Neon brings frontier-level capabilities to a faster, lower-cost model, we paired it with strong real-time safeguards against cyber and biosecurity misuse comparable to our Carbon protections, while declining far less legitimate work in these areas, refusing for instance just 1.98% of tasks on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and 0% on Terminal-Bench-Science. Advancing alignment and disciplined model behavior: In internal coding use, alert rates from our chain-of-thought and action misalignment monitor remained below the already low baselines set by Carbon, suggesting improved alignment propensity for Neon — and that same monitor is deployed to protect Neon across external surfaces. Neon is trained to complete multi-step work without cutting corners, fabricating results, or overstepping user boundaries — continuing to improve the balance between following through on requests and staying within scope. It matched Carbon with 0.0% cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 and took shortcuts on just 2.45% of tasks on our coding cheating evaluation (the lowest rate of any Gemini 4 model). It also achieved a 0.09% misaligned action rate on our agentic safety suite and a 99.2% pass rate on our agent honesty evaluation. On our agentic behavior evaluation, Neon builds on Carbon’s strong baseline by further reducing under-service by 43%–56% and overreach by 15%–35% across different effort levels. Protecting users from indirect prompt injection attacks: On Gray Swan's IPI benchmark, Neon is more resilient than other models in its class when malicious instructions are planted in the web pages, emails, documents, or code it accesses. We found that with real-time safeguards at its highest thinking level, Neon resisted every attack within this Gray Swan benchmark, matching the 0.0% attack success rate reached only by other Gemini models. For more details, see the Gemini 4 Neon model card . Built for deeper analysis In the Gemini app, Gemini 4 Neon excels at work that requires frontier-level reasoning and fast responses. Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs. Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data. Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund. Where Neon sits in the Gemini 4 family Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency. Neon delivers frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently. Start building with Gemini 4 Neon today Gemini 4 Neon begins rolling out today: For developers: Build with the Gemini API paid tier in Google AI Studio and Android Studio , if you’re a paid Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can try Neon in Google Antigravity and all Pro and Ultra subscribers can try it in AI Studio. For enterprises: Use Gemini 4 Neon in Gemini for business (via the API or model drop-down) and Google Antigravity. For consumers: If you’re a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscriber, you can select Gemini 4 Neon from the model drop-down in the Gemini app . For cybersecurity defenders: Eligible Fairwind Program members will begin receiving access over the next few days. To request access to the Fairwind Program, contact your Cloud account team. Get the latest news from Google in your inbox Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. Check your inbox to confirm your subscription. You can also subscribe with a different email address . Your information will be used in accordance with Google's privacy policy. You may opt out at any time. new tab) Facebook (opens in a new tab) Article link Copy link Share At MAI, our mission is to build you the very best models in the world and keep every developer and every enterprise at the frontier of capability. But as token spend skyrockets, we know that you also want models at a price point that lets you run agents 24/7 doing real engineering work. That’s why today we’re releasing a family of seven new world class models at a truly exceptional price-performance. Here’s the lineup: MAI Cyber 2 Flash beats GPT-6 Astra’s quality at less than 2% of the cost per task on the CyberGym-E2E benchmark. MAI Code 2 reaches 98% of the coding quality of GPT-6.1 Sol at about 40% of the price. And against Opus 5.5, it reaches 96% performance for just 5% of the price. MAI Code 2 Flash shows comparable performance GPT-6 Luna at 65% of the price, and Haiku 5.5 at 20% of the price. MAI Image 2.7 is #1 on Artificial Analysis image editing, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. MAI Realtime 1 outperforms GPT-Realtime 2.1 and starts at just $0.01 per audio minute. Dragon Copilot Transcribe is built on MAI Transcribe 2, the world’s fastest and most accurate multilingual transcription model, and already powers 10 million patient encounters a month with multilingual error rates halved. Decision 1.1 is the latest decision model from Microsoft, 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Maia 200 , Microsoft’s second-generation AI accelerator, is now in production running our largest models, achieving 1.7x more tokens per watt.  Frontier cyber defense built to run 24/7 Security, alignment and containment are the most important priorities for agent development in 2027 and beyond. That’s our top priority. We need to run monitoring and control agents defending and patching live production systems 24/7. That’s why MAI Cyber 2 Flash was designed to deliver frontier intelligence at a fraction of the cost. Built with Microsoft’s decades of proprietary data and world-class security expertise, our models help defenders stay safe in this new era where attackers have cheap and abundant offensive tools. MAI Cyber 2 Flash builds on earlier MAI Cyber models that defenders already rely on. MAI Cyber accounts for almost 40% of scans in MDASH, and 90% of scans that started with MAI continued to use it. Our latest model is now priced 86% lower on output tokens than MAI Cyber 1.1 Flash, giving existing MDASH customers a stronger model at a lower price. Incredible coding performance at a fraction of the cost MAI Code 2 is built for the best price-performance for everyday enterprise coding tasks. Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1, SWE-Atlas and FrontierCode v1.1), MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT-6.1 Sol at 40% of the price, and 96% of Claude Opus 5.5’s performance at just 5% of the price. We’ve built these models to prioritize the coding work our customers do every day. They’re explicitly not yet tuned for harder problems, like fundamental science research and very long horizon agentic work. MAI Code 2 also been tuned to generate great dashboards and visualizations. In a blind, side-by-side evaluation of frontend work, developers preferred MAI Code 2 over GPT-6 Sol 64% of the time. Try MAI Code 2 in GitHub Copilot today. Read more here . MAI Code 2 Flash is designed for high-volume, everyday tasks like code explanations, targeted edits, routine fixes, and rapid iterations, while bringing quality at a much lower cost. It performs comparably to GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5 at 65% and 20% of the price, respectively, across three coding benchmarks measuring day-to-day, high-volume routine coding tasks (DeepSWE 1.1, Terminal Bench 2.1 and SWE-Atlas). It’s available in GitHub Copilot and in a limited-access preview in Microsoft Foundry . The best image and transcription models in the world MAI Image 2.7 is the best image editing model in the world, taking the #1 spot on Artificial Analysis, outperforming GPT Image 2.6 Sunburst (max) at just one-fifth of the price. At text-to-image generation, our model is ranked #4, making us the second-best lab. And MAI Image 2.7 Flash brings world class image generation for high-volume scenarios at ~$10 per 1,000 images. Both are available in Microsoft Foundry here . MAI Realtime 1 is our first live speech-to-speech model, designed for natural, low-latency conversations. In our evaluations, it outperformed GPT-Realtime 2.1 across external and Dynamics 365 benchmarks. It’s priced for enterprise-scale use, starting at a budget-saving price of $0.01 per audio minute. You can try it out in MAI Labs and register your interest here . Dragon Copilot Transcribe , built on MAI Transcribe 2, is now live in Dragon Copilot, powering 100% of doctor–patient conversation transcriptions. It covers 10 million encounters a month, halves error rates in multilingual workflows, and is in the hands of a third of US physicians. The leading Decision model in the market Decision 1.1 provides model routing integrated right into your applications so that the bigger, pricier models are only used when you really need them. On the Artificial Analysis Decision Index Microsoft is ahead of Jev, Google and OpenAI, while being faster and cheaper. Used by 4,000 customers, it’s 50x faster and 79x cheaper than GPT-6.1 Sol. Customize models for your business We’ve heard again and again from leaders that no one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model. And if you build on open weights, can you really trust where they came from, or how they’ll behave when you use one as the foundation for your most valuable IP and data? We heard you. We started with Custom Models. AT&T developed an MAI custom model for 5G network operation analytics and it outperformed GPT-6.1 Sol at 1/50th of the cost. On complex scenarios, they found that Code 2 delivered frontier-level performance at a significantly lower price than alternatives. Today, we’re taking a big step forward with MAI Licensed Weights : models under your control. Take a frontier MAI model, customize it using your proprietary data if you want to. Then run it securely in your own Azure environment. You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents. So that’s MAI, a family of world class models with exceptional price performance: the world’s best image editing model; the world’s best transcription model; frontier cyber defense at 2% of the cost; and world class everyday coding models at a price you can scale. And crucially all of it with Your IQ. Your agents. Your weights. All under your control. This is Frontier Intelligence you can trust, from the company you can trust. title: DNS resolvers are the wrong place to fight piracy
body_text: Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy | Tech Stackups Skip to main content Tech Stackups Home Topics Comparisons Guides Articles AX Search Quad9 Is Leaving France: Why DNS Resolvers Are the Wrong Place to Fight Piracy November 18, 2026 Â· 21 min read Al Smith Technical writer On Tuesday, November 24, 2026, Quad9 will stop answering DNS queries from France. Quad9 is the Swiss non-profit behind the free 9.9.9.9 resolver, which blocks malware and phishing domains. It is not leaving because of costs or lack of users. It is leaving because a Paris court fined it for refusing to block a list of pirate sports-streaming domains on behalf of beIN Sports. With around 20 similar cases still pending in France, leaving the country is the only option Quad9 can afford. Cloudflare, which runs the competing 1.1.1.1 resolver, called the departure "a canary in the coal mine" , and the post reached the front page of Hacker News . In that thread, Quad9's CTO John Todd asked readers to write "a long-form, well-reasoned statement of why France is taking the wrong path", with plenty of sources, and to send it to policymakers. This is our attempt. Every claim below links to a primary document, a court ruling, or contemporaneous reporting. What Quad9 is, and why it matters â A DNS resolver turns a name like example.com into an IP address your computer can connect to. Most people use their ISP's resolver without knowing it. A public resolver is one anyone can point their device or network at instead, such as Google's 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1, Cisco's OpenDNS, or Quad9's 9.9.9.9. Quad9 has a few properties that make it unusual: It is a non-profit. It was founded in 2017 by the Global Cyber Alliance, IBM, and Packet Clearing House , and moved its legal seat to ZÃ¼rich in 2021 , hosted by SWITCH, specifically so that its privacy promises would be backed by Swiss law. As John Todd put it at the time: "Privacy policies which are not backed by law are empty promises." Security filtering is its main purpose. Quad9 refuses to resolve domains that threat-intelligence feeds flag as malware, phishing, or botnet infrastructure. Its about page claims 670 million+ blocks a day across 230+ resolver clusters in over 110 countries . It keeps no user records. Quad9 does not know who its users are, and that is the point. Organisations have come to depend on it. Mullvad shut down its own public encrypted DNS service on November 2, 2026 and moved Mullvad Browser users with default settings to Quad9, funding Quad9 instead. (Mullvad Browser users in France will now be migrated to a resolver that disappears three weeks later.) Quad9's announcement lists dozens of French networks it sees traffic from, including the interministerial digital directorate DINUM, France Travail, CEA, Institut Pasteur, RENATER, EDF, SNCF, AP-HM hospitals in Marseille, France TÃ©lÃ©visions, Thales, and Airbus's Stormshield . Quad9 can't tell any of them it is leaving. As Cloudflare points out , when a resolver disappears, users don't see an error message. "Their Internet will simply stop working." How France got here â The law: Article L.333-10 of the Code du sport â The legal basis for all of this is Article L.333-10 of the French sports code . It was created by Law 2021-1382 of October 25, 2021 , the same law that merged HADOPI and the CSA into the new regulator Arcom . L.333-10 lets a sports rightsholder go to the president of the Paris judicial court and obtain "dynamic" blocking orders, meaning orders that cover sites already identified plus new mirror domains notified later through Arcom, against "toute personne susceptible de contribuer Ã y remÃ©dier" (any person able to help stop the infringement). That last phrase is what puts DNS resolvers in scope. In July 2026 , Parliament passed Law 2026-725 on professional sport , which amended L.333-10 and added an automated real-time blocking system run by Arcom. TorrentFreak reported that under the new system "ARCOM's agents no longer approve each block in advance." Quad9 called it "recklessly dangerous." The cases: from ISPs to everyone â The timeline shows how the circle of targets has widened: Date What happened Dec 2023 Canal+ sues Cloudflare, Google and Cisco under L.333-10 to force DNS blocking of football piracy sites. MayâJun 2024 The Paris court orders the three resolvers to block ~117 domains . Google complies. Cisco pulls OpenDNS out of France on June 28, 2024, citing a court order "issued under Article L.333-10 of the French Sport code" ( archived notice ). SepâOct 2024 New orders expand blocking by Google and Cloudflare. Dec 2024 Canal+ wins three orders against Quad9 and Vercara (Premier League, Champions League, Top 14 rugby). Because it can't geolocate users, Quad9 blocks the domains for the whole world : "we have to block these sites for all users, in all areas." May 2025 A beIN request against Google, Cloudflare and Quad9 is rejected for lack of evidence . Quad9 didn't defend that case at all, citing lack of resources. Mar 2026 The Paris Court of Appeal rejects five appeals by Google, Cloudflare and Cisco (RG 24/09372), the first appellate approval of DNS blocking under L.333-10: "Any filtering measure can be circumvented, and this possibility does not render the measures in question ineffective." The same month, the court issues simultaneous orders against 19 ISPs, Google, Cloudflare, Quad9 and VPN providers . Apr 2026 Canal+ obtains orders against Whalebone's EU-funded DNS4EU resolver , which complies by blocking "globally across our resolver tiers." May 13, 2026 beIN Sports obtains an order (RG 26/02207) requiring Quad9 to block IPTV sites showing the WTA women's tennis tour until the season ends on November 14. It starts with 6 domains and grows to 58 via Arcom notifications. Jul 2026 14 new Canal+ orders for the 2026/27 season target ISPs, Google, Quad9, DNS4EU, Cloudflare, VPNs, and Bing. Oct 7, 2026 The court refuses penalties against Cloudflare, NordVPN and Surfshark because each had made some effort to block. Cloudflare kept 1.1.1.1 out of it by acting through its CDN instead. Oct 21, 2026 The court imposes a â¬1,000/day penalty on Quad9 (RG 26/11882). Oct 22, 2026 Quad9 announces it will leave France on November 24. The ruling itself â The 21 October judgment is short and worth reading. A few details matter: The â¬580,000 figure was beIN's request, not the penalty. beIN asked for â¬10,000 per day per domain still reachable; across 58 domains that is â¬580,000 a day. The judge set â¬1,000 a day in total, running until the end of the WTA season on November 14. The judge used Quad9's malware filtering against it. Quad9 argued it could not implement geolocated blocking. The court (para. 16) replied that Quad9 "appears to contradict itself" because it already "applies automated filtering strictly limited to cybersecurity to neutralise malicious domains on a global scale." The fact that a resolver can drop a name for everyone was treated as proof it can drop a name for France. Refusing to try was enough. Paragraph 18: "Bound by an obligation of means, the Quad9 foundation states that it implements none in order to execute the decision. This circumstance alone justifies the imposition of a penalty." â¬1,000 a day for three weeks is survivable, about â¬24,000. Twenty more cases like it, each running for a full football season with ever-growing domain lists and Arcom's new automated system feeding them, is not. Quad9 says : "Quad9 cannot survive the accumulation of penalties yet to be assessed in 20 other pending cases." Why Quad9 can't just comply â Quad9 is often asked why it doesn't just block the domains. It has three options, and none of them work. 1. Block globally. This is what Quad9 did for Canal+ in December 2024 and what DNS4EU does today. It means a French court decides what a user in Brazil, Kenya or Germany can resolve, for the commercial benefit of one company. Quad9's announcement asks how France would react if other nations imposed their laws on French users through DNS. The answer is obvious, and the reverse should be too. Nothing limits this to sports either: once global blocking is accepted, every court in every country can add names to everyone's resolver. 2. Geo-block France. Quad9 has already tried this, in Germany. In the Sony Music v. Quad9 case , Quad9 used geoIP blocking for German users while the case continued. Sony's lawyers used a VPN to reach the content "from Germany" anyway, the court agreed this was non-compliance, and Quad9 was fined for contempt. GeoIP is a probabilistic guess about where an IP address is, not a legal fact about where a person is. A resolver that keeps no user records has no reliable way to define a "French user." As Quad9 told TorrentFreak : "There is no legally useful way for us to define a French user." Even the French order is geographically complicated: heise notes it covers the overseas departments and Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon but excludes New Caledonia, Wallis and Futuna, and French Polynesia. 3. Pay and fight. Quad9 won in Germany. The Dresden Higher Regional Court held in December 2023 that DNS resolvers get the same liability privilege as access providers, and the German civil rights group GFF said "the judgement puts the onus on rights holders." But winning took "several years, six figures of cost to Quad9, and massive wasted time," and the opposition, in Quad9's words, "has more lawyers than we have money and time." As Quad9 wrote in 2025 , compliance costs that are routine overhead for Google are, "for small, mission-driven nonprofits like Quad9, â¦ an existential threat." That leaves leaving. Why DNS blocking doesn't work â The argument against resolver blocking isn't only about Quad9's survival. Even on its own terms, it does not do what the rightsholders want. It doesn't remove anything. The DNS only holds pointers. Quad9's Dresden write-up puts it this way: "The DNS does not contain content - it is a system designed for delivery only of pointers." The pirate server stays online and keeps serving everyone who reaches it some other way. The Internet Society's 2025 guide for legal professionals says the same thing. It takes seconds to bypass. Quad9 notes there are thousands of other open resolvers . Users can also run their own, or use encrypted DNS over HTTPS ( RFC 8484 ), which looks like ordinary web traffic. Arcom's own December 2025 study for the National Assembly says 20% of French internet users already use an alternative DNS resolver and 29% use a VPN. Quad9 compares DNS blocking to "holding a piece of newspaper in front of a stadium full of people to block the view of a concert." It is blunt. DNS works at the level of whole domains. A resolver can't block one infringing stream on a shared host without blocking everything else on that name. The IAB's RFC 7754 , the IETF's standard reference on blocking and filtering, says: "From a technical perspective, there are no perfect or even good solutions -- there is only least bad." ICANN's security committee revisited the question in SAC127, "DNS Blocking Revisited" (2025), warning implementers to minimise overblocking and avoid affecting users outside their jurisdiction. France's own registry operator, AFNIC, made the core point years ago in its scientific council's report on the consequences of DNS filtering : "Le DNS n'a pas Ã©tÃ© conÃ§u pour filtrer les contenus." (The DNS was not designed to filter content.) It is opaque. When a resolver is forced to lie, the user sees a site that doesn't load. They have no way to tell whether the site is down, their network is broken, or a court ordered the block. There is a standard for being honest about this: RFC 8914 Extended DNS Errors defines code 16, "Censored", for answers withheld "due to an external requirement imposed by an entity other than the operator." But nothing in the French orders requires resolvers to use it. Blocking at scale causes real collateral damage. France is not the only test case. Italy's Piracy Shield system blocked Google Drive for much of the country in October 2024 . A RIPE Labs study of Piracy Shield found more than 500 unrelated sites blocked and concluded that "IP-level blocking is an indiscriminate tool with consequences that outweigh its benefits." In Spain, LaLiga's IP blocking of shared Cloudflare addresses knocked innocent sites offline every match day, leading Cloudflare's CEO Matthew Prince to call the approach "bonkers" . The same RIPE study found most European piracy is hosted in Europe , which is where enforcement belongs: at the hosting provider. Measured by its own goals, the French system has a mixed record. Arcom reports 12,606 sports domains blocked since 2022, 6,496 of them in 2025 alone (up 71%), while piracy fell 4% in 2025 and 34% since 2021. The number of blocks is growing much faster than piracy is shrinking, and Arcom's figures don't separate the effect of resolver blocking from ISP blocking. Every one of those domains has to be found, blocked, and then found again when it reappears under a new name. OONI's 2025 measurement of French ISP blocking found that of 542 domains tested, 291 were blocked by at least one ISP but only 132 by all four. The European Commission's own 2025 assessment of its live-events piracy recommendation concluded the effects "have been limited and have not allowed to significantly curb the volume of online piracy of live events." What France loses â Driving Quad9 out of France doesn't hurt pirates at all. The people who lose are the ones who chose a resolver for security. French users lose a malware filter. Quad9 exists to stop people resolving phishing and malware domains. Users who move to an unfiltered resolver, or to their ISP's resolver, lose that protection. Users who move to an unknown free resolver may be trading it for one that sells their browsing data . As Cloudflare puts it, "Penalizing transparent services only pushes users toward less accountable corners of the web." Critical infrastructure may break silently. Hospitals, utilities and local authorities on Quad9's list will lose DNS if their IT teams miss the announcement. Embedded devices with 9.9.9.9 hard-coded may be hard to fix. The choice of resolvers shrinks. OpenDNS left France in 2024, and Quad9 leaves now. An Internet Society report cited by TorrentFreak warned that small and non-profit resolvers are the most likely to be pushed out, leaving the field to the largest companies, which can afford to fight or to build per-country infrastructure. Cloudflare can satisfy the court by blocking at its CDN; Quad9 has only a resolver. France's own digital sovereignty goals suffer. France promotes privacy-respecting European infrastructure, yet its courts are driving out a Swiss privacy-focused non-profit while US giants remain. It's not just France â Quad9 is the clearest casualty so far, but the same process is underway across Europe. Belgium: DAZN obtained an order against Cloudflare, Google and Cisco in March 2025, and OpenDNS left Belgium in April 2025 before returning when the order against Cisco was suspended. In August 2026, the Brussels business court upheld the core of the order , with fines of â¬100,000 per match day capped at â¬20 million per company. Cisco says its public DNS "does not allow for the implementation of selective, geolocated and dynamic blocking as required by the order." Cloudflare, Google and Cisco have appealed ahead of the January 2027 deadline. Italy: AGCOM fined Cloudflare â¬14.2 million in January 2026, 1% of its global revenue, for not blocking via 1.1.1.1. Prince threatened to pull servers and free services from Italy: "Play stupid games, win stupid prizes." Spain: A Barcelona court upheld LaLiga's right to block Cloudflare IP addresses. Germany is the counter-example. Courts there rejected resolver blocking for both Quad9 and Cloudflare . The EU level: A study commissioned by the European Parliament's legal affairs committee proposes a binding regulation that would require blocking within 30 minutes across DNS resolvers, VPNs and CDNs. John Todd's warning on Hacker News is that "the EU and EC are looking at this issue right now and I expect will look to France as a case study of how to do things for the rest of the region." That is why France matters beyond France. If its model becomes the EU template, every public resolver in Europe will face the choice Quad9 faced: lie to all users worldwide, build unreliable geolocation infrastructure, or leave. The counter-arguments â The Hacker News discussion wasn't one-sided, and the counter-arguments deserve answers. "Hosting providers are unreachable, so courts move up the chain." One commenter argued that pirate hosts are bulletproof and ignore courts, so going after the intermediaries is the only lever left. Another asked the Quad9 CTO directly where the problem should be attacked. This is the strongest point. But the RIPE data shows most of the hosting is in Europe and within reach of European courts, and the commenter's logic leads to blocking at the last link in the chain that cannot fight back. That is not the same as the link that can actually stop the infringement. "Friction works. Most people won't bother to switch." Some argued that DNS blocking is good because it nudges the majority while staying easy to bypass for those who know how. The Paris Court of Appeal used essentially this reasoning. But Arcom's numbers say a fifth of French users already use alternative DNS, the friction is gone the moment one person changes a router setting for a household, and the cost is paid by resolvers that never had anything to do with piracy. "Cloudflare is a hypocrite." Several commenters pointed out that Cloudflare's CDN fronts many pirate sites. That may be true, and it is an argument about Cloudflare's CDN, which French courts can already reach and have. It says nothing about whether a resolver should lie. "The yellow pages would be held responsible." One commenter asked whether we'd accept a phone directory that kept listing a drug dealer's new address. The analogy fails because a resolver is not a curated directory. It's closer to the operator who connects you to whatever number you dial. Quad9 has "no association with these domain names, nor with the operators of the websites." Making the operator liable for every number dialled is how you end up with no operator. What you can do â If you use Quad9 in France , check whether you do at on.quad9.net , and switch resolvers before November 24. Check routers, VPN configs, DHCP settings, Pi-hole upstreams, and any devices with 9.9.9.9 or 149.112.112.112 hard-coded. Whatever you switch to, read its privacy policy first. If you're in France or the EU , do what John Todd asked: write something long-form , ideally in French, make it indexable, and send it to your representatives. Quad9 specifically suggests telling Arcom that its mandate is to balance rightsholders' interests against citizens' digital rights, and that "balance cannot be claimed when the privacy and security of digital users are the collateral damage." If you work on infrastructure , push for transparency wherever blocking does happen. RFC 8914's "Censored" error code exists so users can tell a court-ordered block from a broken network. If you can afford it , Quad9 accepts donations for its legal defence. Its appeal against the May order is still pending at the Paris Court of Appeal. The canary â Quad9 put it this way : "Once the tools of censorship are built, they are rarely used sparingly or justly." The French system started with football. It now covers tennis, rugby, MotoGP and Formula 1, has expanded from ISPs to resolvers, VPNs, CDNs and search engines, and runs through an automated system in which no human approves each block. Each step was reasonable on its own. Together, they have pushed a non-profit security service out of the country while the piracy continues. The sports-rights industry has a real problem. DNS resolvers are the wrong place to solve it, and France is about to find out what the internet looks like when the trustworthy resolvers leave first. Estonia’s Digital Nomad Bet Pays Off As E-Residents Generate €125M All stories → More Latest Issue Culture Fintech Profiles European Business Magazine Awards 2026 About Executive Education Daily News Feed Media OutReach ACCESS Newswire Search Search European Business Magazine Search Home Business AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial Business AI News AI Agents Ask Better Questions Than KPMG Accountants in Landmark Audit Trial By EBM Newsdesk November 18, 2026 25 views 0 comments LONDON, November 18, 2026 — Artificial intelligence has taken another significant step into the world of professional services after KPMG revealed that AI agents examining the accounts of a major UK-listed company sometimes investigated financial issues more deeply and asked better questions than its human audit team. The experiment, conducted by KPMG UK using more than 100 AI agents, marks an important development in the application of artificial intelligence to one of the most labour-intensive areas of the financial services industry. It also raises an uncomfortable question for the accountancy profession: if machines can increasingly perform the analytical work traditionally undertaken by highly trained professionals, how quickly will the economics of auditing change? According to the Financial Times , the project, codenamed Project Exponential, examined the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company. The AI agents worked alongside a conventional audit team, undertaking tasks across the audit process rather than simply assisting with isolated administrative functions. Join The European Business Briefing New subscribers this quarter are entered into a draw to win a Rolex Submariner. Join 40,000+ founders, investors and executives who read EBM every day. Subscribe KPMG UK head of audit Cath Burnet said the technology had, in several instances, gone considerably deeper into issues than the regular audit team, identifying areas requiring further investigation and asking questions that human auditors had not necessarily raised. The findings suggest that AI’s potential in professional services may extend well beyond improving productivity. It could fundamentally change how complex financial information is examined, interpreted and challenged. From supporting accountants to conducting audits Project Exponential represents a shift from using AI as a supporting tool towards deploying autonomous agents across an entire audit workflow. The agents collected information, analysed and documented data, developed draft conclusions and observations, and suggested subsequent steps. They were also able to work alongside one another, effectively dividing responsibilities and coordinating elements of the investigation. The technology was developed over approximately four months. However, KPMG was careful to distinguish the experiment from a formally approved statutory audit. Although an audit partner signed off on the experimental exercise, its findings were not used as the basis for formally approving the company’s accounts. Human oversight remained essential. During the trial, an auditor had to intervene when one AI agent failed to correctly match regulatory requirements with the company’s documentation. The episode illustrates both the capabilities and limitations of current AI systems when dealing with complex regulatory frameworks. KPMG plans to expand the initiative to as many as 20 larger audits, although the firm acknowledges that the technology is not yet sufficiently mature to be deployed across thousands of engagements. Data quality also remains a significant obstacle, with some businesses lacking the clean, structured information required for AI agents to operate effectively. A challenge to the Big Four business model? The implications for the accountancy industry could be substantial. Traditional auditing relies on large teams of junior accountants undertaking detailed and repetitive work, supervised by experienced managers and partners. AI agents potentially offer a different operating model, automating significant portions of data collection, analysis and documentation while allowing senior professionals to concentrate on complex judgements and exceptions. For firms such as KPMG, Deloitte, PwC and EY, the attraction is clear: faster audits, potentially lower operating costs and the ability to analyse much larger volumes of financial information. However, whether those savings will ultimately be passed on to clients remains uncertain. KPMG has acknowledged the potential for significant time savings but has not confirmed whether AI-driven efficiencies will translate into lower audit fees. Human judgement remains the final safeguard The transition also presents regulatory and professional challenges. The UK’s Financial Reporting Council has warned that the use of AI must not undermine auditor independence, integrity or professional scepticism. There are also concerns about data security, over-reliance on automated conclusions and the possibility of AI generating inaccurate or fabricated information. The fundamental responsibility for an audit opinion remains with the human auditor, regardless of the technology used. The KPMG experiment does not establish that AI can replace accountants or independently deliver a reliable statutory audit. It does, however, demonstrate that AI agents are beginning to challenge professionals in areas that were once considered dependent on human expertise. For the accountancy profession, the question is no longer simply whether AI will become part of the audit process. It is how much of that process will eventually be performed by machines — and what role human accountants will play when it does. title: We need smart people who give a shit
body_text: 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit • VioletPixel VioletPixel Justin Michael's notions and miscellanea Blog About Now Contact Feed Tuesday, November 17th, 2026 @ 7:01 PM PST 🧠 We Need Smart People Who Give a Shit Something I learned a long time ago, something that's been proven to me time and again, is that the world is held together by smart people who give a shit. This truth always comes into stark focus when I learn how a complex system functions—or, rather, how it barely functions. When I worked at Stripe I learned a lot about various banking and money movement systems, and it's terrifying how flawed and fragile these systems are. ACH is a great example. It's a complex system we rely on every day that is just barely good enough to function. It's old, riddled with flaws, and encumbered with legacy baggage. And yet, despite all of those problems, ACH usually works great and is generally considered to be safe, cheap, and reliable. The reason there's a mismatch between the technical reality of the ACH system and how it functions in practice is due to a single factor: smart people who give a shit. Every problem with ACH is fixed, patched, bypassed, overridden, routed around, or manually handled by people who have two things: Intimate knowledge of the system The drive and determination to force the system to work Those two things feed into each other. You have to care about a complex system to dive deep enough to learn how it works, and when you know a lot about how a complex system works you care more about it, especially if the system is important or critical infrastructure. Now, you can replace "ACH" above with a myriad of other complex systems—everything from huge infrastructure to nice-to-have apps—and everything I said remains true, both about the systems themselves and the people who keep them running. The world runs on these systems, and they depend on smart people who give a shit. Take those people away, and the systems collapse. And collapse is what we're starting to see. Some recent examples of various failures from just this past week or so: Microsoft 365 , Air Traffic Control , United Airlines' systems , the NSA's network , many major banks , Apple's systems , and more. We're told these failures and problems are not related. They're not the result of a cyberattack. They're not the fault of generative AI. I guess that depends on how you look at it. I don't have inside information about what's going on, but my experience dealing with complex systems tells me there's a common through line to all of these disruptions: there aren't enough smart people who give a shit. So where did they go? Capitalism has never been particularly kind to smart people who give a shit (or people in general... but I digress). Capitalism does, however begrudgingly, recognize that smart people who give a shit are required to build and maintain complex systems that serve capitalist goals. Thus, those people have been accommodated and incorporated into the system by virtue of their necessity and, in many cases, their rarity. Now, though, generative AI is here. To the people running the show—leadership and management—it seems like they can get the same or better value (and even more output!) from a machine. The machine is cheaper, works longer, doesn't take sick days or vacations, doesn't ask for any benefits, and never pushes back against a bad idea. People who don't do the actual work—the people who aren't in the trenches—have a hard time telling the difference between a flawed system held aloft by the drive and determination of smart people who give a shit and slop provided by generative AI. To them it's all just output: words you can read, code that runs, and pixels that look nice to their eye. It's all the same to them, so why does it matter where it comes from? It matters because generative AI isn't smart, and it doesn't give a shit. What seems like intelligence is an illusion propped up by a massive amount of data strip-mined from the commons with weights that nudge the output toward a generally desirable shape. What seems like care, concern, and attention is just generative AI doing what it's designed to do: telling you what you want to hear. The math and logic that power LLMs are as cold, unfeeling, and indifferent as the laws of physics. Smart people who give a shit notice things. They connect dots. They notice when things don't feel right. They know when something is about to go off the rails, and they know how to get things back on track. They know how to handle edge cases. They know how to manually handle a unique situation. They know what the right thing to do is, and they know when they need to put in extra effort or time to make something happen. Generative AI falls far short in these areas, but this is the glue that holds complex systems together. More prompting and more output isn't a substitute for this. It's hard for capitalist leadership to internalize any of that, though. It would be such a relief for them, such a burden lifted, to replace all those smart people who give a shit with generative AI. It would be so much easier to win at capitalism if generative AI lived up to the hype, and there's so much pressure for leadership and management to believe that the hype is real. Thus, a lot of the smart people who give a shit have been laid off, and the ones that remain are hollowed out. Telling people to stop doing the job they signed up for in favor of babysitting LLMs so they can do that job instead is a great way to make people less smart about the system they used to work on and give less of a shit about it. Every prompt moves them one step further away from the system they used to know inside and out. Every generated output that becomes part of the system means those people understand less about how the system actually works. Those people are robbed of the things that make them smart (the struggle of building and learning) and the things that made them gave a shit (a sense of ownership and close connection with the system). We've moved from a world dependent on complex and fragile systems held together by smart people who give a shit to a world of complex and fragile systems run by generative AI. The people running the generative AI are not as smart, nor do they give as much of a shit. There are, of course, exceptions (which is why a lot of things are still humming along), but we are on a course where the number of smart people who give a shit are decreasing, and that's a big problem. As long as the number continues to go down, more systems will fail. I think what we have here is a hot stove moment for capitalism. When you tell a young kid a stove is hot and they shouldn't touch it, you'll find there are two kinds of kids. For one kind of kid, the warning is the lesson, and they don't touch the stove. For the other kind of kid, the only lesson that works for them is being burned. They have to touch the stove at least once to learn the lesson. Capitalism was told the stove was hot, but their hand is on it right now. Unfortunately, we're all getting burned. ← 🛰️ Voyager 1: Almost One Light-Day Away VioletPixel : Justin Michael's notions and miscellanea Blog About Now Contact Feed This site is view source friendly! The year has been defined by global debates on what it means to be human when AI is blurring the boundaries between people and machines. 'Human' is defined in the Cambridge Dictionary as ‘having the qualities, faults, and feelings that people have, as opposed to gods, animals, or machines’. In 2026, many public figures defended humans and humanity in the age of AI. Bill Gates, Chair of the Gates Foundation, made the case for “human reserved jobs”, such as caregivers, that should never be taken by machines, in a widely read essay . Commenting on the selection of ‘human’ as Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year, he said: “AI is making us think harder about what it means to be human. It could help us cure diseases, improve education, and give people more time to spend on the things that matter most. "But we need to make deliberate choices about how it fits into our lives, including where we want people to remain at the center. The measure of AI’s success should be how much it improves human lives.” ‘AI godfather’ and Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton has warned that “we’re creating alien beings. I’m willing to be selfish and choose humans.” And in his Magnifica Humanitas letter, Pope Leo XIV spoke of new forms of “dehumanization” and the “pressing duty to remain profoundly human”. Actors Scarlett Johansson and Cate Blanchett, musicians Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes and Billie Eilish, and authors Jodi Picoult and Jonathan Franzen challenged an "assault on human creativity" as the Human Artistry Campaign and Artist Rights Alliance opposed machine-generated replicas and theft of human-generated content by large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, Project Hail Mary author Andy Weir has wondered whether he "might be among the last generation of fully human writers". The Authors Guild has launched a ‘Human Authored’ kitemark for books, supported by Professor Dame Mary Beard and Malorie Blackman. As AI deepfakes simulated humans, Matthew McConaughey became the first Hollywood actor to pre-emptively protect himself against unauthorised digital reproduction by trademarking clips of his voice, his face and even his catchphrase ‘alright, alright, alright’.  Taylor Swift followed suit, trademarking her voice and image in April. Professor Rachel Adams, an expert on AI governance and human rights at the University of Cambridge, said: “AI brings us back to questions that we’ve asked for millennia: who are we, what does it mean to be human? The answer to these questions has never been fixed or stable, but the act of asking it is something we have in common. “AI is going to be a profound test for humanity. There’s a real risk that it deepens existing inequalities, but it also has the potential to solve them."  Dr Tom McClelland, a philosopher of science at the University of Cambridge, said: “I think ‘human’ is a really interesting choice because right now our understanding of humanity is changing. “We're trying to understand the difference between a human mind and an artificial mind, between living beings like us and artificial beings that we're creating. What sets us apart, is it consciousness, creativity or compassion? “All the rhetoric around AI is about what's inevitably going to happen. But to young people growing up in an AI-enabled world, my advice would be that nothing is inevitable. What happens in the future of AI is up to us. It's up to you." Lexicographer Colin McIntosh of the Cambridge Dictionary said: “AI is changing how we talk about being human. It’s this renewed interest in the idea of being human that captured the zeitgeist and made ‘human’ the Cambridge Dictionary Word of the Year.” Adapted from the Cambridge University Press & Assessment website .
