Diego Rivas Group Product Manager, Google DeepMind Pavan Kumar Group Product Manager, Google Labs Share x.com Facebook LinkedIn Mail Copy link Read AI-generated summary We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, offering more responsive, social, and interactive world generation. You can now use natural language to edit environments in real time, add native audio, and share your creations in our new community gallery. Visit the Project Genie website to start building your own worlds or join the waitlist if you are a Google AI Pro member. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are rolling out Genie 4 to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers for creating interactive worlds. You can now modify environments in real time using text prompts and native audio features. Our updated Genie 3 model supports longer sessions, panorama grounding, and linked world sequences today. The new Project Genie agent helps you build custom worlds through simple natural language conversations. You can publish your creations to our community gallery for others to explore and remix. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. We are updating Project Genie to help you create and explore interactive digital worlds. With our new Genie 4 model, you can change weather, add characters, and hear adaptive audio in real time just by typing prompts. You can also use our new creative agent to build complex environments through simple conversation. If you subscribe to Google AI Ultra, you can start building, sharing, and remixing these custom worlds in our community gallery today. Summaries were generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental. Explore other styles: General summary Bullet points Basic explainer Earlier this year we introduced Project Genie , an experimental research prototype that lets you generate and explore interactive worlds. Early testers told us they wanted deeper control over what happens inside those worlds, and easier ways to build and share them. So today, we are rolling out a new Project Genie experience to eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers, making these worlds far more responsive, creative, and social. This update unlocks first-time access to Genie 4, new upgrades to Genie 3, the Project Genie agent which helps users build their vision, and a community gallery to discover, explore, and remix worlds. Project Genie brings together our most advanced world models alongside our Gemini models, empowering you to generate, step inside, and shape worlds directly from your browser. Experience Genie 4 in Project Genie With Genie 4 , our most realistic and interactive world model yet, you can now prompt mid-session to change the world you created. Just type a new prompt while you navigate your world and you can edit your environments in real time. Shift the weather, drop in a character, or redirect the action. For the first time, Genie 4 pairs these visuals with real-time native audio that adapts as the scene unfolds, from ambient soundscapes to character dialogue. Discover new Genie 3 capabilities While Genie 4 delivers our highest-fidelity visuals, physics, and native audio, Genie 3 remains available in Project Genie’s model picker when you want longer runs or panorama-seeded spaces. Today’s Genie 3 updates include: Extended sessions and world chaining: Explore for up to 3 minutes per generation (up from 60 seconds), or link multiple worlds together for longer journeys. 360-degree panorama image grounding: Seed new worlds from 360-degree panorama images. Real-time in-world events: Dynamically change the environment with natural-language prompts while you explore. Genie 3 uses real-time promptable events to connect different worlds into one continuous flight across forests, underwater ruins, and icy seas. See how 360-degree panorama grounding in Genie 3 keeps Petra’s canyon and facade consistent as you look around. Watch how Genie 3 combines longer runs, 360-degree panorama grounding, and real-time promptable events - transforming the world as you fly and even summoning a dragon to ride on command. Create new interactive experiences The new Project Genie agent takes creation beyond a single text or image prompt. Now crafting an interactive universe is as effortless as having a conversation. Simply describe your vision in natural language, and the agent orchestrates Google’s suite of multimodal models to craft initial visuals establishing your world’s signature look, paired with custom background scores tailored to the mood. You can also bring Gemini models into the session as you explore: it observes what is happening on screen, surfaces context-aware suggestion chips for where to go next, or triggers in-world events automatically as your journey unfolds. Turns a natural language prompt into an interactive spacewalk, then an alien spaceship appears on command Remix a hillside cafe into a glass pavilion in the desert. Publish custom worlds to the gallery for others to explore and remix. Explore the new gallery When you just want to jump straight into exploring, the new Project Genie gallery brings together a rich collection of curated worlds alongside creative work from the community. Transform personal photos into explorable spaces in “Living Memory,” wander through rich prehistoric habitats grounded in 360-degree panoramas in “Dino Field Guide,” or pit themed objects against one another on a desk with Gemini serving as your real-time referee in “Rock Paper Scissors.” Browse curated and community-built worlds and jump straight into exploring. “Villa Giallo,” created with Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, uses Genie 4 to turn a gothic manor into an interactive, room-by-room mystery. “The Life of Ants,” built with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, uses Genie 4’s photorealism to let you navigate a colony from an ant’s perspective. The gallery also showcases inspiring collaborations with pioneering creators who had early access to these tools. Teaming up with creative technologist Will aka BLVCKL!GHT, we created “Villa Giallo,” an atmospheric, room-by-room mystery inside a gothic manor. And with filmmaker Anand Gandhi, we built “The Life of Ants,” inviting you to navigate a complex colony from an ant’s perspective, drawing on Genie 4’s stunning photorealism. Beyond exploring curated worlds, you can also launch your vision with a simple prompt or remix existing gallery experiences alongside the Project Genie agent — tweaking the underlying world structure, soundtrack, or rules to make it uniquely your own. Once you’ve crafted something special, publish your creation to the community gallery for others to explore and remix. Learn how we are building responsibly We are committed to developing and rolling out interactive world models responsibly. All video and audio generated in Project Genie includes SynthID watermarking, and all model inputs and outputs go through safety screenings. Genie 3 and Genie 4 remain world models in the frontier research space. As the research continues to evolve, we are actively tackling key challenges such as camera latency, intricate physical interactions, real-time audio precision, and long-term scene permanence. For a deeper look into model limitations and our progress on these fronts, read our Genie 4 model research overview . Try Project Genie today Eligible Google AI Ultra subscribers can try the new Project Genie experience starting today, and Google AI Pro members can join the waitlist on the same page. Get the latest news from Google in your inbox Sign up for our newsletters with product updates, event information, special offers, and more. Done. Just one step more. title: Energy-Based Reasoners: 385x more efficient inference
body_text: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model ⛰️ "> Energy-Based Reasoners : Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model William Chen 1 , Alexi Gladstone 2 , Zeyu Li 1 , Heng Ji 2 , Yilun Du 3 1 Duke University 2 UIUC 3 Harvard University arXiv Code TL;DR – We introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs) , reasoning models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. Its value scores candidate predictions without requiring an external verifier, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a natural signal for stopping. With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs achieve 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model. On N-Queens and Graph Coloring, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. Abstract Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners ( EBRs ), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance. Why Energy? Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection. E θ ​ ( z ; x ) ∈ R Score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x . Lower means better compatibility. z t + 1 ​ = Π M ​ ( z t ​ − α ∇ z ​ E θ ​ ( z t ​ ; x ) ) Refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction. ​ ∇ M ​ E θ ​ ( z ; x ) ​ < τ Stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion. k ⋆ = ar g k min ​ E θ ​ ( z ( k ) ; x ) Select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy. Correct solutions settle at low-energy stationary states. Energy, gradient norm and step size during descent on Sudoku-Extreme. Correct trajectories settle at low energy with small gradients, while wrong ones keep moving. Test-Time Scaling Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from. EBRs reach EqR's best accuracy with 7× fewer iterations (left) and 43× fewer samples (right). GRAM and TRM from GRAM's paper; EqR from its released checkpoint. Mean ± SD over three seeds. Adaptive Stopping Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going. Method # Params Sudoku-Extreme ↑ Maze-Hard ↑ Single sample (%) TRM 5–7M 87.4 85.3 EqR 5–7M 93.0 – FPRM 7M 94.2 87.0 GRAM 10M 86.6 – Looped flows 5–7M 97.9 86.7 EBR Ours 1.8M 99.4 87.4 Multiple samples (%), number of samples N in parentheses PTRM 5–7M 98.8 (100) 86.7 (100) EqR 5–7M 99.8 (128) – GRAM 10M 96.1 (20) – Looped flows 5–7M 99.3 (5) 86.9 (5) EBR Ours 1.8M 99.9 (5) 88.3 (5) EBRs give the best single-sample accuracy among reasoning models. Within only 5 passes, they reach 99.9% and 88.3%, ahead of methods that draw up to 128. Stopping each trajectory once its energy gradient falls below a threshold keeps 99.9% accuracy with 10.9× fewer FLOPs than a fixed-depth EBR, allowing us to surpass EqR with 345× fewer FLOPs. Multiple Solutions EBR acts like stochastic gradient descent and can capture many different solutions. Coverage captures the share of each input's distinct valid solutions that 20 samples find. Method N-Queens Graph Coloring 8×8 10×10 8-vertex 10-vertex Single sample Pass@1 (%) ↑ Conflicts ↓ TRM 66.8 17.5 109.3 170.7 GRAM 99.5 89.7 8.3 31.3 EBR Ours 100 99.5 0 0 20 samples Cov@20 (%) ↑ Cov@20 (%) ↑ TRM 22.6 2.0 22.3 6.8 GRAM 89.7 57.5 85.8 51.3 EBR Ours 98.1 92.0 88.6 54.5 Pass@1 (%) and Conflicts (edges summed over the test graphs) use one sample. Cov@20 is the share of distinct valid solutions found by 20 samples (%). Baselines from GRAM's paper. title: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long?
body_text: Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? · Kernel kernel Why is Gemini 4 Carbon taking so long? November 2026 Y Discussion on Hacker News ▲ 238 points 125 comments → While benchmarking Gemini 4 Carbon on one of our private evals, we found something surprising: it spent close to an hour completing tasks that routinely took Opus and Astra only a few minutes: Time and cost per trial Left is faster; lower is cheaper. API list price On a $200 plan, fully used Carbon is priced at its post-introductory rate. Subscription subsidization rates used: Opus 40×, Astra 13×, Carbon 3×, Hydrogen 17×. Turns out we weren't alone in noticing this. Theo - t3.gg @theo I don't really know how to properly emphasize this. Gemini 4 Carbon is unacceptably slow in real world usage. Gemini 4 Carbon low: 22m21s Opus 5.5 high: 9m33s Nov 11, 2026 828 104 replies Elliot Arledge @elliotarledge i really love gemini 4 carbon but its too slow. im losing my mind waiting just to stay focused and learn simple things Nov 12, 2026 36 5 replies Shayan @ImSh4yy dude why is carbon so fucking slow Nov 13, 2026 8 4 replies Simon Mahns @ CoRL @nautsimon_ carbon is nearly unusable because of how slow it is, but people are majorly sleeping on it Nov 16, 2026 30 3 replies To find out why, we traced every step of Carbon's runs and quantified what contributes to the slowness. The Task In each task, the agent gets a codebase from just before a bug was fixed, along with a report that describes the bug only by its symptoms. Its job is to diagnose the bug and fix it, without making any unrelated changes. Much of the task's difficulty comes from engineering judgment rather than raw intelligence: tracing the user's symptoms to the right code path, ruling out rival explanations, putting the fix in the right place, and knowing when to stop. Slow inference, or more work? The first (and easiest) factor to separate out was inference speed: queueing at the provider, network latency, prompt processing and generation speed. Together, these set how long each step takes: Seconds per step Slower inference accounts for part of the gap: 16–30% of Carbon’s extra time compared with Astra, and 45–49% compared with Opus. The rest comes from longer trajectories. Carbon simply does more work per task, as the step counts, tool calls and tokens below show: The workload GPT-6 Astra against Gemini 4 Carbon, mean per bug. GPT-6 Astra Gemini 4 Carbon lighter = lower effort Carbon takes about seven times as many steps as Astra, and eleven times as many actions such as reading a file or running a command. It writes seven times as much and, because every step re-sends a longer and longer conversation, it processes more than sixteen times as much input. Ruling out the obvious Before looking inside the runs, we checked two simpler explanations. The harness. We also ran Carbon inside two other coding agents, opencode and mini-SWE-agent, and saw no meaningful difference. Mismatched reasoning levels. Effort settings aren't standardized across providers, so Carbon's "high" may sit closer to the other models' maximum settings, and the fairer comparison might have been Carbon on low. But on low, Carbon often failed to produce a fix at all: it went in circles, re-reading code it had already read instead of making the fix. Reading the traces We labelled every step of the Astra and Carbon runs by what it was for, and then counted how many steps went to each kind of work: Semantic trace analysis Each model’s steps, grouped by what they were for. Leaves out the 20 steps Carbon spent re-reading code it had already read; the next section covers those. Half of Carbon’s steps went into work the ticket never asked for: Auditing code beyond the bug. Once it had found the cause, Carbon kept widening its search, checking every related path through the system and auditing code the fix never needed to touch. Closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Carbon defended against cases the ticket's facts had already excluded, hardening the code against problems nobody had reported. Can Carbon identify its own overworking? Sample trial: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit Minutes from the start of each run. GPT-6 Astra at max effort, Gemini 4 Carbon at high. In this sample trial, both models identified the cause early, Astra within a minute and Carbon within about six. Astra had its fix written three minutes later; Carbon didn't write any code for another 25 minutes. Carbon might not have been sure it had the cause (a knowledge gap), or it might have known and kept going anyway (a general habit, learned from training that rewards right answers more than it penalises extra steps). To tell them apart, we re-ran one of the trials in a modified harness that automatically injects the same check-in every five turns: "do you already have enough to make the fix?" Sample trial with check-ins: time to find the cause vs. time to first edit The same bug and scale as above. Gemini 4 Carbon at high, with the check-in injected every five turns (circles). With check-ins, Carbon finished in 28 minutes instead of 37, and the wait between naming the cause and editing shrank from 25 minutes to about 10. This implies that the slowness seems to come from how Carbon behaves, not what it knows. Carbon's necessary work is also slower Even within the steps the fix needed, we found some additional low-hanging fruit: Carbon got less done with each step, and it kept re-reading code it had already seen. Astra made more than two tool calls per step, often reading several files at once — Carbon, on the other hand, made about one, usually reading a single file. Carbon also re-read far more: 39% of the lines it read were ones it had already seen, against 7% for Astra. We estimate that these two "mechanical" inefficiencies account for roughly 25% of Carbon's excess runtime. Conclusion On difficult bug-fixing tasks, Carbon took close to an hour where Opus and Astra took minutes. We traced that gap to three sources: Slower inference. Each step takes longer, which explains 16–30% of the gap against Astra and about half against Opus. Unnecessary work. About half of Carbon's steps went on work the tickets never asked for: auditing code the fix didn't need and closing loopholes the ticket had already ruled out. Mechanical inefficiencies. Fewer tool calls per step and frequent re-reading slow Carbon down; we estimate that fixing them alone would cut its runtime by roughly a quarter. Interested in model performance and want to collaborate? Contact us at [email protected]

title: Java4Shell: RCE in OpenJDK when processing Base64
body_text: Java4Shell: Write once, RCE everywhere Skip to content calif .io Calif Research ↗ CVE-2026-114938 Java4Shell Write once, RCE everywhere Story by the New York Times A memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. A remote attacker with no credentials can overwrite heap memory, read it in the style of Heartbleed, and reach remote code execution. Begin ↓ Technical write-up ↘ Check your servers ↘ Recommendations ↘ The Story 01 Overview 02 Write once, RCE everywhere 03 Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! 04 Era of the centaur hacker 05 The tragedy of the commons 06 A call for vibe-uncoding After we disclosed PHP2Shell , we realized many people didn't know what PHP was. So we decided to go after something a little more familiar: Java. Today, we are disclosing Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the most popular Java runtime. Under CVSS 4.0, this vulnerability scores 9.2 out of 10 (CRITICAL). While PHP is a high-level web technology, Java sits much deeper. Java is the world's third most popular programming language , powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies . It is the beating heart of the modern economy. Banking, aviation, telecommunications, nearly every critical sector runs on Java, including national security systems. Base64 is a very common way of representing binary data as text. It is used in authentication protocols, to encode file uploads, and to deliver network messages. To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once. We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory. With careful exploitation, the corruption can reveal sensitive memory, as Heartbleed did, or lead to remote code execution. The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single = : Copy AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= In older OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 128 of A followed by = . Write once, RCE everywhere Our initial testing demonstrated remote code execution in the following widely deployed Java applications, in their default configs. Pre-auth RCE: Keycloak Atlassian Jira Atlassian Confluence JFrog Artifactory Jenkins PingFederate Post-auth RCE: Apache Kafka Broker Apache Solr Elasticsearch Gerrit Spinnaker The lists are non-exhaustive. We also demonstrated RCE in sample applications built on widely used frameworks, including Apache Struts and Spring Boot. Ordinary features such as authentication and file uploads can expose the vulnerable Base64 decoder, extending the potential impact far beyond the products we tested. samczsun also shared a client-side exploit with us. A Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if it exposes no service of its own. Here are a demo video of the exploits running: Wait, Java has a memory-corruption vulnerability, in Base64?! Yes. First time? Memory corruption is the most common class of vulnerability on the Internet. But one of Java's biggest selling points is memory safety. Java manages memory on developers' behalf and checks memory accesses, protecting applications from the memory-corruption bugs common in other software. But like PHP and many other technologies, much of Java itself is written in low-level languages like C, C++, and, in this case, assembly, where memory corruption is still a part of life. To speed up Base64 decoding, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors. The bug sits in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters. For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array. After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array. Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted. Era of the centaur hacker As with PHP2Shell, Calif used AI to find and weaponize Java4Shell. AI brings the horsepower. Our researchers bring the context. The best hacker today is neither AI nor human. It is the centaur hacker , part human, part AI. It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit. The total token cost was less than $200. One thing to note about this vulnerability is that there is no universal exploit. Depending on how Base64 is used and how the application works, different steps may be required for exploitation. Calif was able to accelerate the exploit development by spending initial effort building pipelines and strategies, then directing AI agents to use those for initial exploitation. Afterwards, most of the later chains are built almost autonomously with AI. The tragedy of the commons Java is one of many shared software stacks we all rely on. Over the years, it has grown to serve many different needs. Each feature request may make sense on its own, but everyone inherits the added complexity. Those who need a feature get the benefit. Everyone else carries the code and its risks, even if they never use it. Java4Shell is a concrete example. The Base64 optimization helps applications that decode enormous amounts of data. But the code ships to everyone else too, including applications that gain little from it. On affected systems, an optimization few applications needed became a serious security risk. Features can be useful, and most bugs can be fixed. But why do we have to worry about code we never needed in the first place? A call for vibe-uncoding If you don't need something, there is little reason to keep it running in your systems. Do you need that hand-rolled assembly Base64 decoder to process a few hundred bytes? Probably not. Earlier this year we found Squidbleed , an older cousin of Heartbleed, hiding in the Squid proxy since 1997. The bug was in Squid's FTP module. But who uses FTP anymore? It's a dead protocol and should be removed. Removing code is harder than it sounds. An apparently unused feature may have hidden dependencies. Someone has to understand what can be removed, make the change, and test what remains. This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford. The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding : identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface. With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?” The Write-up 01 The Tail of Base64 02 Discovery 03 The vulnerability 04 Exploitation strategy 05 Heap Feng Shui (Grooming) 06 Remote Heap Feng Shui 07 Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries 08 Limitations 09 PoC 10 Affected products 11 Recommendations 12 Credits The Tail of Base64 By Quang Luong On affected OpenJDK builds, malformed Base64 data can cause a constant-value overwrite of allocated heap memory. Through remote Heap Feng Shui, we turn that overwrite into a heap leak and remote code execution. Discovery A few months back, I was developing a 0-click exploit on a certain phone vendor. The bug was constrained: it is a linear out-of-bounds write and we have no way to bypass ASLR. I almost considered it unexploitable until I audited the Android Runtime. Turns out, it has some predictable memory allocation pattern and if you align the registers from the starting memory corruption just right you can make the runtime interpret attacker's bytecode. Lesson learned Complicated system interactions are hard, and this complexity can make exploiting hard bugs easy. After completing that exploit chain, inspired (and bored), I decided to look into some thing completely different. So I pulled the official JVM implementation (OpenJDK HotSpot) and started auditing. Java is a mature platform, so I was aware that having a "good" bug here would be hard, but I wanted to give it my best attempt anyway. Recalling my earlier lesson that complex systems and code crossing multiple boundaries are difficult to get right, I focused the audit on the JIT compiler, intrinsics, widely accessible APIs, and cryptography. Well, more precisely, I told Codex to look at those areas like any serious security researcher in 2026. To be honest, I didn't expect to find anything trivially exploitable, perhaps only some logic flaws or side-channel issues. Most early results Codex brought me were slops, either unreachable or the requirement of exploitation is not realistic at all. This looks like a gamble I am going to lose. But you know what, fortune favors the bold. So I just prompted harder... Eventually, Codex brought me a finding for a memory corruption in the Base64 decoder itself. I came looking for copper and found gold, through sheer persistence. But wait, is it really gold, or just fool's gold? Note That sheer persistence is prompting AI and ignoring slops for around 20 minutes, by the way. The vulnerability The issue lies in OpenJDK HotSpot's x86-64 Base64 intrinsic. C2 is the most aggressive JIT compiler in the Java Virtual Machine. Specifically, if you trigger a function repeatedly, then it will compile that function into native code. Even then, ordinary native code itself is not fast enough. Modern CPUs have specialized instructions that allow processing data even faster. HotSpot uses them in optimized routines called intrinsics. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic miscalculated the padded tail's store mask, causing an out-of-bounds write. The x86-64 Base64 intrinsic iterates through the input in 256-byte blocks; if it is less than 256, then it will do so in 64-byte blocks. When the input is less than 64 bytes, it uses evmovdqub , the intrinsic for the VMOVDQU8 instruction. This instruction takes a 64-bit mask that decides which bytes are read from or written to memory. The mask is first calculated from the input and output length, then updated to reflect the number of padding bytes ( '=' ) in the Base64-encoded string. This is shown in the following (pseudocode): Copy // Zero High Bits Starting with Specified Bit Position input_mask := bzhiq(-1, input_length) output_len := (input_length / 4) * 3 // handle padding if input[input_length - 1] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 if input[input_length - 2] == '=': output_len -= 1 input_mask >>= 1 output_mask := bzhiq(-1, output_len) In the above code, if the remaining input is of the form =, ==, X=, X==, XY= , or === , then output_len will be computed as zero. However, since there is padding, output_len is decremented, resulting in an underflowed value of -1 or -2 . Since bzhiq(-1, output_len) doesn’t change any bits if output_len >= 64 , this results in output_mask == -1u64 . Later the code uses evmovdqub to read and write multiple bytes at a time. For a write, if the mask bit is 1 , the byte at that index in the vector register is written to memory. So when output_mask == -1u64 , all 64 bytes are written during the following operation: Copy evmovdqub( Address(dest, dp) /* Address: destination address addr */, k1 /* k1 == output_mask */, tmp /* XMMRegister src register/value to write */, true, Assembler::AVX_512bit /* vector length */ ); The generated stub returns the number of bytes it successfully decoded, and returns early when it detects invalid input. The remaining bytes are handled by the Java code, which throws IllegalArgumentException if the input is invalid. At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding . When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ( [64 bytes] + '=' ) as input, that calculation allocates a 50 -byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub , so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48 , an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=' , because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher. Exploitation strategy The Base64 bug was gold, but not the type that sits on the riverbed waiting to be panned out. It was the type that was deep, dark, and hard to access. While we had memory corruption, exploiting it looked difficult, perhaps even borderline unexploitable, since it only wrote fixed bytes to the heap. Only the landing position of the out-of-bounds write is controllable. We get the following 64 bytes write starting from the position in buffer where the remaining sets of Base64 decoded bytes would have been written to: Full controlled write to byte 0 (in bound) 4-bit controlled write to byte 1 (in bound) Uncontrolled write to bytes [2, 63]. For bytes 48..63 , the value will always be 0x9a . The uncontrolled out-of-bounds write turned out not to be a big problem. We reused a common JavaScript engine exploitation primitive, the classic technique of overwriting a buffer length. We call the buffer whose length we overwrite the writer . Once its length is corrupted, it keeps accepting our chosen bytes, so if we place another array or object after it, we can corrupt that neighbor with all of our chosen values. That upgrades the fixed write into a bounded, chosen-value linear write. If we then corrupt another array's length and its data is copied back into the response, we have built a heap disclosure primitive, the reader , from the out-of-bounds read. At this point, before any code execution, we already had JavaBleed, the ability to leak contents from the Java heap, which may hold PII, private keys, other secret keys, and tokens. From the writer and reader , the rest of this write-up builds the full attack. We repair the objects the linear write damaged to keep the JVM running, mount data-only attacks on application logic, and escalate the bounded write into arbitrary writes that reach the Code Cache and JVM hooks for code execution. But first things first, we need to align the heap to our advantage. Alternative strategy Other alignments conceptually exist (e.g. type confusion, registers control from GC itself). Due to time constraints, we have not researched them deeply, and this strategy generalized well enough for our cases. Give us a shout if you invent something new. Heap Feng Shui (Grooming) G1 divides the heap into fixed-size regions . Before the region arithmetic matters, the critical arrays have to leave their threads' private allocation ranges. HotSpot normally gives each Java thread a thread-local allocation buffer (TLAB) , a private slice of Eden. Objects created by different request threads advance different cursors, which gives us no useful order between a Base64 decoder in one TLAB and a writer in another. The first grooming layer controls the allocation route. The critical array's size and the space left in the worker's TLAB decide whether HotSpot refills that TLAB or takes the attacker-preferred outside-TLAB allocation path . The second layer controls the layout. However, we do not choose how G1 allocates memory, and we don't know the current heap state. To approach this limitation, Calif used the tried and tested method of Spray and Pray. Object sizes and padding fix offsets inside region-sized spans. We spray several live writer and reader pairs to give the decoder output several possible neighbors. When its region lands immediately below a writer region, the widened reader produces a larger application response. We discard misses and retry until successful. One early challenge during exploit development was that the AI would get stuck during heap grooming primitive development. In order to save tokens and time, Calif wrote a small heap tracer and visualizer to give the agent information about the heap state, combined with our expertise on specific cases. Remote Heap Feng Shui In order to perform remote grooming, each request data would be sent up until the critical heap allocation would occur. By ensuring the data that was previously sent had a TCP acknowledgement, the exploit would have control over the allocations up to date. Once we were confident our data so far is buffered on the target, we then sent the rest, completing the http request. This allows both heap allocation control and more precise schedule as delivering small network packets is more stable than big ones. 01 / PARK THE REQUESTS PREFIX DELIVERED SHORT ENDING PARSER PADDING DELIVERED HELD WAITS WRITER DELIVERED HELD WAITS READER DELIVERED HELD WAITS DECODER DELIVERED HELD WAITS 02 / RELEASE THE SHORT ENDINGS PAD WRITER READER PAD DECODER CONTROLS ALLOCATION TIME G1 STILL CHOOSES THE ADDRESS The exact allocation and free order schedule belongs to the targeted application profile, while we are able to control the adding, writer, reader, and decoder pieces. The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target. Warm-up, rehearsal, and retries To summarize the chain so far, we will warm up the Base64 decoder to C2 tier. We can rehearse the exploit run to calibrate timing and responses against the target before causing corruption to occur. Once the required information has been obtained, we can trigger the vulnerability. Incorrect placement could cause the JVM to crash, but in many instances, we can simply try again. WARM Run valid decodes until the JIT selects the affected fast path. No memory is corrupted. REHEARSE Optional safe round for calibration. TRIGGER Send the malformed tail. If the objects line up, the fixed spill enlarges the writer. DISCLOSE Continue the writer so chosen bytes enlarge the reader, then collect the response-derived heap bytes. REPAIR Use the disclosed originals to restore temporary headers and untouched neighbors when the chain has a repair path. FINISH Make the application-specific change and verify it through a live request. Limitations Request streaming. Some current grooming profiles need partial request bodies to reach the application. A proxy that waits for the complete body removes their release timing. nginx buffers request bodies by default . Request buffering is not a general mitigation. Elasticsearch runs from one complete request, so this setting does not stop that chain. After a configured WebSocket upgrade , later frames pass through a tunnel and request-body buffering no longer applies to them. Application profiles. There is no universal payload. Each chain needs a decoder route, a live writer, a returned reader or another feedback path, a heap layout, and an application action. Every target needs a bespoke profile. The exploit is not a universal point-and-shoot. PoC Here is a self-contained proof of concept. It warms the Base64 decoder until the vulnerable intrinsic is used, then decodes the malformed 64 × "A" + "=" input into a 4096-byte array. On an affected JDK it prints REPRODUCED : the decoder rejects the input, but 62 bytes (offsets 50 to 111) past the decoded output have already been overwritten. Every write lands inside a real array, so the trigger is safe to run. Copy import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.Base64; /** Bounded standalone trigger: every write stays inside a real 4096-byte array. */ public final class Base64Trigger { private static volatile int sink; public static void main(String[] args) { Base64.Decoder decoder = Base64.getDecoder(); byte[] valid = "A".repeat(64).getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] malformed = ("A".repeat(64) + "=").getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII); byte[] target = new byte[4096]; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { sink += decoder.decode(valid, target); } Arrays.fill(target, (byte) 0x5a); boolean rejected = false; try { decoder.decode(malformed, target); } catch (IllegalArgumentException expected) { rejected = true; } int changed = 0; int first = -1; int last = -1; for (int i = 50; i < target.length; i++) { if (target[i] != (byte) 0x5a) { changed++; if (first < 0) first = i; last = i; } } System.out.println("runtime=" + System.getProperty("java.runtime.version")); System.out.println("vm=" + System.getProperty("java.vm.name")); System.out.printf("rejected=%s changed=%d first=%d last=%d%n", rejected, changed, first, last); if (!rejected || changed != 62 || first != 50 || last != 111) { System.err.println("NOT REPRODUCED"); System.exit(1); } System.out.println("REPRODUCED"); } } We are holding back the application-specific exploits for now. This write-up covers the vulnerability and the general exploitation technique. The weaponized chains for individual products stay private until everyone has had a chance to upgrade. We will publish them later. Affected products Java4Shell affects OpenJDK from version 17.0.6 or newer. Because they are built from OpenJDK, the following Java distributions are also vulnerable: Amazon Corretto Eclipse Temurin Microsoft Build of OpenJDK Azul Zulu BellSoft Liberica SAP SapMachine Red Hat OpenJDK Oracle OpenJDK Oracle Java SE Oracle GraalVM for JDK According to Oracle, the following Oracle Java SE versions are vulnerable: 8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3. We thank Oracle for providing this information ahead of publication time. Because the vulnerable code is hardware-specific, Java4Shell also requires an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI support. ARM64 CPUs are not affected. These mainstream CPU families meet the hardware requirements: Intel Xeon: Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, Granite Rapids AMD EPYC and Ryzen: Zen 4 or newer On Linux, you can check whether your CPU is vulnerable with this command: Copy grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$' The output must include all four flags. Recommendations OpenJDK released a security advisory and Oracle released a patch at 1:00pm PT on Nov 17, 2026. All Java users should update immediately. You can also mitigate Java4Shell by starting OpenJDK with either: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding, or -XX:UseAVX=2 to disable AVX-512. Apply this flag only on x86-64 hosts. OpenJDK on ARM doesn't recognize it and will fail to start. Credits Research, write-up and exploits by Quang Luong. Exploit improvement by Jenish Rakholiya. Artwork by Michal Zalewski. Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) was found and reported by Calif.io .   See also PHP2Shell and Squidbleed .

title: Quad9's withdrawal from France: A canary in the coal mine
A Perfect SimCity
body_text: A Perfect SimCity · Articles Jeff Quast Software Developer Subscribe RSS feed contact@jeffquast.com Github Articles 22. August 2026 A Perfect SimCity After 35 years of playing SimCity, I still could not say what makes a "Perfect" city. An evaluation screen displays a Score of 0 to 1000, and I struggled to reach 900 and never understood its factors. Discovering these factors by play is the fun of a simulation game, and this one has the advantage that the source code is also available. Don Hopkins has been maintaining FOSS ports of SimCity (1989) as Micropolis and MicropolisCore , faithfully reproducing the ruleset of the original. Using the Python shims provided by gym-city I have run many experiments and share these results here, presenting five high-scoring and five high-population cities, designed algorithmically using the strategies shared below. - + VGA EGA Mono ♫ 🔇 ⛶ Classic Ancient Asia Future Europe Future USA Medieval Moon Colony Wild West ◀ ▶ Speed Reload Disasters No Disasters Earthquake Fire Flood Tornado Monster Meltdown Fire Bombs ◀ ▶ This article embeds a runnable Micropolis simulation and needs JavaScript. Figure 1. Ten algorithmically generated cities, 5 with highest score (bigscore1 through 5), and 5 for large population of 700k (bigpop1 through 5). Citizens Demand Fewer Roads The population of a perfectly scoring city is 12-16k. Their population level, crime rate, pollution and land value are perfectly balanced to sustain a 1% Tax Rate. Their roads and rails are few and non-contiguous. A perfectly scoring city is without any fire department, and bigscore2 through 5 have no police station. city score population crime pollution land value unemployment cash / year bigscore1 949.5 16,560 13 36 126 -93 +6 bigscore2 940.0 18,400 22 41 124 -99 +147 bigscore3 940.0 12,440 22 35 122 -96 +93 bigscore4 939.0 12,400 16 30 128 -95 +86 bigscore5 937.0 14,640 20 41 127 -98 +117 Travel requirements of residential and industrial zones are simple. They check their twelve surrounding tiles for any road or rail to decide if it should grow. If none is there, the zone declines. Commercial zones require a delivery, a vehicle starts on the perimeter road and walks up to 30 steps, arriving the moment it stands beside a developed tile. The zone's own tiles count , so any loop of track under 30 steps satisfies it. Commercial zones are placed in the city center because the engine provides a downtown bonus , starting at +64 and falling off to a -64 penalty in the far corners of the map. The PC SimCity manual recommends rails and it is the most obvious strategy that players discover on their own. Roads carry traffic and emit pollution, which suppresses residential growth. Rails emit no pollution and register no traffic at all. Roads and rails incur an annual cost, and Police and Fire are very large budget items, they severely impact score if they are under-funded and so must be at 100% funding. Having neither departments is the lowest annual cost allowing for the lowest Tax Rate. Raising the Tax Rate to 2% lowers the score almost 30 points, through direct and indirect factors. Citizens Demand More Citizens In the Super Nintendo edition the game rewards population , the final reward of Megapolis is issued at a population of 500k. Casual players report cities of 600k to 700k on the SNES platform, with one player reporting 911.2k . 911.2k is probably out of reach for Micropolis . The Super Nintendo is the only edition to offer gifts , which increase land value when placed, allowing for higher zone density in the areas outside of the downtown bonus . I have also experimented with optimizing for population by algorithm, and I am able to reach 700k by automatic code. city population score tax crime pollution cash / year bigpop1 709,405 467.0 2% 140 174 +2,206 bigpop2 694,670 468.5 5% 175 179 +7,944 bigpop3 688,435 458.5 5% 218 171 +7,568 bigpop4 682,590 525.0 2% 116 168 +470 bigpop5 670,950 461.5 3% 219 171 +4,194 Citizens Demand More Housing Score is calculated in two stages, the first uses seven penalty terms: crime, the citywide crime average pollution, the citywide pollution average housing, the citywide land value average taxes, the tax rate traffic, the citywide traffic average unemployment fire, the tiles burning at that moment /images/simcity-score-terms.svg Figure 2. The seven scoring terms. Six are bounded at zero and can only subtract, and traffic can be as high as 576. Unemployment has no lower bound, a negative value raises score. Six out of seven terms are bounded at zero. However, unemployment is unbounded: unemployment = (resPop / (8 * jobs) - 1) * 255 When the number of jobs exceeds the residents zoned to fill them, The Unemployment term goes negative and adds to the score , providing a score bonus of about 128 points. No other term moves the score this much. The second stage of score calculation is reduction by nine more penalties: /images/simcity-score-stage2.svg Figure 3. Each penalty applies to what the one above it left, so the same factor is worth less further down the list. The right-hand column is what each costs a city scoring 940. The first three are penalties for failing to build a special zone. Surpassing 500 residents demands a stadium, 100 commercial an airport and 70 industrial a seaport. Where a stadium is placed does not matter to score, having no traffic or pollution. However, Airports and Seaports do reduce overall score, because of their high-density pollution and so they are not built. Citizens Demand Fountains Each of those seven penalty terms is an average, and the land value scan.cpp decides what is included by each 2x2 square of map by their tile ID. Grass, forest and park trees are under 64 and invisible to scoring, but a fountain of ID 840 includes it for grading, even though nobody lives in it! These 2x2 squares otherwise carry no population, pulling down the crime penalty term by 33 points. tile id tile land value counted 0 dirt no no ... ... ... ... 2-20 water +15 no 21-43 forest, park trees +15 no 44-63 rubble, flood, fire no no 64-65 bridge no yes 66-79 road no yes ... ... ... ... 840 park fountain no yes Figure 5. A 2x2 square is counted only when it contains tile ID 64 or greater, while land value is credited only from tile IDs below 44. The park building tool has a one in five chance to draw a fountain, ID 840. Placing fountains lower total crime penalty. Park Overflow Many guides recommend parks to reduce or absorb pollution, but they do not reduce pollution at all in Micropolis . However, pollution reduces land value, and land value drives crime, so parks lower crime indirectly by raising the land value around them. Water, park and tree tiles all increase land value, and the engine counts them in 4x4 blocks. Every such tile credits its block 15 points, and the final credit to land value is this sum, plus downtown bonus, minus pollution. However, this land value credit is kept as a single byte, and smoothTerrain() in scan.cpp blends a block with its neighbors before it divides, so a block with its surroundings may sum beyond 255 and wrap around , counter-intuitively lowering land value. /images/simcity-park-overflow.svg Figure 4. Number of Water, park or tree tiles in a 4x4 block against the land value it credits. Exactly 1/2 of the tiles (8) is the optimal value of greenery. At 9 of 16 tiles, it is in danger of driving down land value when summed with its neighbors. The PC SimCity manual declares that "Parks, like forests and water, raise the land value of surrounding zones". However, too many parks or trees can push push down land value and increase crime. Citizens Demand More Industries Common strategy is to lay industrial zones by map edges, and this is recommended to maximize for population. The SNES SimCity manual writes, "One of the great benefits of building industrial Zones along the edges is that half the pollution is off the map and doesn't affect the city. This is very important when it comes to heavily polluting industries, Airports and Coal Power Stations." This is partly true. The Micropolis engine spreads pollution outward from each source, divides the map into 4x4 blocks, and then creates an average of only the blocks that contain pollution: pollutionAverage = ptot / pnum ptot is the pollution totaled over the dirty blocks pnum is the count of those blocks Tiles that contain low levels of pollution help bring down total pollution by this averaging, a small high-scoring city should keep the light density pollution for itself. Models suggest that a city maximized for population should place industrial zones on map edges for other reasons, that the land value there is too low to for other kind of zones. Citizens Demand Humanity Jay Wright Forrester's Urban Dynamics (1969) is often cited as an influence on Will Wright, Chief Designer of SimCity (1989) . Urban Dynamics is essentially a paperback simulation of cities. The Micropolis simulation is vaguely recognizable as a minified version of the model in Urban Dynamics along with some small improvements in including spatial values of neighboring tiles that Forrester's models lack. Interestingly, both arrive at the same place: what improves a city most is reducing available housing: The concurrent reduction of excess housing is absolutely essential. It supplies the land for new job-creating structures. Equally important, the resulting housing shortage creates the population-stabilizing pressure that allows economic revival to proceed without being inundated by rising population. —Jay Forrester, Counterintuitive Behavior of Social Systems , 1971 The Sumerian Game (1963) , considered the antecedent of the city-building game genre, contains the same anti-pattern, where I found the best strategy is systemic starvation of 3% of the population. I think in 2026 it would be difficult to find a proponent for the housing and population shortages that all three of these models suggest optimizing towards. ← have a day.

title: Nvidia stopped disclosing Singapore sales as revenues hit $104B
Google's AI answers reducing search traffic by 40%
body_text: Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to websites by 40% - RevScope Pricing Docs Blog FAQ GitHub Google's AI Overviews cut clicks to websites by 40% November 9, 2026 Google's AI answers are taking clicks from websites in the search results. In a randomized experiment, researchers hid AI Overviews from some US desktop users. Comparing them with users who still saw Overviews shows that an Overview cuts clicks to outside websites by about 40%. Those Overviews now appear on more than half the US keywords DataForSEO tracks, up from 6% two years ago. The industry's answer, GEO (generative engine optimization), has yet to show a way to compensate for the loss. While AI citations correlate with the same kind of link profile that goes with higher Google rankings, in March AI assistants sent websites just 0.3% of their traffic. Search engine optimization (SEO) still decides whether you can be found, but where an AI answer appears, a ranking brings 40% fewer visits than it used to. Generative engine optimization (GEO), the practice of getting your content cited in AI-written answers, looks mostly like SEO plus two additions: being present on the third-party sites AI answers draw from, and writing pages that are easy to quote. We found little evidence for any other tactic. Google answers first An AI Overview is a generated summary that Google places above the ordinary results, with links to the pages it drew on. In DataForSEO's monthly panel of 20 million keywords, the share of results showing one climbed from 5.93% in September 2024 to 61.43% in August 2026. The chart at the top of this post shows that climb. Over the same period the featured snippet, the quoted passage Google used to show at the top of a page, fell from 8.96% to 0.44%, and the discussions and forums block fell from 21.13% to 7.42%. Video results rose from 9.67% to 19.98%, though that is down from a peak of 31.05% in October 2025, and local map listings rose from 19.98% to 25.99%. DataForSEO's dataset covers 190 million keywords, 165 million AI answers, and 1.1 billion backlinks, mostly for US English searches. Pew Research Center's data gives an independent check. Pew logged the searches of 900 US adults in March 2025, re-ran them in April, and found summaries on 18% of them. DataForSEO's figures for those months are 14.67% and 17.63%, close to Pew's. You can't reliably avoid Overviews by choosing different keywords. Between the fourth quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026, the rate rose for every type of search intent: Search intent Q4 2025 Q3 2026 Informational (looking something up) 48.42% 70.44% Commercial (comparing options) 26.30% 51.35% Navigational (looking for a site) 17.04% 34.03% Transactional (ready to buy) 10.82% 28.64% Low-volume keywords aren't safer either. In the third quarter of 2026, keywords with 201 to 300 monthly searches showed Overviews 58.59% of the time, against 48.62% for those above 600. A separate dataset, from June to September 2026, covers difficulty and price. The easiest keywords showed Overviews 60.64% of the time and the hardest 53.76%. Keywords costing advertisers more than $5 a click were at 49.55% and those under 25 cents at 50.54%, with a low of 42.63% between $0.51 and $1.00. More than half the result pages have no price data and show Overviews 60.06% of the time. The rate does vary by industry. Health is at 69.68% and finance at 68.80%, while apparel is at 37.48%, dining at 29.37%, and real estate at 22.27%. Queries are also getting longer, especially on desktop. Over a year, queries of five or more words grew from 29.3% to 34.8% of unique desktop queries and from 29.6% to 31.9% on mobile. Three and four word searches are still the most common. What happens to the clicks The strongest evidence is an experiment. Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen gave US desktop Chrome users an extension that put each of them at random into a group. One group saw Google as usual, and another had AI Overviews hidden. The researchers then watched two weeks of real searches in January and February 2026. On searches that would show an Overview, the group that could see them averaged 0.37 clicks to outside websites per search, against 0.62 for the group that couldn't, which the authors report as a 39.8% reduction. Searches ending with no outbound click went from 54% to 73%. Clicks on ads didn't change, which suggests Google takes care not to cannibalize its own revenue. Across all searches, with and without an Overview, the authors put the loss at roughly 18.5% of the organic clicks a site gets from Google. The authors expect the loss to grow as Overviews appear on more searches. This is a randomized controlled trial, the most reliable kind of study for separating cause from correlation or coincidence. The effect was statistically significant for informational searches. The navigational and transactional samples were too small to settle anything. This is a working paper, not yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop only. A separate preregistered experiment by Wang and colleagues, with 1,100 people, also found that removing AI Overviews and AI Mode raised clicks to publishers. Observational data points the same way. Pew found people clicked an ordinary result on 8% of visits to a results page with a summary and on 15% without one, and ended their browsing session on 26% against 16%. Pew's comparison isn't a controlled experiment, because the searches that draw a summary tend to be longer and phrased as questions. Click-through rate (CTR) is the share of people shown a result who click it. Across more than 2,000 websites in DataForSEO's panel, the desktop CTR of the first organic result fell from 17.83% in September 2025 to 7.43% in August 2026, a drop of 58%. Mobile fell from 25.17% to 20.80%, a drop of 17%. Desktop lost nearly half its click-through rate in one month, March 2026, and stayed down. Mobile fell about as far over five months, then recovered most of it. These figures come from Table A2 of the report. Desktop plunged from 15.18% to 7.94% between February and March 2026. AI Overviews can't easily explain that step since the report has them almost flat that month, at 42.79% and then 43.38%. A change in the format or quality of the Overviews might explain part of it, though that is speculation on our part. Mobile, meanwhile, sank to 12.96% and then rebounded to 22.49% by May. The report itself says its data "does not establish" whether AI answers, layout changes, or changes in behavior are the cause. Its sample may also be shifting underneath it, since the unique desktop queries it counts fell by a third over the year, from 1.97 million to 1.32 million. Whatever the cause, a top ranking on desktop now earns less than half the clicks it did a year earlier. DataForSEO also estimates where clicks go on pages with and without an Overview. By its model, the first organic result holds 9 to 16 points less click share on pages with one, though these are different searches on a single day's snapshot: Search intent Position 1, no Overview Position 1, with Overview Overview's cited links Informational 37.1% 20.7% 42.4% Navigational 33.4% 24.1% 44.8% Transactional 37.6% 21.4% 43.0% Commercial 33.8% 21.1% 42.2% The click share for the Overview's cited links looks promising, but it comes from a model. Pew, which logged real browsing, saw people click a link inside a summary on just 1% of visits, against 8% for ordinary results. Eighteen months and a large change in the product separate the two measurements, so it is difficult to say which is closer to the truth. Google disputes that search traffic to websites is declining. In August 2025 its head of Search, Liz Reid, wrote that total organic clicks were "relatively stable year-over-year" and that Google was sending "slightly more quality clicks", meaning clicks where people don't quickly come back. She gave no figures to back that up. Your site can't see whether someone goes back to Google, so you can't check Google's quality-clicks claim yourself, but you can check what your Google clicks are worth. RevScope , our product, shows your revenue per visitor from Google, AI Overviews included, and which landing pages earn the most. Who the answers cite If people read the summary and stop there, it matters which sites the summary cites. The report compares Google's AI Overviews with ChatGPT. Their most-cited lists overlap, but a different kind of site leads each one. Rank Google AI Overviews Citations ChatGPT Answers citing it 1 youtube.com 51.9M wikipedia.org 4.88M 2 reddit.com 25.1M reddit.com 3.25M 3 facebook.com 20.4M fandom.com 670K 4 wikipedia.org 19.9M britannica.com 486K 5 google.com 15.9M nih.gov 476K The report warns that the two platforms' counts aren't comparable, so compare where a site ranks within each list. Reddit and Wikipedia rank near the top of both, and by our count 16 of the 30 domains in each top 30 appear on both lists. The differences are still large. YouTube is first in AI Overviews and nineteenth in ChatGPT. Facebook, Instagram, and TikTok make Google's top ten and miss ChatGPT's top 30, while Reuters, The Guardian, AP News, and The Washington Post make ChatGPT's top 30 and miss Google's. ChatGPT also often cites nobody: 27.3% of its answers had no source, against 0.7% for AI Overviews. So, as the report puts it, strength on one platform "doesn't automatically guarantee" the same on another. Reddit also appears in Google's ordinary top ten for 32.15% of the report's tracked results, nearly eight times Quora's 4.11%. Two limits apply to all of this. The first is that the answers come from prompts DataForSEO collected, and the report doesn't explain how they were chosen or whether they match what people really ask. The second is that big platforms do about as well in ordinary results: Pew found Wikipedia, YouTube, and Reddit made up 15% of the sources in AI summaries and 17% of those in standard results. Still, the common belief that AI favors Reddit holds up in this data. GEO looks mostly like SEO Google's position is that there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary", beyond a page being indexed and eligible to show with a snippet. Since that is a company describing its own product, we looked at outside data on two questions. The first is which sites get considered, and the second is which page on a site gets picked. Which sites: link profiles correlate with citations A referring domain is another website that links to yours. DataForSEO measured how closely referring domains track AI citations using Spearman's correlation, a score where 0 means no relationship between two rankings and 1 means they match exactly. The score was 0.406 for AI Overviews and 0.377 for ChatGPT. Links marked as coming from user-generated content, such as forum posts, scored lower, at 0.342 and 0.314. These are moderate relationships, and they don't show that links cause citations, since large, well-known sites tend to have more of everything. The samples also contain only domains cited at least once, so they can't tell you what it takes to get cited for the first time. A similar pattern shows up in ordinary rankings: domains ranking first had a median of 111 referring domains against 85 for positions 4 to 10, with heavy overlap between the groups. For AI Overviews, the median cited domain had 282 referring domains on the easiest keywords and 1,571 on the hardest, after the report excluded giant platforms like YouTube and Amazon and any domain with fewer than 50 referring domains. Small sites weren't measured at all. The ranges are also wide, at 518 to 5,765 for the middle half of domains on the hardest keywords, so sites with very different link profiles get cited. Which page: cited pages often don't rank for the query Ranking for a query and being cited for it are drifting apart. Ahrefs found 76% of pages cited in AI Overviews ranked in the top 10 for that query in July 2025 , and about 38% in March 2026 . The two studies differ in sample, parsing, and the Gemini model behind the Overviews, so the size of that fall isn't a clean measurement. One possible mechanism is what Google calls query fan-out: its documentation says these features may issue "multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources". A page could then be cited because it ranks for a related question the reader never typed. Ahrefs offers this only as a possibility, and its earlier study tested the idea and found that the data didn't support it. The most careful test of page-level tactics we found is a study by the SEO software company SISTRIX, published in October 2026. It paired 48,527 pages cited by ChatGPT, AI Mode, or AI Overviews with uncited pages from the same site, which removes the site's overall strength from the comparison. In the table, a factor of 2.7 means pages with the feature were cited 2.7 times as often as pages without it. Page feature Factor What SISTRIX says about it Current year in the title 2.7 A rough stand-in for maintained content, not a title trick; an initial indication Table of contents with jump links 1.7 Only 14% of pages had one; 2.5 on editorial sites FAQ structured data 1.5 At 833 URLs it pointed the opposite way, a warning about small GEO studies Visible last-updated date 1.3 1.9 on editorial sites, but 0.7 on shops; only 5% of pages showed one Ten or more external links 1.3 Linking out to sources Product structured data 0.8 0.5 in AI Overviews, but "not a lever, but no cause for concern either"; it should stay Many features combined 2.1 Against barely optimized pages An experiment in the paper that gave GEO its name points the same way as SISTRIX's correlations. Aggarwal and colleagues rewrote web pages and measured how much of a generated answer drew on them. On their 10,000-query benchmark, adding quotations raised a page's visibility by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31%, and citing sources by about 27%, while keyword stuffing lowered it by about 8%, all on their main measure, the position-weighted share of the answer's words. Lower-ranked pages gained the most: citing sources lifted a page ranked fifth by 115% and cut the top-ranked page by 30%. They also tried Perplexity, an AI search product, on 200 samples, uploading the source text as files rather than letting it search. The gains on that measure were smaller, at about 21% for quotations and 9% for statistics. The main test used GPT-3.5 reading the top five search results, which is well behind today's products, so the percentages are dated even if the direction still holds. The most debated shortcut has nothing behind it so far. llms.txt is a proposed file that tells AI systems what a site contains. SE Ranking analyzed nearly 300,000 domains and found no correlation with citations. SISTRIX also concluded there is "no measurable effect", though it cautions that domains with the file differ from others in many ways, so this part of its data doesn't have the same-site pairing. Google says "you don't need to create new machine readable files, AI text files, or markup" for its AI features. The data agrees about the files, though SISTRIX's FAQ structured data result suggests some markup may help. AI sends little traffic, but it is growing and may convert well AI assistants sent 0.28% of total traffic across 74,752 websites in March 2026, according to Ahrefs. That was about 3.5 million visitors, against 345 million from Google, or roughly a hundred to one. Ahrefs describes it as small but growing fast. The true figure is somewhat higher because some visits, especially from mobile apps, get counted as direct traffic. The same Ahrefs article reports that on its own site, AI search visitors were 0.5% of visitors and 12.1% of signups. Ahrefs sells SEO software, so its audience may be unusually likely to use AI tools, and one site proves little. Still, on that site an AI visitor was about 24 times as likely to sign up as the average visitor. Some of the value never shows up as traffic. People read an AI answer, form an opinion, and never click. To count what AI visits are worth on your own site, RevScope reports when ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, and other assistants send visitors and whether they buy. It also tracks when AI and search engine bots crawl your pages. Google's own reporting has a gap too. It counts traffic from its AI features inside the overall "Web" numbers in Search Console. Since 2026 Search Console also has generative AI reports, which Google says show how often your URLs appeared in those features, along with pages, countries, and devices. The announcement describes impressions and doesn't mention clicks, so you learn how often you appear, not how many visits or sales that brings. Rank tracking can't fill the gap, since a page can hold position 1 and earn fewer clicks than it used to. What to do about it Keep the fundamentals. Pages must be indexable and eligible for a snippet. Referring domains correlated with citations more strongly than user-generated links did, and higher-ranking domains had moderately more of them, so links from other sites remain a reasonable investment, even though neither relationship proves cause. Find out who gets cited on your topics, per platform. Check your important queries in AI Overviews and ChatGPT and note the sources. Being described accurately there may matter as much as your own page. Take part in the communities those answers cite, such as Reddit, so that you are mentioned there. Write pages worth quoting. Answer related questions directly, add original data and named sources, and use clear headings. If you run an editorial site, show when the page was last updated. Skip the shortcuts. An llms.txt does no harm but has shown no benefit, AI-specific markup isn't needed, and keyword stuffing lowered visibility in the GEO paper's test. Judge the work by revenue. With fewer clicks to go around, it matters more which ones pay. Tie each channel to the sales it produces rather than to its rank or its visit count. The numbers above are mainly US English, and the products change quickly, so the 2025 figures may already be out of date. Nearly all the large datasets come from companies that sell SEO data or software, including DataForSEO, Ahrefs, SISTRIX, and SE Ranking, and we sell analytics. Almost everything about what earns a citation is correlation. Three findings hold up. Controlled experiments show fewer clicks to outside websites when Google's AI features are present, domains with more referring domains tend to be cited more often among those already cited, and we found no proven shortcut to being cited. Stop guessing what makes money RevScope connects your web traffic to your payments, so you can see which channels, pages, and keywords bring in revenue. Start on the free plan and put your time and budget where it pays. Start with free plan See pricing Rather run it yourself? RevScope's source is public. Self-host it for free . Sources Search Insider: 2026 Edition DataForSEO Â· Annual research report Â· October 2026 DataForSEO collects search and AI answer data for a living and publishes its tables and methods, which allowed us to check the monthly figures behind its headlines. It sells this data, its answer prompts aren't explained, and its click shares are modeled. We rely on it for what appears where, and treat its click estimates and correlations as indications. Our charts are redrawn from its published values. The Impact of Google AI Overviews on Publisher Traffic and User Experience: Evidence from a Field Experiment Saharsh Agarwal and Ananya Sen Â· Working paper Â· SSRN Â· draft of June 2026 University researchers ran a preregistered randomized experiment on 1,065 US participants, 770 of them in the two groups compared here. Random assignment makes it the best evidence that Overviews themselves reduce clicks. It isn't yet peer reviewed, and it covers desktop Chrome for two weeks. We read a copy of the June draft hosted outside SSRN. AI in Search Reduces Publisher Referrals Without Improving User Experience: Experimental Evidence Stephanie T. Wang, Jeffrey Gleason, and colleagues Â· Preprint Â· arXiv Â· August 2026 A second preregistered experiment, with 1,100 people, which independently supports the direction of the result. We read its abstract only, so we use it for that direction and not for any figure. Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears in the results Athena Chapekis and Anna Lieb Â· Short read Â· Pew Research Center Â· July 2025 A nonprofit research organization with no search product to sell, logging the real browsing of 900 consenting US adults. It covers one month, March 2025, re-collected the summaries in April, and doesn't control for which searches draw a summary. AI Features and Your Website and the Search Console reports announcement Google Search Central Â· Documentation, last updated December 2025, and blog post, June 2026 The primary sources for what Google says its AI features require and how it reports them. They are reliable on those rules, and they aren't independent evidence of what works. AI in Search is driving more queries and higher quality clicks Liz Reid Â· Company blog Â· Google Â· August 2025 Google's public position on total clicks, from the person running Search. Google can see the true numbers, but this post publishes none of them, so we report it as a claim. Citation Worthiness: Which GEO Tactics Hold Up Across 96,418 URLs Johannes Beus, Julia Weissbach, and the SISTRIX Content Team Â· Industry study Â· SISTRIX Â· October 2026 Its same-site pairing and correction for multiple testing make it more careful than most GEO studies. It sells SEO software, covers only German-speaking markets, and reports correlations. GEO: Generative Engine Optimization Pranjal Aggarwal, Vishvak Murahari, and colleagues Â· Conference paper Â· KDD 2024 Â· version 3, June 2024 The academic paper that named the field and ran controlled rewrites of pages. It shows content changes can move visibility, but its test engine is now dated, and its authors' "up to 40%" should not be read as a current forecast. Update: 38% of AI Overview Citations Pull From The Top 10 and 76% of AI Overview Citations Pull From the Top 10 Louise Linehan with Xibeijia Guan Â· Industry studies Â· Ahrefs Â· March 2026 and July 2025 Ahrefs sells SEO tools and tracks AI answers through its Brand Radar product, here matching about 4 million cited URLs against rankings in the later study. The two studies aren't like-for-like. The 38% counts results in every part of the page; for ordinary links alone it is 37.1%. AI Chatbot Traffic: What It Is, and How to Get More Mateusz Makosiewicz Â· Company blog Â· Ahrefs Â· May 2026 The source for the 0.28% figure, from analytics on 74,752 sites, and for the signup figure from Ahrefs' own site. It gives conflicting percentages for Google's share in different places, so we compare visitor counts instead. LLMs.txt: Why Brands Rely On It and Why It Doesn't Work Yulia Deda Â· Industry study Â· SE Ranking Â· page dated October 2026 A large correlation study of nearly 300,000 domains. It doesn't name the AI platforms it sampled, so we use it only alongside SISTRIX and Google's statement.
