Help Frequently asked questions Moderators' noticeboard Report a bug Browser Extension Install on Chrome Install on Firefox Contents move to sidebar hide Beginning 1 Background 2 Acceptance screen and continued-use rule 3 Privacy policy and terms clauses Toggle Privacy policy and terms clauses subsection 3.1 Marketing use 3.2 Corporate transactions 3.3 Arbitration and class-action waiver 3.4 Data kept after closing a wallet 3.5 2023 and 2026 versions 4 Government-verification carve-out 5 Login.gov and paying without signing in 6 TreasuryDirect move and Senate letter 7 References Toggle the table of contents ID.me terms required for IRS sign-in Page Discussion English Read Edit Edit source View history Give feedback Tools Tools move to sidebar hide Actions Read Edit Edit source View history Give feedback General What links here Related changes Printable version Permanent link Page information Cargo data Appearance move to sidebar hide From Consumer Rights Wiki Taxpayers who sign in to Internal Revenue Service (IRS) online services with ID.me , a private-sector sign-in provider, [ 1 ] [ 2 ] use it under ID.me's own Terms of Service, which send disputes outside small claims court to a neutral arbitrator instead of a judge or jury unless the user opts out within 30 days of accepting them. [ 3 ] ID.me's Privacy Policy says it "may use information for marketing purposes" & may transfer information in a sale, merger or other corporate transaction, [ 4 ] though it says information from state or federal government identity verification is not used for marketing for ID.me Shop, its shopping-discount site, unless the user consents or meets another listed exception. [ 4 ] [ 5 ] Login.gov , which the U.S. government maintains, also works for IRS sign-in, [ 2 ] & the IRS's Direct Pay service takes bank-account tax payments with "No sign-in required". [ 6 ] ID.me replaced the traditional login for Treasury 's savings-bond site TreasuryDirect on October 28, 2026, [ 7 ] & on October 29, 2026 senators Ron Wyden & Elizabeth Warren asked Treasury & the IRS to explain why they continue to use ID.me "instead of the government-run Login.gov platform". [ 8 ] Background [ edit | edit source ] The IRS describes ID.me as "a private sector sign-in provider for secure access to government and non-government websites". [ 2 ] ID.me's Terms of Service say the company provides "a level of assurance to businesses and government agencies" that a user's identity and attributes are verified "based upon widely-recognized standards", [ 3 ] & that "ID.me does not charge members any fees for registering and/or using the Service or Website." [ 3 ] The IRS sign-in page says taxpayers "need an ID.me or Login.gov account" to access tax information online. [ 1 ] The IRS says it uses these sign-in providers "to protect your privacy and data through identity verification". [ 2 ] One account covers the IRS online services: "Individual Online Account, Business Tax Account, Tax Pro Account, e‑Services and more". [ 1 ] ID.me's Privacy Policy says some partners, "such as the IRS", may require identity verification "to a higher level of certainty" under National Institute of Standards and Technology guidelines. [ 4 ] Treasury's savings-bond site TreasuryDirect says it uses ID.me because it "aligns with Treasury security requirements and those used by the Internal Revenue Service". [ 7 ] The IRS said on December 7, 2021 that it was "using ID.me to provide verification services". [ 9 ] It announced on February 7, 2022 that it would "transition away from using a third-party service for facial recognition", [ 10 ] & said on February 21, 2022 that taxpayers could still choose biometric verification "through ID.me’s self-assistance tool". [ 11 ] Acceptance screen and continued-use rule [ edit | edit source ] A user accepts ID.me's Terms of Service , with the Credential Policy made available at that time, by selecting "I agree" or "taking another affirmative action clearly identified as acceptance when these Terms are presented to you". [ 3 ] The Terms say ID.me's Credential Policy "gives further details of how we accomplish our identity proofing". [ 3 ] The Terms say the company keeps a wallet for each user "that contains your identity and group affiliation information". [ 3 ] ID.me's personal-information obligations are governed "at all times" by the Credential Policy & Privacy Policy. [ 3 ] A taxpayer emailed consumer advocate Louis Rossmann a screenshot of the "UPDATED TERMS & CONDITIONS" screen the taxpayer said they saw while signing in to IRS.gov through ID.me, showing ID.me & IRS logos and one button, "Accept Terms & Continue". ID.me's Privacy Policy dated November 2, 2026 says by using the platform "you agree that ID.me. determines how personal information may be used" for the user's wallet. [ 4 ] The policy's May 7, 2026 text lacked it. [ 12 ] The current Terms, Version 10.1.0 dated November 13, 2026, count continued use after revised Terms take effect as "acceptance of those changes", "Unless we expressly state otherwise"; a user who disagrees may stop using the Service & close the wallet first. [ 3 ] Version 10.0.3, dated March 3, 2023, said continuing use after notice "will indicate your agreement to all changes", "Unless otherwise noted by us". [ 13 ] The Credential Policy, Version 10.1, published July 1, 2024, requires users to reaffirm acceptance of "the prevailing Terms of Service, Privacy and other Policies and any other required agreements" "at least once every 5 years" or face credential suspension. [ 14 ] Public radio program Marketplace reported that Nancy Kim, a professor emerita at Illinois Tech's Chicago-Kent College of Law, said she found nothing reassuring in ID.me's terms, pointing out that although they state ID.me won't sell data, ID.me can change them. [ 15 ] Privacy policy and terms clauses [ edit | edit source ] Marketing use [ edit | edit source ] ID.me's Privacy Policy says: We may use information for marketing purposes. We may use your information to send promotional messages and newsletters via email, or otherwise alert you to products or Services we think might be of interest to you, including for ID.me Shop. [ 4 ] ID.me Shop, a page of deals & discounts, says it "is part of the Amazon Associates program and other affiliate programs" & "may earn money when you buy products through links on Shop". [ 5 ] Corporate transactions [ edit | edit source ] The policy also says: We may share your information in connection with a corporate transaction. We may disclose or transfer your information as part of, or during negotiations for, any purchase, sale, lease, merger, or any other type of acquisition, disposal, or financing involving our brands. [ 4 ] Arbitration and class-action waiver [ edit | edit source ] A capitalized notice atop ID.me's Terms of Service says they contain "A MUTUAL ARBITRATION PROVISION, JURY TRIAL WAIVER, AND CLASS-ACTION WAIVER" & that users may opt out "WITHIN THIRTY (30) DAYS OF ACCEPTING THESE TERMS". [ 3 ] Section 20 covers disputes "arising out of or relating to" the Terms, the Privacy Policy, the website or the service. [ 3 ] A dispute not resolved within 45 calendar days after the notice of dispute is received goes to arbitration , where "a neutral arbitrator will resolve all Disputes"; both sides give up suing before a judge or jury, individually or in a class action, except in small claims court. [ 3 ] Subject to an age exception, a valid opt-out & "nonwaivable statutory rights", disputes proceed "solely on an individual basis". [ 3 ] A user may opt out by emailing a notice titled "Opt-Out Notice" to [email protected] within 30 calendar days "after you first accept these Terms" or within 30 calendar days "after a material change to the Opt-Out Provisions takes effect". [ 3 ] Section 10 caps ID.me's aggregate liability at $1,000.00 "To the extent allowed by law". [ 3 ] Version 10.0.3, dated March 3, 2023, had the same cap, & its notice listed "A BINDING ARBITRATION CLAUSE AND A CLASS ACTION WAIVER" with no opt-out. [ 13 ] The opt-out appears in Version 10.1.0, in a copy last updated September 18, 2025 whose opt-out text matches the November 13, 2026 version. [ 16 ] [ 3 ] Data kept after closing a wallet [ edit | edit source ] Closing a wallet directs ID.me to deactivate the credential & "purge the associated data from active use", but ID.me "does retain" account & verification history "for up to three (3) years". [ 4 ] Use of the credential with state or federal government agencies "will be stopped" if the account is deleted. [ 4 ] Information given "in connection with a public sector agency" for verification "may be retained for up to three (3) years after wallet closure", "unless applicable regulations require a shorter retention period". [ 4 ] ID.me reserves the right to keep data from "certain high-risk transactions, particularly in government and healthcare settings", "exclusively for fraud prevention and government audit purposes". [ 4 ] The policy says biometric deletion requests "may be subject to an internal investigation prior to completion", "where determined as necessary to protect the platform against fraud", followed by "ID.me reserves the right to decline such requests". [ 4 ] Marketplace reported that Kim said ID.me can keep a user's data for up to three years even after a deletion request. [ 15 ] 2023 and 2026 versions [ edit | edit source ] ID.me Privacy Policy clauses, earlier and current Clause Earlier: Privacy Policy Version 7.1.5, dated December 1, 2023 [ 17 ] Current: Privacy Policy Version 7.1.8, dated November 2, 2026 [ 4 ] Marketing use of information Included [ 17 ] Included [ 4 ] Disclosure or transfer in a corporate transaction Included, in the same two sentences as the current text [ 17 ] Included [ 4 ] Government-verification carve-out [ edit | edit source ] ID.me's Privacy Policy adds after its marketing clause: Please note, if you are using ID.me Services in connection with legal identity verification for a state or federal government agency, or in association with Electronic Prescriptions for Controlled Substance Services, ID.me does not use any Personal Information provided as part of your verification for any type of marketing or promotional purposes related to ID.me Shop without your consent, or unless you otherwise use your ID.me credential for verification with any ID.me customer who is not a state or federal government agency customer, use your ID.me wallet in connection with ID.me Shop, ID.me Jobs, or ID.me Rx, or otherwise opt-in to receiving marketing communications from ID.me. [ 4 ] ID.me's policy says the company "may share" a user's name, date of birth & contact details for reporting with the government agency the user verifies for, & that verifying "constitutes consent" to it. [ 4 ] Terms of Service 10.1.0, dated September 18, 2025 & November 13, 2026, "do not provide consent to marketing calls or text messages". [ 16 ] [ 3 ] The August 18, 2026 IRS help page said ID.me "will not share, sell, rent or trade" personally identifiable information "with other parties, except to verify your identity and eligibility"; [ 18 ] the October 29, 2026 version points readers to "their privacy policies at Login.gov and IDMe". [ 2 ] Login.gov and paying without signing in [ edit | edit source ] The IRS help page last reviewed or updated on October 29, 2026 says that "The U.S. government maintains the Login.gov system", & that taxpayers who cannot verify their identity with one provider should "try the other provider". [ 2 ] The version last reviewed or updated on August 18, 2026 named only ID.me as the sign-in account. [ 18 ] The IRS sign-in page says to "choose ID.me" for anyone who does not have "an SSN, U.S. address, and smartphone, or tablet with a camera", SSN being a Social Security number. [ 1 ] Login.gov is provided by the federal General Services Administration (GSA). [ 19 ] Login.gov's privacy page says a user who creates an account & verifies their identity consents to Login.gov "collecting, using, keeping, and sharing your personal information" as its policies describe, "including to verify your identity and to help detect and prevent fraud". [ 20 ] Login.gov's Rules of Use say customer-support feedback may be used "for other purposes as we see fit, such as for marketing", though Login.gov "will not reveal your personal information outside of the Login.gov service" except "as required by applicable law or as stated elsewhere in these terms". [ 19 ] They also say disputes "shall be governed by federal law" & that no fees are charged for registering or using the service. [ 19 ] In a 2026 blog post, GSA wrote that Login.gov's privacy protections let people access government services "without their information being used for commercial purposes". [ 21 ] Direct Pay, the IRS service for paying taxes from a bank account, lists "No sign-in required"; people who have never filed, or who last filed over six years ago, are told they "can pay another way". [ 6 ] Taxpayers who cannot register online can have a tax return or tax account transcript mailed; the IRS lists "transcripts of past tax returns" & "tax account information" among their tax records. [ 22 ] TreasuryDirect move and Senate letter [ edit | edit source ] ID.me became available for TreasuryDirect logins on September 13, 2026 & replaced the traditional TreasuryDirect login on October 28, 2026. [ 7 ] TreasuryDirect says Login.gov "cannot be used to log in to your TreasuryDirect account", & a user who declines to let ID.me share their verified identity information cannot log in. [ 7 ] Its FAQ states neither TreasuryDirect nor ID.me "sells, rents, or shares your personal information with third parties for marketing or advertising purposes". [ 7 ] An ID.me spokesman wrote to Marketplace , "We do not sell, rent, or trade users’ personal information". [ 15 ] On October 29, 2026, Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., & Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee Ranking Member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., demanded that Treasury halt "a rushed transition" to ID.me for Americans trying to access their savings bonds online. [ 8 ] The senators wrote: Americans should not have to provide sensitive personal information to ID.me as the price of accessing essential government services when a secure government-operated alternative is available [ 8 ] They asked the agencies to delay the ID.me requirement until after the 2027 tax filing deadline. [ 8 ] Their letter, dated October 27, 2026, said federal law requires agencies to implement "a single sign-on trusted identity platform" developed by the General Services Administration, citing 6 U.S.C. § 1523(b)(1)(D). [ 23 ] It said ID.me was awarded a five-year agreement with a ceiling of more than $1 billion for identity verification, authentication, and fraud prevention services. [ 23 ] The letter requested a response by November 9, 2026. [ 23 ] Trade publication Biometric Update reported that two Treasury orders for ID.me subscriptions were placed under "a five-year Treasury blanket purchase agreement for ID.me identity verification and authentication services" with "a ceiling of approximately $1.03 billion", and that "Federal procurement records show about $93 million obligated against the vehicle so far". [ 24 ] An August 31, 2026 memorandum from the Office of Management and Budget , M-26-18, says agencies offering other identity solutions must promote Login.gov as the default option for new account creation "for any user population that Login.gov is able to serve". [ 25 ] The IRS said in an emailed statement, quoted by news site FedScoop, that "Taxpayers can use Login.gov or ID.me" ahead of the 2027 filing season. title: AI is killing All About Berlin
body_text: AI is killing All About Berlin - Nicolas Bouliane N icolas B ouliane Blog Projects Recipes etc. AI is killing All About Berlin Posted on May 26, 2026 Psst! There is an update to this post . This is the traffic to All About Berlin , the website that I run since 2017, and live from since 2020. After 7 years of growth, it has lost 70% 75% of its traffic to Google AI Overviews. When you Googled something, you used to get a link to my website. Now you get a page of ads, then an AI-generated answer trained on my content, then finally a link to my website. This has a devastating impact on traffic. What it means to be first on Google It’s hard to fund my work with only a quarter of my audience. Soon, I will need another way to pay my rent. Instead of writing new guides, I already spend my days preparing for that future. It’s not just about the money. I have poured 8 years of my life into making something good and useful. Strangers’ faces light up when they learn that I run All About Berlin. Local and federal government offices refer people to my guides. The Berlin immigration office uses my data about themselves . It inspired two government portals and a few similar websites in other cities. If my work just get mixed into an AI-generated answer, I lose my voice and my audience. My carefully chosen words lose their meaning. No one shakes my hand and buys me a beer. No one tells me how their citizenship application went. This is not an isolated case. Many website owners have reached out in private to commiserate. Some have paywalled their work. Others have given up and moved on. They keep the websites online, but they no longer update them. It’s just not worth it. It will get worse. Last week, Google has made two announcements: AI-generated answers will replace search results entirely, and they have ads in them. 1 This is the future of the internet. No websites, just a chat box with ads. I don’t know where All About Berlin fits in that future. This was also discussed on Mastodon , Hacker News , LinkedIn and Twitter . If you are affected, reach out . Let me know how you are doing. You are not going through this alone. , Katie Bo Lillis , Sean Lyngaas , Davis Winkie , Zachary Cohen Updated Nov 17, 2026, 10:33 PM ET Published Nov 17, 2026, 10:31 AM ET Updated Nov 17, 2026, 10:33 PM ET PUBLISHED Nov 17, 2026, 10:31 AM ET The National Security Agency (NSA) headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 2010. Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images Federal agencies National security Digital security See all topics Facebook Tweet Email Link Threads Link Copied! Follow The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail. Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. title: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review
body_text: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Skip to content Antitrust Cyber Investments Markets Surveys Buyers Guide Geopolitics Newsletters Subscribe About Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Oct 13, 2026 Editor’s Note: Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, yet finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, according to a working paper by Harvard Ph.D. candidates Fiona Chen and James Stratton covering 718 firms. The paper, a job-market paper with no indication of completed peer review, measures what happens at the human checkpoint once drafting speeds up. Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and Cooley’s redaction agent, still in development with Google Cloud, both keep a lawyer at a comparable checkpoint, and neither announcement reports a measure of that review stage. For eDiscovery, privacy and compliance professionals, the study suggests a measurement approach for legal AI buyers: consider approved work product, revision rates and reviewer time alongside drafting output. It also shows that AI authorship can leave metadata in collaboration systems that records and legal hold programs may need to reach. Watch for a revised version of the paper and for any legal vendor that publishes review-stage figures, keeping in mind that the study examined software, not legal work. Content Assessment: Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review Information - 92% Insight - 90% Relevance - 88% Objectivity - 90% Authority - 92% 90 % Excellent A short percentage-based assessment of the qualitative benefit expressed as a percentage of positive reception of the recent article from ComplexDiscovery OÜ titled, "Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review." News Analysis – Artificial Intelligence Beat Harvard researchers find AI coding agents shifted the bottleneck to code review ComplexDiscovery OÜ Staff Engineers at firms that adopted AI coding agents added about 30 percent more code, but finished work did not measurably rise and getting code through review took 49 percent longer, a Harvard working paper found. In the study’s data, the extra coding produced no detectable rise in finished work, and code review became the bottleneck. Fiona Chen and James Stratton, both Ph.D. candidates at Harvard University, measured that pattern across 725,938 workers at 718 companies. Two legal AI announcements this month, Harvey’s motion-to-dismiss workflow and a court-filing redaction agent Cooley is developing with Google Cloud, place a lawyer at a comparable review step, and neither reports a measure of it. What the Harvard data measured How much weight that pattern can bear depends on where the numbers came from. Chen and Stratton built the study on data from Jellyfish, a company that sells an analytics platform tracking engineering activity, and joined it to LinkedIn employment records collected by Revelio Labs. The sample runs from January 2021 to March 2026 and covers Jellyfish client firms that consented to research use of their data. The paper’s tables list 68.3 million Jira issues, 200.9 million commits, 49.1 million pull requests and 21.3 million calendar events, though only 213 of the 718 firms supplied calendar data. The design is a staggered difference-in-differences comparison, which tracks month by month how outcomes changed at adopting firms against firms that had not yet adopted. A comparison like that is only as good as the reasons adoption dates differed, and here the authors point to a process legal and security teams will recognize, because they sit inside it. The paper says timing was shaped mainly by when firms learned about the tools and by how long procurement took, meaning sourcing, legal and security approvals and pilot programs. One interviewee’s firm approved a tool in about a day; another interviewee put the average approval time at six to 12 months. The authors call those procurement delays plausibly unrelated to how fast a firm was growing, which they argue supports comparing early and late adopters. They acknowledge one known imbalance, that larger firms adopted earlier, and they control for firm size. If some hidden difference remains, the authors say, it would more likely make AI look more productive than it is, not less. A bias in that direction would make the flat output result, if anything, generous to AI. The current version of the paper is dated Aug. 4, 2026, and the first was dated Jan. 7. Chen circulated it as her job-market paper, and nothing in the version reviewed for this article indicates journal acceptance or completed peer review. Her website lists coverage links to The Wall Street Journal and The Economist, and legal trade press picked it up this month, including an Oct. 12 eDiscovery Today post by Doug Austin that relayed an Ars Technica report. Drafts went up and finished issues did not With that provenance in view, the coding results are large. Lines of code added rose by 1,494 per worker-month against a baseline of 5,017, about 30 percent. Commits rose 20 percent, and pull requests, the bundles of code submitted for review, rose 23 percent. The authors note that these estimates capture the added effect of agents at firms that already had AI coding assistants, not the effect of AI from a standing start. Output is where the gain stops. The paper counts finished work as Jira issues resolved, and an issue counts as complete when its code is deployed to production. Agents moved that measure by 0.12 issues per worker-month on a 3.67 baseline, with a standard error of 0.17. That result is statistically indistinguishable from zero, and the 95 percent confidence interval rules out an increase above about 12 percent of the baseline, well short of the 30 percent rise in code written. The authors tested the obvious escape route. If engineers had shifted to larger tasks, a flat issue count would understate real output. So the researchers labeled a 0.5 percent sample of issues by size with GPT-4o and extended those labels to every issue with a text-embedding model. They found no shift in average issue size, and pull requests did not grow larger either, which the authors use to set aside the simplest explanation for what happened in review. Where the shortfall shows up: the review queue The paper locates the shortfall in code review. The time from pull request submission to merge rose 3.45 days on a 7.03-day baseline, a 49 percent increase. The share of pull requests receiving a formal change request increased by about 12 percentage points from a baseline of 13 percent, nearly doubling, and review comments per pull request rose 35 percent. The share of workers doing any code review rose 14 percent from a base of about 29 percent, while the share writing code showed no measurable change. AI review tools did not remove the bottleneck. By March 2026, nearly 80 percent of the firms had used one, yet AI generated only 23.3 percent of review comments, and only 10.8 percent of pull requests received even one AI comment. The authors write that the bottleneck persists after firms adopt such tools. The paper’s interviews show what that looks like on a team: a junior software engineer described a project where only one senior engineer could approve changes and could review the interviewee’s code only once a week. “After some outages that were caused by AI-generated commits, there were also new rules requiring senior engineer approval for AI-generated code, which created even more review bottlenecks,” the engineer said, in a quote the authors say they lightly edited for clarity. That account fits the model the authors use to explain their numbers, which has two channels. In the first, faster drafting sends more code to a fixed pool of reviewers, a problem that moving labor into review can largely relieve. In the second, the rise in change requests and comments, which faster drafting alone does not explain, reads through the model as a sign of lower-quality drafts. That problem, the authors say, would require better technology. Anyone buying an agent should care which channel dominates, because the two call for different spending. Employment did not move either Nor did the coding gains show up as job cuts. The estimates rule out a decline in overall employment larger than 2.9 percent. A noisier estimate rules out a decline in engineering employment larger than 13.8 percent. The authors caution that these are short-run effects measured in partial equilibrium, which could mask job losses at competing firms, and that the assistant estimate for engineering employment shows upward pre-trends that make it hard to read causally. Legal AI tools are designed around a similar checkpoint Those software results arrive as legal AI tools adopt a related design, and the Harvey and Cooley announcements both follow it: automate a first pass, then keep a lawyer at the checkpoint. Harvey’s workflow, co-developed with LexisNexis and announced Oct. 7, is the drafting case. Harvey says the multi-step process of reading the complaint, researching and drafting a motion to dismiss “commonly takes 40 to 50+ hours of work” and that its tool produces the research and a first draft “in a matter of hours.” The announcement describes “human checkpoints at the moments where a lawyer’s judgment matters most,” but it does not state how long lawyers spend at those checkpoints or how long it takes to reach a motion ready to file. Cooley’s Oct. 8 announcement applies the same posture to a different task, since its agent recommends redactions rather than drafting arguments. Cooley says the agent is still being developed and that attorneys make all redaction determinations before a filing goes to the court, which puts the human checkpoint at the last step before submission. As ComplexDiscovery reported Oct. 10, the announcement carries no error rate. For a motion filed in federal court, the checkpoint is a legal duty rather than a design choice. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 11(b), an attorney presenting a motion certifies several things about it to the best of the attorney’s knowledge, information and belief, “formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances.” Its legal contentions must be “warranted by existing law or by a nonfrivolous argument for extending, modifying, or reversing existing law or for establishing new law.” Its factual contentions must have evidentiary support or, if specifically so identified, be likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for further investigation or discovery. A first draft can arrive in hours, but that inquiry stays with the attorney, and the software evidence raises the possibility that review could absorb some of the drafting savings. The paper’s method carries a second lesson, this one for information governance teams. The researchers identified agent use partly from traces inside the firms’ own systems, including bot accounts tied to AI tools and signatures such as “Co-authored-by” lines in commit messages and pull request descriptions. AI authorship can leave its own metadata trail in collaboration systems. That trail is a record that a retention schedule and a legal hold may need to reach. None of this means legal work will behave like software, and the limits of the comparison matter. Document review is not code review, a production is not a pull request, and Chen and Stratton studied no legal work. A separate National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, revised in September 2026, reports a similar falloff using data on over 500,000 GitHub developers. Its authors, Mert Demirer, Leon Musolff and Liyuan Yang, found a 240 percent cumulative rise in commits from autonomous agents shrinking to 30 percent for actual releases. That paper carries its own disclosure: Demirer and Musolff each previously held a postdoctoral research position at Microsoft, which owns GitHub, and each now works as a paid research consultant for the company. Two software studies point to a pattern in software, not a finding about law firms. Document review offers a partial precedent Discovery practitioners have argued a version of this question before, and Austin’s post draws that comparison. He wrote that discovery has seen a similar debate over generative AI review, with some practitioners saying manual validation offsets the gains and others, including him, saying statistical sampling of the kind used in predictive coding is enough. For coding agents, though, he wrote that the extra review time may be warranted, since code that is 90 percent correct can still fail to run. His comparison suggests a useful split between two kinds of legal output. Population-level work such as first-pass relevance review can be validated by sampling. A single filing is different, because its citations, factual assertions and sensitive data generally need direct examination when one fabricated citation or one missed Social Security number is the failure. Buyers can turn that split into a test. Ask a vendor which kind of output its agent produces, then ask for the downstream measure rather than the drafting one: hours from upload to an approved work product, the share of drafts a reviewing attorney sent back and reviewer time per matter. Budget review capacity before scaling drafting volume, and log what reviewers change, because that log shows whether the bottleneck is volume or quality. Read the paper’s limits as closely as its findings Those questions apply to the paper’s own sourcing, too. The data partner has a commercial interest in the subject, and the relationship runs deeper than a data license. Jellyfish describes itself as an “AI Impact Platform,” and the authors have published on its blog: a Sept. 25, 2025, post by Chen and Stratton described itself as “part of our ongoing work with Jellyfish.” The paper thanks the Jellyfish team “for their partnership” and states that Jellyfish reviewed the manuscript only to check for proprietary disclosure, not for scientific content, and that the conclusions are the authors’. Its funders were the Stripe Economics of AI Fellowship, a Harvard Kennedy School program on wealth distribution and the Schmidt Sciences AI at Work Program. Jellyfish has also promoted an earlier version of the work. A Jan. 28 post on its blog by Nicholas Arcolano called it “a preliminary version of a new paper from our collaborators at Harvard Economics, Fiona Chen and James Stratton,” based on 100,000 software engineers across 500 companies. That post, and a March 17 Jellyfish press release after it, reported that AI was making coding faster and that “code quality doesn’t seem to be suffering.” The August version, built on a larger sample running through March 2026, reads the near-doubling in change requests through its model as a possible sign of lower draft quality. The two descriptions rest on different versions and samples, so they need not conflict, but a reader relying on Jellyfish’s summary would miss the quality question the current paper raises. The paper also carries small internal inconsistencies that do not touch the headline agent estimates. Its introduction rounds the sample to about 700 firms and 700,000 workers, and its main text describes 17 interviews where an appendix describes 21. Other limits are structural rather than clerical: the underlying data are proprietary, and use of AI tools through individual licenses goes unrecorded. None of those caveats overturns the central result, though the March 2026 data cutoff means a revision could move the figures. What the paper offers is a standard the two legal announcements discussed here do not meet: named authors, a disclosed method, a confidence interval and a measured checkpoint. If an agent cuts 40 hours of research and drafting to a few, how many of those hours reappear on the desk of the lawyer who signs the motion? [exclude_from_rss] [taq_review] [/exclude_from_rss] Industry News - Technology Beat Slush 2026 brings a smaller, sharper bet on European startups to Helsinki ComplexDiscovery Staff Finland marks the International Day for Failure today, a custom that began in 2010 when a student group at Aalto University proposed celebrating failure instead of lamenting it, Yle reported. Five weeks from now, a startup event that Aalto says its student community helped spark will test how far that appetite for risk can carry European technology. Slush 2026 runs Nov. 18 and 19 at Messukeskus, the Helsinki Expo and Convention Centre, with Investor Day and a founders' program on Nov. 17. The organizers have branded this edition a bet on Europe. The program published so far pairs that slogan with a sitting head of state, a European commissioner, a deliberately smaller crowd and a rebuilt startup competition. ComplexDiscovery will attend and report from Slush for the second consecutive year. A smaller crowd, by design Behind that program sits an unusual organizer. Slush is a not-for-profit owned by the Startup Foundation, a Finnish foundation that receives most of any profit the event makes, according to the organization's own description. It began in 2008 as a 250-person gathering. Its 2026 FAQ projects 5,800 startups and 3,300 investors, and its homepage advertises 12,000-plus attendees, 200-plus speakers and 600-plus side events across what Slush calls Slush Week. Students and recent graduates run the operation, supported by a volunteer corps that Slush's own pages put at between 1,600 and 1,800 people. Selectivity runs through the whole event. Slush says it does not pay speakers and speakers do not pay it, and every company seeking to attend must complete an application that the Slush team reviews personally. This year the headcount is smaller on purpose. When Slush named Noora Saksa chief executive on Jan. 27, it said the 2026 event would cut its audience by 10 percent to better serve its core of early-stage startups. Personal recommendations will tailor the experience to each company's growth stage, the announcement said. Saksa, who first joined Slush as a volunteer in 2021, framed the stakes in economic terms. "Startups are our best bet for GDP growth in Europe," she said in the announcement. She also set a goal there of at least two European technology companies in the global top 10 by market capitalization by 2050. Announcements that set the 2026 program The same rethinking reached Slush 100, the pitch competition whose earlier formats date to the event's 2008 founding year. This year's winner receives €500,000 with no equity taken, replacing the €1 million investment from venture firms that winners received from 2022 through 2025, according to Slush. "A flat €1M at a fixed valuation and standard terms no longer fits most startups," Saksa said. Dropping the investor-led model also opens the contest to founders from outside Europe and the U.S., Slush said. From over 1,400 applicants, Slush named 100 companies and then 20 semifinalists, who pitch on the Startup Stage on the first morning before three finalists compete for the prize. Slush also created Slush 20 Under 20, a program for builders who have not yet turned 20. The first list, published this month, names 20 people from over a dozen countries, the youngest of them 15, who together have raised over €10 million from venture investors, according to Slush. Anthropic, Index Ventures and Sifted support the program. "Europe's first €1T company could be founded by a teenager," Saksa said. Off the stage, Slush has changed address. Since July, it has worked from Kasvutalo, or Growth House, in Helsinki's Kamppi district. That is the new name Slush and the startup community Founders House gave to Sähkötalo, an Alvar Aalto building completed in 1973 as head office of the city's electricity utility. A Sept. 2 release counts about 50 companies and communities in the building, around 30 of them startups, investors and startup communities. "Every leading tech hub in Europe has its own startup district," Saksa said in the release. Who is on stage, and why practitioners should listen Those year-round moves feed a November program whose speakers are now partly public. Slush has published what it calls its first batch of 2026 speakers and says the stage program is full. The roster includes two officeholders, Alexander Stubb, Finland's 13th president, and Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European commissioner for startups, research and innovation. It also features Jessica Livingston, co-founder of Y Combinator; David Silver, former lead of DeepMind's reinforcement learning team and now chief executive of Ineffable Intelligence; and Matthew Prince, co-founder and chief executive of Cloudflare. Beyond Prince, cybersecurity professionals will find two security-company founders on the list. Eoin Hinchy ran security operations for 15 years at companies including eBay, PayPal and DocuSign before co-founding Tines, according to his Slush biography, and Madeline Lawrence is co-founder of Aikido Security. Legal technology arrives through Ross McNairn, whose company Wordsmith builds AI software for corporate legal departments. Paolo Fois of Lexroom is also listed, and his Slush biography says over 15 percent of Italian legal proceedings pass through Lexroom, without explaining how that share is measured. The third legal name is Joshua Browder of DoNotPay, whose speaker biography describes the service as "the world's first robot lawyer." That phrase has a regulatory history. In a September 2024 complaint, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) alleged that DoNotPay did not test whether its AI lawyer service performed at the level of a human lawyer. The commission voted 5-0 on Jan. 16, 2025, to approve a final order, which the agency announced Feb. 11. The order requires DoNotPay to pay $193,000 and bars it from claiming its service performs like a real lawyer without sufficient evidence to back that up, according to the FTC. For eDiscovery and information governance teams weighing AI vendors, the lesson reaches beyond one company, because a federal regulator has already required one legal AI provider to support its performance claims with evidence. Every vendor claim heard in Helsinki deserves the same scrutiny. Company law has its own advocates on the program. Simon Schaefer, Iwona Anna Biernat and Vojtech Horna appear for EU-INC, a movement Schaefer co-founded in late 2024, according to his Slush biography. The European Commission has since proposed an EU-level company form under the EU Inc. name, which it describes as optional and digital by default. In its March 18 release presenting the proposed regulation, the Commission called on the European Parliament and the Council to agree on it by the end of 2026. In Parliament, the file has hit a delay: a vote in the legal affairs committee planned for Oct. 8 was postponed, with a new date around Oct. 19, Agence Europe and Table.Briefings reported. Attendees planning their days should know that Slush's public pages, as reviewed Oct. 13, list speakers and opening hours but not a session-by-session schedule. The media page says the agenda launches in the fall, and for 2025 Slush published its full stage agenda on the Slush Platform, the same online tool attendees use to book meetings. The main event opens with the Slush 2026 Opening Show at 10 a.m. Nov. 18. What Slush's own research claims, and what it cannot Whatever the final schedule, Slush's sales pitch rests on research it publishes itself. The Slush Startup Report 2026, released in May with data partner Dealroom, compared 2,108 European companies that first attended Slush in 2022, 2023 or 2024 with 229,866 European peers matched on founding year, country and growth stage. Every company in the Slush group was founded in 2016 or later and had not reached a Series B round when it first attended. After that first attendance, 26.4 percent of the Slush companies raised institutional capital, against 7.5 percent of benchmark peers measured over what the report calls the equivalent post-2022 period, which the report presents as a 3.5-times premium. On investor quality, 5.6 percent of the Slush companies were backed by a fund in the top 0.1 percent of Dealroom's global investor ranking, against 0.8 percent of peers. Readers should weigh those figures against the report's own caveats. The two groups start in different places. Nearly half the Slush companies, 48 percent, had no institutional backing when they first attended, while 89 percent of the benchmark companies were bootstrapped. The report acknowledges that already-backed companies raise money at higher rates in both groups, which is why its aggregate premium exceeds the premium within either subgroup. Among companies with no outside funding at first attendance, 17 percent of the Slush group raised venture capital afterward, against 5.6 percent of peers. Among those already backed, the rates were 35 percent and 23.2 percent. Its methodology also concedes that matching cannot account for how ambitious, well connected or ready to raise the attending companies already were. The findings are correlational, the report says, and its matching "cannot separate who attends from what attending does." The report closes by telling readers the data suggests the trip is worth taking, which marks it as research produced by the organization that sells the tickets. Two other Slush studies frame this year's message. In a February survey of 310 Finnish founders and operators, 53 percent of respondents said they were considering or actively planning to move business operations abroad, and 56 percent named general attitudes and culture as obstacles to growth. Slush says the respondents represent about 10 percent of Finland's active startups. It sent 10 reform proposals to Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who said his government would review them in its April budget framework discussions. An October 2025 study with Dealroom and Accel found that 68 of 459 former full-time Slush staff members, or 15 percent, had gone on to found companies. Finland's stage carries geopolitical weight Slush makes its case for European founders from a city whose venues carry their own history. Investor Day on Nov. 17 takes place at Alvar Aalto's Finlandia Hall on Töölö Bay, where Slush's Investor Day page promises over 2,000 venture investors. Leaders of 35 states gathered there for the 1975 Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. They signed the Helsinki Final Act on the summit's last day, Aug. 1, 1975, according to the Finnish Heritage Agency and Switzerland's National Museum. Finland's own position has shifted since then. It became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, and Stubb took office as president on March 1, 2024. Helsinki also hosts the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, which counts 35 participating states, all of them members of the EU or NATO. For security teams with Finnish operations, the country's Cybersecurity Act, which implements the EU's NIS 2 Directive, began phasing in obligations for covered entities on April 8, 2025, according to Traficom. Those entities then had until May 8 of that year to register and until July 8 to establish risk-management procedures, although public administration entities received no separate transition period for that risk-management obligation, the agency said. The technology record behind the event runs deep. Linus Torvalds, who enrolled at the University of Helsinki in 1988, started work on the kernel later named Linux in the fall of 1991, according to the Computer History Museum. Satellite company ICEYE, whose co-founder Rafal Modrzewski is on the 2026 speaker list, launched its technology in Finland and now serves defense clients worldwide, according to Slush's Helsinki page. What ComplexDiscovery will be watching ComplexDiscovery's coverage from Helsinki last year followed similar threads, examining how Harvey scaled domain-specific legal AI, how the BORDERLAND gathering approached dual-use defense technology, and what data provenance meant for information governance teams. Four threads stand out for 2026. The first is evidence: when legal AI founders cite adoption or accuracy figures on stage, record the claim and its basis, because statements made on stage can resurface in sales materials and procurement files. The second is corporate form: if EU Inc. advances, counterparties incorporated under a new EU-level form are likely to raise registry and records questions for diligence and discovery teams, in this publication's assessment. The third is resilience, because defense, space and infrastructure companies on the program, ICEYE among them, work in sectors where cybersecurity, export controls and data sovereignty overlap. The fourth is timing. Two of the 20 Slush 100 semifinalists build products around sensitive information: Foundation Clinic, which Slush lists as "the health-data platform for European healthcare," and GraceX, pitched as "your company's brain" with privacy built in. In this publication's assessment, companies at that stage are where security, information governance and discovery needs first take shape, which makes Slush a place for providers in those fields to see what early-stage clients will ask of them. The International Day for Failure, as Yle describes it, aims to take the stigma out of mistakes so that people feel free to create and innovate. Slush is now asking Europe to place a larger bet on its own builders, while its own research concedes it cannot separate the founders who walk in from what the room itself does for them. Which claims made on Helsinki's stages next month will your organization be ready to verify before it relies on them? For cybersecurity, data privacy, regulatory compliance and eDiscovery professionals, the more telling names include founders from Tines, Aikido Security, Wordsmith and Lexroom. They share the program with DoNotPay's Joshua Browder, whose company operates under a 2025 Federal Trade Commission order barring unsupported claims that its service performs like a real lawyer. Organizers of the EU-INC movement will also speak while the Commission's EU Inc. proposal remains before Parliament and the Council. ComplexDiscovery will report from Slush for a second consecutive year, testing which on-stage claims, from legal AI adoption figures to the organizer's own fundraising research, arrive with evidence attached. [exclude_from_rss] [taq_review] [/exclude_from_rss] Industry News - Technology Beat Slush 2026 brings a smaller, sharper bet on European startups to Helsinki ComplexDiscovery Staff Finland marks the International Day for Failure today, a custom that began in 2010 when a student group at Aalto University proposed celebrating failure instead of lamenting it, Yle reported. Five weeks from now, a startup event that Aalto says its student community helped spark will test how far that appetite for risk can carry European technology. Slush 2026 runs Nov. 18 and 19 at Messukeskus, the Helsinki Expo and Convention Centre, with Investor Day and a founders' program on Nov. 17. The organizers have branded this edition a bet on Europe. The program published so far pairs that slogan with a sitting head of state, a European commissioner, a deliberately smaller crowd and a rebuilt startup competition. ComplexDiscovery will attend and report from Slush for the second consecutive year. A smaller crowd, by design Behind that program sits an unusual organizer. Slush is a not-for-profit owned by the Startup Foundation, a Finnish foundation that receives most of any profit the event makes, according to the organization's own description. It began in 2008 as a 250-person gathering. Its 2026 FAQ projects 5,800 startups and 3,300 investors, and its homepage advertises 12,000-plus attendees, 200-plus speakers and 600-plus side events across what Slush calls Slush Week. Students and recent graduates run the operation, supported by a volunteer corps that Slush's own pages put at between 1,600 and 1,800 people. Selectivity runs through the whole event. Slush says it does not pay speakers and speakers do not pay it, and every company seeking to attend must complete an application that the Slush team reviews personally. This year the headcount is smaller on purpose. When Slush named Noora Saksa chief executive on Jan. 27, it said the 2026 event would cut its audience by 10 percent to better serve its core of early-stage startups. Personal recommendations will tailor the experience to each company's growth stage, the announcement said. Saksa, who first joined Slush as a volunteer in 2021, framed the stakes in economic terms. "Startups are our best bet for GDP growth in Europe," she said in the announcement. She also set a goal there of at least two European technology companies in the global top 10 by market capitalization by 2050. Announcements that set the 2026 program The same rethinking reached Slush 100, the pitch competition whose earlier formats date to the event's 2008 founding year. This year's winner receives €500,000 with no equity taken, replacing the €1 million investment from venture firms that winners received from 2022 through 2025, according to Slush. "A flat €1M at a fixed valuation and standard terms no longer fits most startups," Saksa said. Dropping the investor-led model also opens the contest to founders from outside Europe and the U.S., Slush said. From over 1,400 applicants, Slush named 100 companies and then 20 semifinalists, who pitch on the Startup Stage on the first morning before three finalists compete for the prize. Slush also created Slush 20 Under 20, a program for builders who have not yet turned 20. The first list, published this month, names 20 people from over a dozen countries, the youngest of them 15, who together have raised over €10 million from venture investors, according to Slush. Anthropic, Index Ventures and Sifted support the program. "Europe's first €1T company could be founded by a teenager," Saksa said. Off the stage, Slush has changed address. Since July, it has worked from Kasvutalo, or Growth House, in Helsinki's Kamppi district. That is the new name Slush and the startup community Founders House gave to Sähkötalo, an Alvar Aalto building completed in 1973 as head office of the city's electricity utility. A Sept. 2 release counts about 50 companies and communities in the building, around 30 of them startups, investors and startup communities. "Every leading tech hub in Europe has its own startup district," Saksa said in the release. Who is on stage, and why practitioners should listen Those year-round moves feed a November program whose speakers are now partly public. Slush has published what it calls its first batch of 2026 speakers and says the stage program is full. The roster includes two officeholders, Alexander Stubb, Finland's 13th president, and Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European commissioner for startups, research and innovation. It also features Jessica Livingston, co-founder of Y Combinator; David Silver, former lead of DeepMind's reinforcement learning team and now chief executive of Ineffable Intelligence; and Matthew Prince, co-founder and chief executive of Cloudflare. Beyond Prince, cybersecurity professionals will find two security-company founders on the list. Eoin Hinchy ran security operations for 15 years at companies including eBay, PayPal and DocuSign before co-founding Tines, according to his Slush biography, and Madeline Lawrence is co-founder of Aikido Security. Legal technology arrives through Ross McNairn, whose company Wordsmith builds AI software for corporate legal departments. Paolo Fois of Lexroom is also listed, and his Slush biography says over 15 percent of Italian legal proceedings pass through Lexroom, without explaining how that share is measured. The third legal name is Joshua Browder of DoNotPay, whose speaker biography describes the service as "the world's first robot lawyer." That phrase has a regulatory history. In a September 2024 complaint, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) alleged that DoNotPay did not test whether its AI lawyer service performed at the level of a human lawyer. The commission voted 5-0 on Jan. 16, 2025, to approve a final order, which the agency announced Feb. 11. The order requires DoNotPay to pay $193,000 and bars it from claiming its service performs like a real lawyer without sufficient evidence to back that up, according to the FTC. For eDiscovery and information governance teams weighing AI vendors, the lesson reaches beyond one company, because a federal regulator has already required one legal AI provider to support its performance claims with evidence. Every vendor claim heard in Helsinki deserves the same scrutiny. Company law has its own advocates on the program. Simon Schaefer, Iwona Anna Biernat and Vojtech Horna appear for EU-INC, a movement Schaefer co-founded in late 2024, according to his Slush biography. The European Commission has since proposed an EU-level company form under the EU Inc. name, which it describes as optional and digital by default. In its March 18 release presenting the proposed regulation, the Commission called on the European Parliament and the Council to agree on it by the end of 2026. In Parliament, the file has hit a delay: a vote in the legal affairs committee planned for Oct. 8 was postponed, with a new date around Oct. 19, Agence Europe and Table.Briefings reported. Attendees planning their days should know that Slush's public pages, as reviewed Oct. 13, list speakers and opening hours but not a session-by-session schedule. The media page says the agenda launches in the fall, and for 2025 Slush published its full stage agenda on the Slush Platform, the same online tool attendees use to book meetings. The main event opens with the Slush 2026 Opening Show at 10 a.m. Nov. 18. What Slush's own research claims, and what it cannot Whatever the final schedule, Slush's sales pitch rests on research it publishes itself. The Slush Startup Report 2026, released in May with data partner Dealroom, compared 2,108 European companies that first attended Slush in 2022, 2023 or 2024 with 229,866 European peers matched on founding year, country and growth stage. Every company in the Slush group was founded in 2016 or later and had not reached a Series B round when it first attended. After that first attendance, 26.4 percent of the Slush companies raised institutional capital, against 7.5 percent of benchmark peers measured over what the report calls the equivalent post-2022 period, which the report presents as a 3.5-times premium. On investor quality, 5.6 percent of the Slush companies were backed by a fund in the top 0.1 percent of Dealroom's global investor ranking, against 0.8 percent of peers. Readers should weigh those figures against the report's own caveats. The two groups start in different places. Nearly half the Slush companies, 48 percent, had no institutional backing when they first attended, while 89 percent of the benchmark companies were bootstrapped. The report acknowledges that already-backed companies raise money at higher rates in both groups, which is why its aggregate premium exceeds the premium within either subgroup. Among companies with no outside funding at first attendance, 17 percent of the Slush group raised venture capital afterward, against 5.6 percent of peers. Among those already backed, the rates were 35 percent and 23.2 percent. Its methodology also concedes that matching cannot account for how ambitious, well connected or ready to raise the attending companies already were. The findings are correlational, the report says, and its matching "cannot separate who attends from what attending does." The report closes by telling readers the data suggests the trip is worth taking, which marks it as research produced by the organization that sells the tickets. Two other Slush studies frame this year's message. In a February survey of 310 Finnish founders and operators, 53 percent of respondents said they were considering or actively planning to move business operations abroad, and 56 percent named general attitudes and culture as obstacles to growth. Slush says the respondents represent about 10 percent of Finland's active startups. It sent 10 reform proposals to Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who said his government would review them in its April budget framework discussions. An October 2025 study with Dealroom and Accel found that 68 of 459 former full-time Slush staff members, or 15 percent, had gone on to found companies. Finland's stage carries geopolitical weight Slush makes its case for European founders from a city whose venues carry their own history. Investor Day on Nov. 17 takes place at Alvar Aalto's Finlandia Hall on Töölö Bay, where Slush's Investor Day page promises over 2,000 venture investors. Leaders of 35 states gathered there for the 1975 Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe. They signed the Helsinki Final Act on the summit's last day, Aug. 1, 1975, according to the Finnish Heritage Agency and Switzerland's National Museum. Finland's own position has shifted since then. It became NATO's 31st member on April 4, 2023, and Stubb took office as president on March 1, 2024. Helsinki also hosts the European Centre of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats, which counts 35 participating states, all of them members of the EU or NATO. For security teams with Finnish operations, the country's Cybersecurity Act, which implements the EU's NIS 2 Directive, began phasing in obligations for covered entities on April 8, 2025, according to Traficom. Those entities then had until May 8 of that year to register and until July 8 to establish risk-management procedures, although public administration entities received no separate transition period for that risk-management obligation, the agency said. The technology record behind the event runs deep. Linus Torvalds, who enrolled at the University of Helsinki in 1988, started work on the kernel later named Linux in the fall of 1991, according to the Computer History Museum. Satellite company ICEYE, whose co-founder Rafal Modrzewski is on the 2026 speaker list, launched its technology in Finland and now serves defense clients worldwide, according to Slush's Helsinki page. What ComplexDiscovery will be watching ComplexDiscovery's coverage from Helsinki last year followed similar threads, examining how Harvey scaled domain-specific legal AI, how the BORDERLAND gathering approached dual-use defense technology, and what data provenance meant for information governance teams. Four threads stand out for 2026. The first is evidence: when legal AI founders cite adoption or accuracy figures on stage, record the claim and its basis, because statements made on stage can resurface in sales materials and procurement files. The second is corporate form: if EU Inc. advances, counterparties incorporated under a new EU-level form are likely to raise registry and records questions for diligence and discovery teams, in this publication's assessment. The third is resilience, because defense, space and infrastructure companies on the program, ICEYE among them, work in sectors where cybersecurity, export controls and data sovereignty overlap. The fourth is timing. Two of the 20 Slush 100 semifinalists build products around sensitive information: Foundation Clinic, which Slush lists as "the health-data platform for European healthcare," and GraceX, pitched as "your company's brain" with privacy built in. In this publication's assessment, companies at that stage are where security, information governance and discovery needs first take shape, which makes Slush a place for providers in those fields to see what early-stage clients will ask of them. The International Day for Failure, as Yle describes it, aims to take the stigma out of mistakes so that people feel free to create and innovate. Slush is now asking Europe to place a larger bet on its own builders, while its own research concedes it cannot separate the founders who walk in from what the room itself does for them. Which claims made on Helsinki's stages next month will your organization be ready to verify before it relies on them? [exclude_from_rss] [taq_review] [/exclude_from_rss] Event Calendar The 2026 Event Horizon: Early Outlook for eDiscovery, AI, and European Innovation ComplexDiscovery Staff As the professional landscape for data discovery and legal technology continues to evolve, the 2026 event calendar offers early evidence of an accelerating convergence between eDiscovery, artificial intelligence, and Europe’s leadership in digital governance. While this preview is not exhaustive, it provides a practical point of reference for professionals engaged in law, technology, and information management as they assess their strategic priorities and learning opportunities for the year ahead. The Shifting Center: eDiscovery Meets AI Across continents, the pipeline of 2026 conferences and summits points to one clear trend: artificial intelligence is rapidly reshaping the conversation, from automated review and advanced analytics to risk management, data strategy, and legal innovation. Traditional benchmarks such as Legalweek in New York, ILTACON in Nashville, and Relativity Fest in Chicago remain anchor points for eDiscovery practitioners in North America, serving as forums for technology launches, best practices, and discussions on the shifting regulatory landscape. At the same time, U.S. cyber risk series such as the NetDiligence Cyber Risk Summits—scheduled for Miami Beach, Toronto, San Diego, and Philadelphia—continue to support lawyers and technologists at the frontline of incident response, insurance, and digital forensics. Europe: At the Forefront of AI and Legal Innovation For professionals seeking global perspectives and direct connection to the heart of regulatory change, the 2026 calendar’s European segment is especially compelling. A suite of focused programs—spanning the Nordics, Baltics, Western Europe, and key legal and digital hubs—demonstrates the region’s expanding influence over the future of law and technology: Latitude59 (Tallinn, Estonia): Ground zero for Baltic innovation, with deep dives into startup ecosystems and legal tech. CyCon (Tallinn, Estonia): A critical juncture for cyber conflict, AI-aided defense strategies, and transatlantic security. Slush 2026 (Helsinki, Finland): Europe’s flagship for startup culture, technology ventures, and the frontiers of AI and governance. DigitalEurope Masters of Digital (Brussels, Belgium): A pan-European forum shaping policy and regulation for artificial intelligence, data, and innovation. Legal Geek Europe (Amsterdam, Netherlands): Celebrated for its fresh approach to legal tech and regulatory trends. Dublin Tech Summit (Dublin, Ireland): Merging data, fintech, and next-gen technologies in an EU context. LegalTechTalk (London, UK): Focusing on AI’s accelerating impact on law, digital transformation, and European compliance. Relativity Fest (London, UK): As eDiscovery’s epicenter in Europe, the London edition stands out for its focus on advanced technologies and regulatory developments. Legal Geek Growth (London, UK): Mapping growth trajectories for tech-savvy legal teams and providers. Legal Operations Exchange (London, UK): A gathering for ops leadership, process improvement, and technology strategy within legal environments. ILTA Evolve EU (Barcelona, Spain): Bringing together international legal technologists to discuss emerging tools and governance. World Agentic AI Summit (Berlin, Germany): Highlighting the road ahead for responsible and agentic AI in law and business. Events are set against the backdrop of established European capitals and tech hubs—including Tallinn, Helsinki, Amsterdam, Dublin, Berlin, Barcelona, and London—reflecting the continent’s vital leadership role not only within the EU but as providers of global insight into data policy, AI ethics, and cross-border eDiscovery. What’s Ahead: Adapting to Change This early listing is designed as a living resource, subject to updates as additional programs, dates, and venues are announced and as organizers introduce dedicated tracks and specialized workshops in response to new developments. It is clear that as digital transformation accelerates, Europe is emerging as a nexus for both regulatory leadership and practical innovation, particularly within eDiscovery and AI-infused legal practice. For data discovery professionals—and those advancing the intersection of law, information, and artificial intelligence—the coming year promises an unprecedented array of opportunities for learning, networking, and collaborative influence. Staying current with evolving event calendars will be essential, whether tracking shifting timelines or tapping into new forums driving the future of legal and data governance across the continent and beyond. As 2026 approaches, forward-looking professionals in eDiscovery, AI, and European legal technology have much to anticipate—and even more to actively shape.
