title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
body_text: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest | ScienceDaily Skip to main content Your source for the latest research news Follow: Facebook X/Twitter Subscribe: RSS Feeds Newsletter New! Sign up for our free email newsletter . Science News from research organizations Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest Date: November 11, 2026 Source: American Heart Association Summary: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation. Share: Facebook Twitter Pinterest LinkedIN Email FULL STORY Popular energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising heart health concerns after researchers uncovered strikingly higher rates of reported cardiac arrest and heart attacks, particularly among young adults. Credit: Shutterstock Energy drinks and stimulant supplements are raising new concerns about heart health after researchers discovered a striking pattern in reports of serious cardiovascular emergencies. Products containing caffeine and other stimulants appeared far more frequently in reports of cardiac arrest, heart attacks, and other heart problems than products without these ingredients. The findings were particularly concerning among younger adults. People ages 18 to 34 accounted for a substantial share of the reported heart problems involving caffeinated products, according to independent, preliminary research presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2026. Researchers emphasized that the findings do not establish that energy drinks or stimulant supplements caused these medical emergencies. However, the unusually high frequency of certain cardiovascular events in FDA safety reports suggests that these widely available products deserve closer examination. Growing Concerns About Energy Drinks and Heart Health The energy drink industry has expanded rapidly, with sales more than doubling over the past decade and exceeding $20 billion in 2024. Despite their popularity, scientists still have limited information about the cardiovascular effects of energy drinks and supplements containing stimulants. Existing evidence suggests that consuming large amounts of caffeine can harm the cardiovascular system. Medical professionals have also documented cases of arrhythmias (irregular heart rhythms) and sudden cardiac death following the consumption of these products. Some of these incidents involved young adults who had no previously identified risk factors for heart disease. A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease indicates that most adults can generally consume up to 400 mg of caffeine daily without significant safety concerns (the equivalent of up to 5, 8-ounce cups of regular black caffeinated coffee). However, caffeine concentrations can differ dramatically between products. Certain energy drinks provide up to three times as much caffeine per fluid ounce as brewed coffee, while some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times the concentration found in coffee. Another concern involves how these products are regulated. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) classifies energy drinks and stimulant supplements as foods or dietary supplements rather than medications. As a result, they are not subject to the same safety testing requirements that medications must meet before entering the market. "These products are marketed as everyday pick-me-ups and sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk," said study author Sai Samayamanthula, a fourth-year medical student at the University of Virginia School of Medicine in Charlottesville, Virginia. "For many healthy people, if these products are consumed occasionally, the risk is probably small. However, individuals who consume energy drinks or other stimulant-containing supplements regularly can quickly exceed the recommended daily limit for caffeine, so it's important for people to know that there may be a risk of cardiovascular harm with these products." FDA Reports Reveal Striking Differences in Cardiac Events To investigate possible cardiovascular safety concerns, researchers examined a federal database containing reports of suspected adverse reactions to foods and dietary supplements. They compared products containing caffeine and other stimulants with products that did not contain these ingredients. The comparison group included commonly consumed products such as soft drinks, smoothies, vitamins, protein bars, and meal replacement shakes. Researchers examined reports involving people ages 13 and older submitted between 2017 and 2025. Several differences stood out in the analysis: Cardiac arrest: Reports involving caffeine and stimulant products were approximately 11 times more likely to mention cardiac arrest than reports involving products without these ingredients. Heart attacks: Heart attacks appeared about 4.5 times more frequently in reports associated with energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Abnormal heart rhythms: Reports involving stimulant products were roughly four times more likely to include ventricular arrhythmias (abnormal rhythm in the heart's lower pumping chambers) or heart palpitations. Other cardiovascular symptoms: The researchers also identified higher reporting frequencies for rapid heart rate (nearly 3 times more often), chest pain (2.71 times more often) and fainting (about 2 times more often). Young adults: Approximately 45% of cardiovascular event reports involving caffeine and stimulant products concerned adults between ages 18 and 34. Men and women: Comparable patterns appeared in reports submitted for both sexes. These differences describe how frequently certain medical problems appeared within the FDA reports. They do not mean that people consuming energy drinks face an 11 times greater actual risk of cardiac arrest or a 4.5 times greater risk of having a heart attack. "Our findings support the case for more systematic safety monitoring of caffeine- and stimulant-containing products. In addition, healthcare professionals should remember to ask their younger patients who have palpitations, chest pain, or fainting spells if they recently or regularly consume these products," Samayamanthula said. Why Young Adults May Be Particularly Vulnerable One of the most notable findings was the large proportion of cardiovascular reports involving younger adults. Researchers have not yet determined why the connection between stimulant products and reported heart problems appeared so frequently in this age group. Several explanations are possible. Younger consumers may use energy drinks and stimulant supplements more often, increasing the likelihood that these products appear in reports of medical emergencies. How the products are consumed could also influence the pattern. Potential contributing factors include the circumstances surrounding their use (for example, consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs). Some individuals may also have previously undiagnosed heart conditions that could make them more susceptible to cardiovascular complications. These possibilities remain uncertain, and additional research will be needed to determine which factors, if any, help explain the unusually high reporting frequency among younger adults. Do Energy Drinks Actually Cause Heart Attacks? Although the results raise important questions about products containing concentrated caffeine and other stimulants, experts caution against interpreting the findings as proof of a direct cause. "This study raises concerns that products with very high amounts of caffeine may be harmful to the cardiovascular system," said Gregory M. Marcus, M.D., M.A.S., FAHA, chair of the 2026 American Heart Association scientific statement on caffeine and cardiovascular disease. "Although there are biological reasons why that connection could be possible, the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events, because other factors may have influenced the results found in this analysis. More research is needed to understand whether these stimulant products are truly responsible for the reported heart-related events." Marcus did not participate in the research. He is a professor of medicine at the University of California, San Francisco School of Medicine and serves as associate chief of the Cardiology for Research program at the University of California, San Francisco Health. Because the analysis relied on reports submitted voluntarily to the FDA, it cannot establish whether the products themselves were responsible for the cardiovascular events. Other health conditions, behaviors, or circumstances may have played a role. How Researchers Analyzed the FDA Safety Reports The research team reviewed 28,345 reports of possible adverse events submitted to an FDA safety database from 2017 through 2025. Of these, 854 reports involved energy drinks or dietary supplements containing caffeine or other stimulants. The remaining 27,491 reports concerned products without caffeine or stimulant ingredients and served as the comparison group. Researchers classified products according to the ingredients they contained. The stimulant category included caffeine, methylxanthines (theobromine, guarana, yerba mate, green tea/coffee extracts) and sympathomimetics (synephrine, yohimbine, ephedra, DMAA, higenamine). Rather than evaluating individual brands, the researchers grouped products by their ingredients. Consequently, the findings apply to broad categories of caffeinated and stimulant products and do not identify any particular brand as more dangerous than another. The researchers also highlighted important limitations in the available data. Reports were voluntarily submitted by members of the public, consumers, healthcare professionals, and manufacturers, meaning that the database does not provide a complete record of everyone who experienced a possible adverse reaction. Just as importantly, the researchers could not determine how many people consumed these products without developing cardiovascular problems. They also could not establish how many people experienced heart problems but never submitted a report. Without those figures, the analysis cannot calculate the actual likelihood of a heart attack, cardiac arrest, or another cardiovascular event among consumers of energy drinks and stimulant supplements. Nevertheless, the findings reveal a potentially important safety signal. Researchers say more systematic monitoring and further studies are needed to determine whether these products contribute directly to serious heart problems, particularly among younger adults who frequently consume them. body_text: Solid 2.0 - The Long Hold | Solid Skip to main content solid 2.0 Learn Blog Community About Back to blog Solid 2.0 - The Long Hold Solid 2.0 reaches stable after five years: async in the reactive graph, server functions, diagnostics built for agents, and a smaller API. Ryan Carniato Â· November 16, 2026 Â· 8 min read 5 years is a long time to work on anything. It took 5 years from my first commit of Solid to 1.0, and it's been another 5 since then. A lot changes in 5 years. Solid 1.0 made a bet that fine-grained reactivity, signals, was the right foundation for building user interfaces. Back then it was an unusual position. Today signals are everywhere. In Angular, in Svelte's runes, in Vue Vapor, and in a proposal before TC39 to put them in the language itself. It even pushed the conversation into React's compiler. More recently that conversation has shifted to AI, arguably an even larger change in how we build. But Solid has always been about building the right things; the performant things. So for us the mission hasn't really changed all that much. The things that we identified as standout about our approach still stand out now. But instead of living in the shadow of more popular solutions Solid 2.0 carves out a path that others can follow. Deliberately this time. Today that solution reaches stable. Async Graph If fine-grained reactivity's greatest strength is knowing the shape of our application, that knowledge shouldn't end with the process, or the machine the code is running on. Real applications are distributed. Real applications are born from data that lives on a server. The coordination of these pieces should be intentional and by design. This starts with bringing async into the graph. A computation can return a Promise or an async iterator, and everything downstream just understands: function Profile ( props ) { const user = createMemo (() => fetchUser (props.id)); return ( < Loading fallback = {<Skeleton />} > < h1 class = {{ stale : isPending (user) }} > { user ().name} </ h1 > </ Loading > ); } fetchUser(props.id)); return ( <Loading fallback={<Skeleton />}> <h1 class={{ stale: isPending(user) }}>{user().name}</h1> </Loading> );}"> This allows authoring by affordance while automating the handling of race conditions. The introduction of async doesn't cause an app refactor. Speculative state is automatically rolled back without manually written processes ensuring the server remains the authority on truth. SolidStart introduce the world to server functions in early 2022, and now they have found their way home to Solid's core, better than ever. Not only do they support highly capable RPC calls over Request/Response but persistent connections over Server Sent Events. And consuming it remains as simple as the code below. import { live } from "@solidjs/web/server-functions" ; const stockPrice = live ( async function* ( symbol : string ) { "use server" ; for await ( const tick of subscribe (symbol)) yield tick.price; }); // in your component const price = createMemo (() => stockPrice ()) stockPrice())"> This is only the beginning of what can be done with Server Functions and we will be announcing some new features (like reactive Server Components) in coming weeks that leverage this capability. Built to Be Written by Agents "But, we aren't writing the code anymore!" We hear you. A system built on constraints by construction ends up with less code to maintain and less edge cases. What used to be considered a DX shortcoming of reactive frameworks are now their greatest strength. And Solid 2.0 goes all in. Every framework now says it "works great with AI", and usually that means models have seen a lot of it. That's a statement about training data, not about the framework. The question that matters is what happens when the agent gets it wrong. In most frameworks a reactive mistake is silent. The app runs, it's just wrong, and the framework can't tell you, because it can't see it either. Solid can. A fine-grained graph knows exactly what was read, where, and what will update. So Solid 2.0's development builds report mistakes as they happen, with a stable code, the location in your source, and the fix: [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] Reactive value read directly in an effect callback will not update. Move it into a tracking scope (JSX, a memo, or an effect's compute function). in <App> âº <Item> âº effect at http://localhost:5173/src/Item.tsx:12:19 [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] what it means and how to fix it: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/solid-js/diagnostics/strict-read-untracked [STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] agent repair guide: node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#strict_read_untracked âº <Item> âº effectat http://localhost:5173/src/Item.tsx:12:19[STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] what it means and how to fix it: https://docs.solidjs.com/reference/solid-js/diagnostics/strict-read-untracked[STRICT_READ_UNTRACKED] agent repair guide: node_modules/solid-js/skills/reactivity-diagnostics/SKILL.md#strict_read_untracked"> These handle everything from strict errors to helpful heuristics. Thanks to async in the graph we can detect waterfalls, poorly constructed effect loops, poorly scaling graph shapes like wide graph fanouts and fan-ins. Today along with linting rules we can provide the best in class direction for agents at compile and at runtime. This area is still evolving as we learn more about how agents build applications with Solid. The hard part, defining the primitives and semantics, is done. We've integrated with new dev tooling, and Chrome's Performance Tracks. And this capability goes beyond development as this observability powers things like our updated Sentry plugin so you can get the same information on your production builds. We've also been looking at alternative syntax. Solid 2.0 adds experimental support for ReactiveScript and TSRX , both aiming to use compilation to further improve agent authoring. One Framework for All I've always been a big believer that React's super power is its composability. That it allowed the ecosystem to build on its humble pieces. However, we've learned a lot since 2013. At that point composable state, async patterns, and server rendering lacked the primitives to build upon and the ecosystem came up with their own solutions. This was fine for a while but tied React's hands and fractured their ecosystem. Something only a framework as popular as React could survive. Newer frameworks have taken more on themselves and tend to only have one metaframework, or one router. We respect React's original positioning but have updated it for 2026. It isn't about restricting the solution but giving developers the primitives to build upon in the way React originally did. Server functions are example of this. Supporting any router, and cache solution for Single-Flight Mutation is another. We retired our metaframework SolidStart, since every primitive needed to build a Solid Metaframework is now provided by the core or by framework agnostic Vite plugins. We believe that building an opinionated layer like a metaframework shouldn't have you needing to re-implement everything again. We've taken care of the hard parts so you can focus on what you care about. And these days a lot of that work is going to be taken on by your agent. This means less to maintain but no loss in capability. And this makes it easier for the ecosystem. Solid 2.0 only requires one Clerk or Sentry plugin since we provide the primitives for Request/Response (built on web standards) and the hooks for observability that work across any library. We've already seen success with TanStack Query and Router being as capable as anything we've built first party, bringing in Tanner's impeccable attention to detail for the APIs people love to use. Less is More Somehow even though Solid 2.0 brings more capability to Solid, we've collapsed the surface area at almost every point. There are less primitives needed to be learnt, less ceremony around handling async. createResource , batch , startTransition , on , produce , createComputed , createMutable are all gone, because we no longer need them. The equivalent code written for Solid 2.0 is shorter and clearer on intent. It informs our ability observe the runtime, provide better compiler errors, and removes the need for as many escape hatches (like createEffect ) that can get us in trouble. This is something we believe important in an age of AI. Safe by construction rather than by exhaustion. Reduce complexity by deriving(reducing) state rather than putting it in a reducer. // async cascading dropdown function App () { const states = createMemo (() => getStates ( "US" )); const [ selectedState , setState ] = createSignal (() => states ()[ 0 ]); const cities = createMemo (() => getCities ( selectedState ())); const [ selectedCity , setCity ] = createSignal (() => cities ()[ 0 ]); return ( < Loading fallback = {<p>Loading ...</ p > } > < select onChange = {(e) => setState (e.target.value)} > < For each = { states ()} > {(state) => <option>{state}</option>} </ For > </ select > { ' ' } < select disabled = { isPending ( cities )} onChange = {(e) => setCity (e.target.value)} > < For each = { cities ()} > {(city) => <option>{city}</option>} </ For > </ select > < p > Selection : { selectedCity ()}, { selectedState ()} </ p > </ Loading > ); } getStates("US")); const [selectedState, setState] = createSignal(() => states()[0]); const cities = createMemo(() => getCities(selectedState())); const [selectedCity, setCity] = createSignal(() => cities()[0]); return ( <Loading fallback={<p>Loading...</p>}> <select onChange={(e) => setState(e.target.value)}> <For each={states()}>{(state) => <option>{state}</option>}</For> </select>{' '} <select disabled={isPending(cities)} onChange={(e) => setCity(e.target.value)}> <For each={cities()}>{(city) => <option>{city}</option>}</For> </select> <p> Selection: {selectedCity()}, {selectedState()} </p> </Loading> );}"> When the framework carries the guarantees, all loading state, race conditions, and cancellation logic disappears and what you are left with is the UI. The Road Here The first discussions of what a Solid 2.0 would look like started at the moment 1.0 was released. We saught feedback from the community on new reactivity ideas . The real effort started in late 2024. We announced the road to 2.0 in February 2025. Over a year of experiments followed, rewriting the reactive core from scratch until the async model held up to everything we threw at it. The beta landed in March, and the Release Candidate in August, with the API frozen. Then 23 release candidates in 14 weeks. In that time alone, 971 pull requests were merged and 753 issues closed. We set one bar for stable. A full week with no regression in ordinary app code, and no crash or hang anywhere. It took a while to get there. By the end, the bug reports coming in were from people(agents) deliberately hunting edge cases in the deepest corners of the scheduler, and finding them. So many people have touched the project over the past 5 years, from working on the initial reactivity prototypes, to testing the latest RC builds on their production apps. I've tried to thank as many of you as I can and attached hundreds of handles in the RC announcement. There are so many. There are also the many great organizations that have sponsored our development over the years: Sentry, Netlify, Google Chrome, JetBrains, Anomaly, Cursor, Code Rabbit, Anthropic, Tembo and so many more. But mostly I want to thank everyone who has believed in the project. We've accomplished great things and there is much more to come. That isn't possible without all of you. Personally, the past 2 and half years have been some of the most difficult of my life, but knowing what we are building that impacts so many people leaves me with a sense of fulfillment. Solid has always been bigger than its core team, and 2.0 is the clearest proof of that yet. Terminal window npm create solid@latest Solid 2.0 is here. Let's build. The Long Hold refers to a diagnostic warning in Solid 2.0. It fires when a hold has been shown( isPending ) but sufficient time has passed since the last input. Holds were at the heart of our async work for 2.0, and we acknowledge it took a while for this all to land. title: What is the best harness for each model?
body_text: Introducing FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 â RUNTA Runta Resources Docs Blog Pricing About Careers Start free with $50 credit Resources Docs Blog Pricing About Careers Social Discord GitHub X LinkedIn All Blog Contents TL;DR Result Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 What We Tested Setup and Scoring Results by Model The Harness Changes the Cost Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less? Where the Cost Comes From What the Best-Value Harnesses Share Limitations and Future Work Conclusion Appendix: Reference Tables References Introducing FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 November 17, 2026 Â· 14 min read Â· Shilin Zhu agents harness evaluation benchmark harbor TL;DR We partnered with Baseten to build the largest-scale harness leaderboard using 83B tokens across 27,280 agent runs. We wanted to answer two questions: when you switch your model, should you consider switching the harness too? What is the best harness for each model? Previously, our v1.0 FrontierHarness leaderboard ranked harnesses on a single model, Kimi K3. V1.1 expands the benchmark to 22 harnesses Ã 5 models Ã 62 tasks Ã 4 attempts, 76Ã the size of v1.0. Through our experiments, we found that you should consider switching harnesses when switching models to maximize your experience. Each model had a different best-value (pass rate vs. cost) harness: Codex CLI with GLM-5.3, Pi with GLM-5.3 Flash, ZCode with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, Oh My Pi with Muse and Alma with Kimi-K3. Cost ranks moved far between models. By cost per task, the median harness moved 11 of 22 places, and Codex CLI went from 1st with GLM-5.3 to 16th with Kimi-K3. Result Figure 1. Cost per task and pass rate of each harness Each point is one harness: further left is a lower average cost per task, and higher is a higher pass rate. The orange line joins the harnesses that no other harness beats in both cost and pass rate. Select a model to filter all figures of this post. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Over all models, four harnesses are on the line: OpenCode v2 (lowest cost per task, $0.561), Pi, Codex CLI and ZCode (highest pass rate, 61.9%). The others cost up to 1.6 times as much and passed 50.6% to 60.2%. Each card names the best-value harness for one model: the lowest cost per pass, unless another harness costs at most 30% more per pass and passes at least 5 points more often. This rule picked ZCode over OpenCode v1 with DeepSeek (25% more cost, 7.7 more points) and Alma over Oh My Pi with Kimi-K3 (9% more cost, 6.5 more points). Why We Built FrontierHarness Eval v1.1 V1.0 ran nine harnesses with one model. Their pass rates were within 17 points of each other, but the median cost per pass differed by 17 times. We thought that this came mostly from the pair of harness and model: a harness that is cheap with one model can be expensive with another. V1.1 runs each harness with five models. What We Tested Harnesses. 18 harnesses. The four DeepSeek Harness profiles have different tool sets, and OpenCode ran at two versions. Each counts separately: 22 configurations. Table 2 in the appendix gives their versions. Models. Baseten served all five: GLM-5.3 ( zai-org/GLM-5.3 ), GLM Flash ( zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash ), DeepSeek ( deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 ), Muse ( meta-models/muse-spark-open ) and Kimi-K3 ( moonshotai/Kimi-K3 ). Tasks. 62 terminal tasks. The time limits are those of the tasks, from 15 minutes to 8 hours. Setup and Scoring Configuration and Runtime We ran the Harbor evaluation with each harnessâs default settings, because we think this is closest to how people use a harness every day. Each harness used the same version and settings with all models, at the maximum reasoning effort. Figure 2. How Harbor and Runta divide the work in each trial Each trial gets a new Runta runtime, which is deleted at the end. Thus no trial can see the files of an earlier trial. Scoring Method Table 1. Methodology This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. A cell is one harness and model pair. We use the two cost metrics of our dashboard : Average cost per task: the mean cost of the priced trials of each task, then the mean over the tasks. Figure 1 and the cost ranks use it (Figures 4 and 5). Cost per pass: the average cost per task divided by the pass rate. The best-value harness uses it (Figures 3, 6 and 7). We pick the best value by cost per pass because we want harnesses at the top left of a chart of pass rate against cost per task: a high pass rate at a low cost. Draw a line from the origin to the point of a harness. Its slope, pass rate Ã· cost, is the passes per dollar. Cost per pass is the inverse of this slope, so the lowest cost per pass has the steepest line. Audits of the trial logs flagged 216 trials for reward hacking, and 163 of them were online lookups. These trials score 0. Table 3 in the appendix gives the count for each harness and model. Results by Model Figure 3. Cost and pass rate of each harness with each model This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. A deeper cell costs less than the others in its column. Codex CLI was the cheapest per pass with GLM-5.3, $0.803, but 12th with Muse and 10th with Kimi-K3. Over all models, it cost the least per pass, $0.937, and Antigravity CLI the most, $1.63. How Sure Are These Results? We drew the 62 tasks again 4,000 times and chose the best-value harness each time. Codex CLI stayed first with GLM-5.3 in 99.6% of the draws. The other four winners are the most likely of several close harnesses: Oh My Pi with Muse (53%), ZCode with DeepSeek (47%), Pi with GLM Flash (42%) and Alma with Kimi-K3 (25%). The Harness Changes the Cost The model sets the general level of the cost, because the list prices of the models differ by 20 times or more (Figure 9). We took the average cost per task of the 110 cells on a log scale, so that a doubling counts the same with each model. A two-way analysis of variance divides the spread of these costs into three parts: Model, 92.8%: the differences between the five models. Harness, 2.3%: the part of the effect of a harness that is the same with every model. Pair, 4.9%: the rest. It also contains noise, because each cell has one value. So with the model fixed, 68% of the variation between harnesses (4.9 of 7.2 points) depends on the pair, or is noise. With the Model Fixed, the Harness Changes the Cost by 1.8 to 5.0 Times Figure 4. Lowest-cost and highest-cost harness for each model Each row is a model, on a log scale of average cost per task. The ratio divides the highest cost by the lowest. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. To test for chance, we shuffled the trials between the harnesses of each model 300 times and calculated the ratio again. âChanceâ is the median of these ratios, 1.2 to 1.8 times. All five real ratios are larger than every shuffle (p = 0.003), so the spread comes from the harnesses, not from the noise of reruns. The largest is with DeepSeek: Cline CLI cost 5.0 times as much as OpenCode v1, for 2.0 more points. With the other models, the cheapest harness per task was at most 0.4 points behind the most expensive one. The Cheapest Harness per Task Changes With the Model Figure 5. Cost rank of each harness with each model (1 = lowest cost per task) Each line is a harness, with the cheapest at the top. The five highlighted lines are the cheapest harnesses per task with GLM-5.3, GLM Flash, DeepSeek, Muse and Kimi-K3. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Codex CLI was 1st with GLM-5.3 and 16th with Kimi-K3. DeepSeek Harness: Creator moved the most, from 1st with Muse to 21st with GLM Flash. OpenCode v1 was 1st with DeepSeek and 13th with Muse. Reruns do not explain these moves. We divided the attempts into two halves and ranked the harnesses by cost in each half. With the same model, the two rankings had a mean rank correlation of 0.71. With two different models, it was 0.26. A Higher Cost Does Not Give a Higher Score Figure 6. Lowest and highest cost per pass for each model This is Figure 4 for cost per pass. After each ratio is the rank correlation of the cost per task and the pass rate of the harnesses, from â0.39 to +0.22. A positive value means that the more expensive harnesses passed more often. This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. The harness with the highest pass rate was 5th to 20th of 22 in cost per task. With four of the five models, the most expensive harness per pass passed less often than the cheapest one. Does a Simpler Harness Cost Less? No. We compared four factors with the cost per pass. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate are not the main cost factors. Steps are. Start tokens: the input tokens of the first agent-loop request: the system prompt, the tool definitions and the task. Tools: the tools that the first request offers. Cache hit rate and steps: the mean over the passed trials. A step is one entry of the agent trajectory. Figure 7. Four factors of each harness and the cost per pass This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Over the 22 harnesses, the rank correlation of the steps per pass and the cost per pass was +0.51 (p = 0.015). For the other three factors, it was â0.03 to +0.02 (p â¥ 0.88). Within each model, tool calls tracked cost as well as steps. Table 4 below and Table 5 in the appendix give the values. Each step sends the context again, so a trial used 2.0 to 4.8 million input tokens on average, by harness, and the largest first request, 21,365 tokens, is less than 1% of that. mini-SWE-agent has the smallest first request, 882 tokens, but took 38 steps per pass and was 17th of 22 in cost per pass. Table 4. Start tokens, tools, cache hit rate, steps and cost per pass of each harness This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Where the Cost Comes From Figure 8. Inference cost of each harness, by token type or by trial outcome This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. All costs are inference estimates at list prices. The pass rate of the harness on the model card has an outline. Over all trials, input from the cache was 42% of the cost, output 33% and other input 25%. Tokens and the Cache The cache makes repeated input much cheaper. Cached input costs 2% (DeepSeek) to 20% (GLM Flash) of the price of other input (Figure 9). Figure 9. List prices of each model (USD for one million tokens) This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. One pair shows the effect of the cache. Cline CLI with DeepSeek (highest cost per task) read 86% of its input from the cache, and OpenCode v1 read 97%. It also sent twice as much input. Input that did not come from the cache was 57% of its cost. Most of the Cost Goes to Trials That Do Not Pass 64.5% of the list-price cost of the scored runs went to trials that did not pass : 52.7% to failures and 11.8% to timeouts. What the Best-Value Harnesses Share The traces of the five best-value harnesses show three common design choices. These are observations, not tests. One shell tool does most of the work. By harness, it got 61% to 93% of the tool calls. Piâs default prompt has four tools and sends file searches to bash : selectedTools: [...(input.selectedTools ?? ["read", "bash", "edit", "write"])], addRule("Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find"); Each request only adds to the one before it. The start of the context does not change, so the provider reads it from the cache: 91.1% to 94.0% of input in passed trials (Table 4). But 18 of the 22 harnesses read 91% or more, so this does not separate the five. Each step pays the full input price for only about 500 new tokens: # Pi, GLM-5.3, merge-diff-arc-agi-task (trial cd2f6dfd) request prompt tokens cached tokens 8 15,954 15,616 9 16,351 15,936 10 16,999 16,320 No subagents and almost no summaries. Each of the five used a subagent in at most 6 trials, too few to tell if subagents help. Of the five, only Codex CLI summarized, in 8 trials (the 11 Alma trials in Table 6 only drop old images and reminders). Codex CLI summarizes at 90% of the window (Table 6): .map(|context_window| (context_window * 9) / 10); The five also share a weakness. Failed runs end with a confident answer. About three in four failed trials ended with a final answer, not at the time limit: from 68% with Pi to 82% with Codex CLI. Few said that the work was incomplete: # Codex CLI, GLM-5.3, cancel-async-tasks (trial 37182b0e) Agent: - Validated with system Python, including concurrency and cancellation-cleanup tests. Verifier: FAILED test_tasks_cancel_above_max_concurrent assert stdout.count("Cleaned up.") == 2 AssertionError: assert 0 == 2 Trials that did not pass took 60% (Codex CLI) to 69% (Alma) of the cost of each harness. A check before the harness stops could save part of it, but we did not test this. Limitations and Future Work Open models, one provider. Closed models can give different results. The cache and the prices are those of Baseten, and another provider can change the cost ranks. We plan two next steps: Closed models. We will add closed models, such as Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra and Gemini 4 Carbon. Long-horizon work. We will study how a harness that runs continuously in the cloud improves itself during long work. Conclusion When you change the model, think about changing the harness too. Test the candidate harnesses with your model on a private dataset of your own tasks, large enough to see past the noise. The model sets most of the cost, and the harness is second. The model explains 92.8% of the variance of cost per task. With the model fixed, the most expensive harness cost 1.9 to 4.9 times as much per pass as the cheapest (1.8 to 5.0 times per task), so compare the cost when you pick a harness. A higher cost does not buy a higher pass rate. For each model, the rank correlation of cost per task and pass rate was â0.39 to +0.22. Size does not predict cost. mini-SWE-agent, the smallest harness, was 19th of 22 by cost per task over all models. Most of the cost, 64.5%, went to runs that did not pass. With the five best-value harnesses, 68% to 82% of the failed runs ended with a confident final answer, not at the time limit. With a cheap model that has a wide range of pass rates, pick a harness with a high pass rate. Pass rates varied by harness, from 54.0% to 69.0% with DeepSeek. But each pass rate has a 95% interval of about Â±10 points, so a gap of a few points is a tie. For harness developers: cut steps, not just prompt tokens. Prompt size, tool count and cache hit rate did not predict cost per pass. Steps did, because every step sends the whole context again. Appendix: Reference Tables Table 2. Harness configurations This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Table 3. Reward-hacked trials of each harness This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. Table 5. Prompt and tools of each harness This figure is interactive and needs JavaScript. References FrontierHarness dashboard Harbor and Harbor Hub , where the ten jobs are stored Introducing FrontierHarness Eval , our v1.0 results Baseten , Model APIs , the inference provider for performant open models Runta Harbor guide and Runta pricing Runta Agent execution layer for token efficiency, secret protection, and governed access. How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
body_text: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification / claude.dev Blog [ H ] HOME [ M ] MODS [ D ] DOCS [ T ] TERMINAL Try Claude Code [ H ] HOME [ M ] MODS [ D ] DOCS [ T ] TERMINAL Engineering How the Claude Code team thinks about verification How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. AUTHOR Addy Osmani CATEGORY Engineering PUBLISHED Nov 16, 2026 READING TIME 10 min How the Claude Code team thinks about verification TREE â Not all tests are created equal: 3 tests worth investing in â How the Claude Code team thinks about verification â Good tests, good results ââââââââââââââââââââââââââââ 00% 10 MIN READ SHARE X.com LinkedIn Email Copy URL Copy markdown On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. Thatâs because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claudeâs work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agentâs performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. NOT ALL TESTS ARE CREATED EQUAL: 3 TESTS WORTH INVESTING IN No matter which test type you choose, there are a few failure modes to avoid. If your tests are flaky youâll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before youâve committed the changes. Now, here are the three types of tests I think are most worth investing in. E2E tests If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to foolâeither the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concretely tell you whatâs broken. FIG A A unit test may show âError: Timeout after 30 seconds,â but an end-to-end test can show a screenshot with a description of whatâs broken. While unit tests are faster and less flaky, itâs possible to pass them and still break the feature. This is because both the agent and the test donât understand the full task. With E2E tests, it is effective to give your agent hands and eyes on the real running system. You can use a skill to boot, drive, and inspect the app with tools like CDP , simulators, or API harnesses. The feature map can serve as a guide and grading rubric for agents as they typically list features from the userâs point of view with descriptions of paths, keyboard shortcuts, selectors, and expected results. Property tests: constraints that canât break A lot of tests are based on what you thought might go wrong. Property tests look at the edge cases that people tend to miss, which is where agents often fail. You start by writing a statement you think canât fail and then use a test library ( fast-check for JS/TS, Hypothesis for Python, proptest for Rust, etc.) to generate thousands of inputs that try to prove otherwise. There are many properties in virtually every software project like: Round-trip encoding : âif you encode X then decode it back, you get X.â This works for parsing and serialization as well. Invariants : Things that must always be true, like âaccount balance can never become negative.â Idempotency : Doing an action (migration, normalization, retry) twice has the same effect as doing it once. Equivalence : Optimized code produces the same result as naive but correct code. Property libraries are a great way to keep agents honest by using edge cases that arenât created with the same bias as the agent that created the original code. They are also particularly helpful for rewrites when the spec has drifted from production behavior and is no longer a reliable source for verification. Differential tests: the old system is the oracle Differential tests are particularly effective for large-scale migration use cases where functionality is expected to remain the same. For these tests, you run both the old system and the new system with the same inputs and see if you get different results. If you do, there is a bug or breaking change that needs to be fixed. The key for differential tests is to use randomly generated inputs or a sample of production traffic. Youâll also want to normalize irrelevant factors like whitespace and keep a list of approved changes for situations where the new environment should differ from the old. HOW THE CLAUDE CODE TEAM THINKS ABOUT VERIFICATION We have previously written about how code review works at Anthropic , but this article aims to go deeper on how we verify our work. Verification means running the change Running the app end to end matters more than tests. You wouldn't ship an iOS change without trying it in a simulator, and the same goes for Claude. Claude can test the whole app the way a human or QA engineer would. Ask it to use the Claude Chrome extension for web changes, an iOS or Android MCP for mobile, computer use for desktop, or to run the service locally for backend work. To codify how to start the simulator or run your app, create a skill called verify. Put it in a .claude/skills/ folder in your repo, as close to the relevant code as you can, and add as many as you need. Claude knows to use the verify skill before committing changes. Then invest in making your verify skill fast and reliable. Ask Claude to iterate on it and stress test it. It's your smoke test harness, so you want it rock solid. When you give Claude a way to smoke test its changes end to end, you get much better results. You'll see it iterate and catch real mistakes faster, the way a human would. This is how we test nearly all changes at Anthropic. Failing tests require human attention Nobody can read every change, so we use failures as one way to decide what needs a person. Claude runs the checks and tries to fix anything that fails. If a check is still failing after three rounds, Claude stops and brings in a human. Code owners write their own checks The people who own the code write the checks for it, and refine them until they flag what the owner would flag. When a check pulls in a reviewer, it should say why, so they don't have to work it out from the diff. Reliability checks trigger on the diff We maintain a reliability checklist with 39 items, each with a trigger that can be read from a diff, a check, and the incidents or PRs behind it. One is â--resume loads old transcripts.â When session storage or message types change, we ask whether a new field loads safely, since older transcripts wonât have it. Claude reads the diff and checks only the items whose trigger matchesâusually 3 to 10âso nobody has to memorize past outages. One reviewer, multiple rounds We don't try to improve reviews by stacking on more reviewers. Adding a second, more expensive, reviewer on top of the primary one is often a worse approach than tuning the primary. Instead, we have a REVIEW.md that says what the reviewer should pay attention to for this code. We also think review and verification rounds should build on each other. We point each pass at context from earlier rounds and past failures rather than re-checking everything from scratch. Itâs cheaper and finds more. Changes can't modify their own checks If a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken. Code Review reads the REVIEW.md file from the base or default branch, never from the pull request's changes . The Claude Code team ensures the rules that gate changes are on a branch that the change can't modify. The Claude Code team also reserves reviews for commits. If someone's pushing while the review is happening, then the review result is no longer useful. A passing review on an out-of-date commit means nothing. The team also runs cheap checks first. If an agent pushes before testing locally, it has spent shared review and CI time when it could have caught the bug itself. On our team, Claude runs the tests, build, and linter before opening a pull request. You can enforce this with a hook that runs the tests when Claude finishes, or a /goal of a passing test suite. Start a new gate in observe mode In our own repos, we stamp each commit with how it was verified. The stamp even includes "none" so we can query for commits that weren't verified. We've also created a commit gate that can block a commit if the session did not contain /code-review or /verify. We've set it up with off, observe, and enforce modes. Observe mode will log what would have been blocked, so that we can review any false positives and ensure no one is impacted. Enforce mode will block the commit. Any commit can carry an explanation in its message as to why it didn't get verified. If commits have been blocked twice in the session, the next one will be allowed through so Claude doesn't get stuck â Claude Code isn't perfect. Test your checks on what actually matters The Claude Code team also regularly reviews the reviewers. We track how many merged changes were reverted, how many changes a maintainer rejected before merging, and a size-matched subset of changes that have stayed clean. This can also be done with a formal evaluation. In our code review post , we described how the Code Review team has set up an evaluation based on previous incidents and reverts. They recreate the repo to the state at the time of review for each example, and provide a one-sentence answer key to what the bug was. Only findings that correctly describe the bug in question get points. They use merged and stable changes as a control to prevent over-flagging. Their tuning set is split out from the fixed test set they use to evaluate their system. They also evaluated the recall rate for raw findings, post-verification, and final review separately. This lets them see if the system is losing bugs it had already found. Any evaluation that treats all these as one end-to-end score won't capture this nuance. In addition to validity, the other dimension we care about is how important it is to make the change. A good reviewer will catch most things that are technically correct, but people care about whether a given bug is a must-fix, a should-fix, or a nit. Code Review has this exact idea, and it will tag things as Important, Nit or Pre-existing . The "pre-existing" tag means that the reviewer shouldn't hold the author responsible for something that was already a bug. Finally, the Claude Code team tunes recall up to the point where the next improvement would be overfitting to the eval rather than actually catching bugs. Turn misses into rules In the Claude Code repo, we have two methods of turning missed cases into rules. The first is extracting patterns in human code review comments and PR reverts to identify common issues. These must occur in at least two PRs and be identifiable from a diff to be considered a potential rule. Three agents will try to disprove them, and they will be reviewed and approved by a human in a PR. The second method is replaying three bug finders against a PR that is associated with a known incident. If at least two find the bug, it's a detectable bug. If the bug is missed on a small diff, this is a gap that is worth turning into a rule in REVIEW.md. Flaky tests get the same treatment. Claude can't skip them, add sleeps or retry until they pass. If it can't find the root cause, it deletes the test and writes down why. Rules need cleaning up too. Test suites, verification steps and .md files only grow if you let them, so we tidy them up on a routine. GOOD TESTS, GOOD RESULTS Weâve found that giving your agent a way to verify its work with a strong feedback loop makes all the difference. Treat your verification layer like you would any other system. Keep it out of reach of the changes they judge, grade them against the bugs that mattered to you, and write down lessons when they miss something so that it doesnât happen more than once, and prune those lessons so they stay worth running. Do that and your job shifts from reading every diff to defining what âdoneâ looks like and reviewing the evidence, which is what lets you run many Claudes at once. title: Interpreting claims that a theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean
body_text: “…and the proof is checked in Lean” | Xena Xena Mathematicians learning Lean by doing. Skip to content Home About Xena Student projects Installing Lean and mathlib Bluesky Useful links. ← A Modern Reorganization of Mathematics “…and the proof is checked in Lean” Posted on November 12, 2026 by xenaproject This post is an attempt to explain in simple terms how to interpret claims of the form “this theorem is correct because it was checked in Lean”. The summary is: there is an important signal that can be extracted from Lean code, but if this code is AI-generated then you need to do some tests first. We explain the tests, and note that in many cases (such as the OpenAI theorem dump) these tests have not yet been systematically done. Introduction Last month’s theorem dump by OpenAI consisted of 722 mathematics papers, around 45% of which came with some Lean code. Three of the (non-Leanified) papers have since been retracted because of a sign error. Some people might say “well, the papers that come with Lean code are definitely correct because that’s how Lean works”. Others might say “well Lean had a soundness bug and could well have more, and AIs will reward hack, so Lean verification doesn’t tell us much at all”. The truth, unsurprisingly, is more subtle, and this post is an attempt to explain it. This post is structured as a sequence of four questions that one needs to ask about a Lean repository, particularly if it is AI-generated, before one can start to make correctness claims of this form. And before I start, let me stress that for many of the papers in the OpenAI theorem dump, these questions have not yet all been answered affirmatively (but there is nothing stopping people from answering these questions, and I have no reason to believe that any of the tests below will fail, it’s just that people didn’t do them yet). Question 1. Does the Lean statement match the informal statement? A Lean repository will typically have a “headline theorem statement”. This will be some computer code which defines the statement (not the proof!) of a theorem. Note the huge difference here between the statement, and the proof. For example here is some fully-compiling Lean code which defines a mathematical statement. import Mathlib def FermatsLastTheorem : Prop := ∀ a b c n : ℕ, n ≥ 3 → a^n + b^n ≠ c^n This code imports Lean’s mathematics library Mathlib and then defines a mathematical statement which looks at first glance like it might be Fermat’s Last Theorem, but which actually is a trivially false statement because in Lean ℕ contains 0 , so a = b = c = 0 and n = 3 gives a counterexample. This does not stop the statement from compiling! It will however stop any proof of this statement from compiling. Lean carefully distinguishes between the statement of a theorem and the proof of a theorem; humans are very good at referring to both ideas as “a theorem”. The first question which one has to ask when judging a pdf which comes with some Lean code is: “what is the statement of the theorem in the Lean code, and does this correspond to the actual theorem statement in the pdf?” For a human Lean expert, this is typically (but not always) an easy question to answer. For example any Lean-competent human mathematician would be able to read the two lines of code above and observe that this was a mis-statement of Fermat’s Last Theorem. Things are, however, not always as easy as this. Currently, because of deficiencies in available libraries, one may have to read many thousands of lines of code just to understand the statement of a formalised theorem. An example of this right now is a PR to DeepMind’s Formal Conjectures repository containing a Lean formalisation of the statement of the Hodge conjecture. At the time of writing, the statement relies on over 10,000 lines of code sitting on top of Mathlib , because Mathlib (which is carefully human-expert-checked and which can be trusted) does not yet have the definitions of things like the cycle class map needed to make the statement. Another example is Axiom’s recent announcement of a formally-verified proof of the classification of finite simple groups . The statement which Axiom’s system proved is here in Tau Ceti, an AI-generated library of Lean code. The file containing the statement imports over 250K lines of Lean code in Tau Ceti (over 900 files). Of these, around 5600 lines of code are crucial because they contain all the relevant definitions (for example, all the definitions of the sporadic simple groups, most of which are still not in Mathlib ). Without human checking, one does not really know for sure that this is definitely the correct statement of the classification (and note that I have not yet met any human who claims to have carefully checked that the definitions of the sporadic groups in Tau Ceti are correct). In fact by far the strongest evidence that we have that this statement is correctly formalized is that Axiom’s code proves it! It is worth noting that of the 290 OpenAI theorems which come with Lean code, around 38 of them have the property that the Lean code does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper . And OpenAI never claimed that it did! They just said “here is some Lean code which goes with this paper”. Sometimes the code just states and proves some intermediate results — my impression is that OpenAI decided to go live when some of the formalizations were incomplete, so just dumped what they had. To give a concrete example: paper 194 claims to prove Lech’s multiplicity conjecture in commutative algebra, with no restriction on dimension, residue field or characteristic; this question has been open since 1960. The headline theorem in the corresponding Lean code can be checked to be Corollary 5.4 of the paper — already an impressive achievement, but not the headline result. Question 2: does the code compile? Once you’re convinced that you understand the statement of the theorem which the Lean code purports to prove, you (or perhaps one of your friends who has access to a beefy machine, if the code base is huge) has to actually compile the code. When Anthropic formalized a proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in Lean , they asked me to take a look at the 13 million lines of code which they had generated. I downloaded it onto my machine, dumped it into a sandbox (because who knows what AI-generated code will do, it can in theory delete all your files) and attempted to compile it; I very quickly ran out of memory. I told Anthropic that I was unable to make any claims about what they had done until I could see the code base compiling, and they gave me temporary access to a machine with 96 cores and 500 gigs of ram. I could then compile the code. Of course, with a more reasonably-sized codebase it is possible to compile the code on a reasonably-sized machine. For example OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier-Stokes problem is 640K lines of code and compiles fine on my laptop. It is probably worth stressing again: do not run random Lean code on your local machine unless you sandbox it first. Lean’s mathematics library is safe to run and build upon because this is human-curated and checked by human experts. AI-generated code is not. Question 3: does the code prove the theorem as stated? I already talked in Question 1 about the importance of checking the statement of a theorem, so we can be sure that the code is proving the right thing. However, there is an added complication here. Ideally the statement of a theorem will be contained in a file which has very few imports beyond Mathlib , so we know we can trust it. But the proof of the theorem will necessarily import thousands and possibly millions of lines of code which nobody wants to read. How do we know for sure that there is no trick hidden in the millions of lines of proof files which redefines x^n to mean 37 , and then proves that a^n + b^n ≠ c^n because the left hand side is 37+37=74 and the right hand side is 37 ? Or which adds a new axiom to mathematics saying that the theorem is true? Put another way — given a Challenge.lean file with only trusted code imported and the statement of a theorem, and a Solution.lean file with millions of lines of untrusted code imported and the proof of a theorem which looks identical , how do we know for sure that somewhere in the millions of lines of code there is no hack which changes the meaning of the statement, changes the rules from just the axioms of mathematics, The one-line answer: lake comparator . You can read more about this answer here . But in short, this tool checks that the theorem stated in a trusted file and the theorem proved via untrusted imports are identical, and that only the axioms of mathematics are used in the proof. Question 4: does the code exploit a bug in Lean’s official kernel? This can happen. There was a soundness bug in Lean’s kernel which was fixed four hours after it was discovered, and a subsequent review of Lean’s code base by OpenAI found several more, all of which were fixed before they were announced publicly. There may in theory be more soundness bugs in Lean’s kernel. However, this does not matter . Why not? Because Lean now has many kernels, created by users, written in many different languages, and at least one of which is formally verified to have no bugs, right down to the assembly level. If you want to make absolutely sure that there is no reward-hacking then again there is a one-line answer: lake comparator --paranoid . A malicious piece of code exploiting an as-yet-undiscovered bug in Lean’s official kernel will not pass this test unless it exploits as-yet-undiscovered bugs in many independent systems all at once. For example this webpage from the Lean kernel arena demonstrates that OpenAI’s resolution of the Navier–Stokes problem is accepted by multiple kernels as well as Lean’s official kernel. One final remark Even if the Lean code compiles and passes all these tests, and is thus overwhelmingly likely to be a correct proof of a theorem, this does not mean that any corresponding pdf also contains a correct proof! The Navier–Stokes lost in translation paper demonstrates the opposite in fact, for the Navier-Stokes write-up; whilst all the tests above have been run for the Navier–Stokes work, there are instances where the pdf proof and the Lean proof diverge. In these cases, who knows if the pdf proof is OK! My understanding is that some experts have been using AI to informalise the Lean proof back into English in order to read the argument, rather than ploughing through the slop in the pdf. Summary/conclusions “It’s true because it’s checked in Lean” can be made to make sense. But one has to do some work beyond “the Lean code compiles”. Your frontier AI model can do all of this work. But it needs to be done, and (depending on the amount of Lean code in the proof) it may be computationally costly. (is the verification in some other proof assistant? couldn’t there be a soundness bug in that?) Like Like Reply xenaproject says: November 12, 2026 at 8:17 am I think I’ll defer to the master and just point you to https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-with-verified-kernels/ Like Like Reply coolio says: November 12, 2026 at 1:48 pm Thanks, I’d seen that blog post, but as someone who doesn’t know much about Lean, it’s a bit hard to interpret, and I’m interested in why *you* find it reassuring. In particular a statement like “Con-leche is the first kernel for Lean written in Lean and proven consistent.” doesn’t on the face of it make a whole lotta sense. How is it not circular to use Lean to prove that a Lean kernel is consistent? If there was a soundness bug, it could be used to prove anything in Lean, in particular that con-leche was consistent, right? Maybe the idea is that the consistency proof can be manually verified to not contain anything “weird” (though it seems this proof was produced by Claude…) Like Like xenaproject says: November 12, 2026 at 10:02 pm I’m really sorry, you need to ask these questions elsewhere (e.g. on the Lean Zulip). In this case, the question is whether a Lean consistency proof of a Lean kernel increases our confidence that the Lean kernel really is consistent. Well, what could go wrong? First, the Lean kernel would need to be inconsistent. Then, the inconsistency would have to be used to falsely prove that the Lean kernel is consistent. All this is possible, but generally speaking, exploiting kernel bugs is a highly nontrivial business. The Collatz example required very careful engineering and a deliberate attempt to prove something false. If we assume good faith on the part of the author of con-leche, the consistency proof of con-leche, though AI-generated, was not produced by instructing the AI to produce a proof of a false statement by any means possible. Under these circumstances, it’s much more likely that the consistency statement is actually true and that the AI generated a correct proof. If you believe this, then the consistency proof is a big improvement over no proof at all. Like Liked by 1 person dorchard says: November 12, 2026 at 10:33 am A very nice summary- thanks. Squircles
body_text: Squircles - Linebender Linebender About Blog Wiki Squircles A squircle is a shape intermediate between a square and a circle. There is no single mathematical definition, rather there are a number of curves that fit this shape. All general squircles are parametrized, and can vary between circle and square. Loading the interactive tester… Superellipse The best known squircle is the superellipse, popularized by Piet Hein. Martin Gardner wrote a detailed narrative of its origin in a Scientific American column in 1977. The text is replicated in https://piethein.com/superellipse/ but that’s missing equations and figures. The superellipse has the formula $|x|^n + |y|^n = 1$ (we’ll use a unit radius for convenience). When $n=2$ it is a circle, and it approaches a square asymptotically as $n \rightarrow \infty$. Measurement There is no standard measurement for squircles. For superellipses, the exponent is the most common parameter. A good choice is the coordinates of the midpoint of the quadrant, assuming a unit radius; here $x$ and $y$ are equal. The conversion formula is simple and intuitive: $x = 0.5^{1/n}$. This measurement is called "gauge" in the interactive demo above, and is the primary parameter; with the exception of some unreachable regions of parameter space, it should be possible to compare different squircle variants with similar gauge. Flat-sided squircles There are two basic approaches to squircle creation. One is a single analytic curve, where curvature reaches zero at the poles, but is otherwise nonzero. The other is mixing straight line segments with corners. A significant advantage of the latter approach is that it can adapt to rectangles of arbitrary aspect ratio without distorting the corner shape. The Apple squircle shape Squircles received renewed attention when Apple changed the icon shape from rounded rectangle to their own squircle in iOS 7 in 2013. There were several blog posts to analyze and recreate the shape. An early analysis suggested that it was a superellipse of exponent 5, but when people extracted the Béziers and looked more closely, that was found to be inaccurate. Rather, it’s a flat-sided squircle. For the raw Bézier path data of the Apple shape, the best source is the PaintCode blog . This blog correctly points out some bugs in that logic, and also has some details on behavior for oval rather than square aspect ratios. The Apple shape has a number of flaws, including one extraneous straight line segment, and a lack of symmetry. However, those flaws are minor, and really only reveal themselves under close analysis. The Apple shape has no additional parameter, so its variation is controlled entirely by the length of the flat side. With no flat side, it has a gauge fixed at 0.809. An extremely detailed analysis of the Apple shape is in The Art of Continuous Corners . The Figma squircle Figma published a blog post, Desperately Seeking Squircles , with an analysis of the Apple squircle and their own approximation. It is influential because Figma is an important design tool, because their writeup was compelling, and because there are any number of open source implementations of it, mostly TypeScript/JavaScript. squircle-path-kit from msurguy figma-squircle from phamfoo corner-smoothing from sanalabs (uses figma-squircle) squircle-js from bring-shrubbery (uses figma-squircle) figma_squircle from aloisdeniel (Dart/Flutter) Lisse from JaceThings The Figma blog contains a plot of the Béziers comprising a cleaned up version of iOS 7 rounded rectangle, revealing three Bézier segments per quadrant. It fixes the straight-line segment and the asymmetry, so is not an exact match. The middle segment is very close to an arc. The other segments are more problematic. They have zero curvature at the endpoints, so are G2 continuous with flat sides, but there is a curvature discontinuity with the middle (arc) section, and their curvature profile is not especially smooth. A reasonable guess is that it was drawn by hand to be approximately smooth. Without a flat side, the Figma squircle is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.854. Gauges up to 1 are of course attainable by adding the flat side. Clothoid squircles The Figma blog suggests “smoothed curvature profiles” which have a piecewise linear relationship between arc length and curvature. It then goes on to approximate them with cubic Bézier segments, but their approximation has fairly significant curvature discontinuities when joining to the circular arc. The clothoid squircle is worth describing explicitly, as it has G2 continuity (as opposed to G1 for the Figma approximation). The behavior is generally similar to the Figma variant. Without a flat side, it is only capable of a gauge between $\sqrt{0.5}$ (0.707) and 0.790. The box decorations corner-shape spec Squircles got a big boost as they’re now standardized in CSS, as the corner-shape property of the box decorations spec . These specify real superellipse corners, with additional tweaks and support for animation. The Chromium superellipse approximation While the CSS spec mandates the actual superellipse shape, practical implementations will generally use a Bézier approximation. A blog post, The corner cases of implementing CSS corner-shape in Blink , gives an efficient closed-form approximation, with two Bézier segments per quadrant. This formula, determined using symbolic regression, is parametrized, and handles exponents 2 and above well. It is exact for placing the midpoint (this is part of the formula), so is well calibrated in that regard. Apple-like behavior with the corner-shape spec The early analysis of the Apple squircle shape as being approximately an exponent 5 superellipse was based on coarse shape only and didn't take into account its flat side. A much better match to the Apple shape is attainable using a superellipse with exponent 3 and a corresponding flat side length to match the gauge. This has G2 continuity and a similar curvature profile. This illustration was made using the Chromium approximation, so it should match the browser. Here's the CSS to accomplish the "close to Apple" squircle shape. Note that the parameter to the superellipse() function is the base-2 log of the exponent, so the value for an exponent of 3 is 1.585. . icon { aspect-ratio: 1 ; border-radius: 46.2% ; corner-shape: superellipse( 1.585 ); } Continuity A superellipse of exponent $n$ has continuity $G(\lceil n \rceil - 1)$. This includes the flat-sided variants, as, for exponent > 2, the endpoint of the quadrant has zero curvature. A perfect circle (and indeed, any even integer exponent) without flat sides is of course the exception, as it has an infinitely high order of continuity. As a general observation, for visual smoothness, the shape should have G2 continuity. Of the variants discussed, only the clothoid and superellipse (for n > 2) have this property. The Chromium approximation comes close; it doesn't have zero curvature by construction when joining the flat part, but does at the corner join by symmetry (unlike the Figma approximation, which has an additional arc there). Other squircles Quite a number of other curves can be pressed into service as squircles if need be. The polynomial spiral (“spiro”) curve can do a reasonable flat-sided squircle with G2 continuity. See the “suitcase corners” section of Raph's thesis , figure 7.2. Conic sections (hyperbolas). These approximate a sharp corner but are only G1 continuous (if flat sided). Fernández-Guasti squircle, defined by $x^2 + y^2 - s^2x^2y^2 = 1$. This is used in engineering but likely not in graphic design. The Wikipedia page on squircles has a “periodic squircle” which has very similar behavior to the Fernández-Guasti one (they are visually near indistinguishable). Related topics The offset curve of a squircle is not a squircle, but (a) it’s close, and (b) concentric squircles might be visually just as appealing or more so; for example a slightly rounded inner corner might look better than a sharp one if the curvature exceeds the stroke half-width. The blurred rounded rectangle approximation is based on applying shading to a superellipse; each iso-line is in fact a superellipse. title: Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine
body_text: Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty sabotage attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine Search Query for Search the web Search with Yahoo Scout Search the web Skip to main Home News Finance Sports More Mail Search the web News US Politics 2026 Midterm Elections Science World Weather Originals ... Advertisement Advertisement Return to Homepage Top Stories: Anthropic IPO live 'GTA 6' launch hit by glitches Nvidia signals caution on China Peltola wins Alaska Senate race Medicare premiums are rising Life in remote Alaska Anthropic's IPO: Key details Apple iCloud outage Nvidia won't reinstate Huang Traveling for Thanksgiving Ukrayinska Pravda Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty sabotage attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine Khrystyna Bondarieva,Iryna Balachuk Wed, November 18, 2026 at 9:05 AM UTC 2 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. Russia reportedly planned mass-casualty sabotage attack in Poland to be blamed on Ukraine Russian intelligence services reportedly planned to carry out a sabotage operation on Polish territory near the border with Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast in late October or early November which they intended to be blamed on Ukraine. Source: Polish newspaper Rzeczpospolita , as cited by European Pravda Details: The newspaper cited senior sources with ties to Poland's military and security services who are familiar with an operation carried out over the past two weeks to foil the Russian plot. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Rzeczpospolita said Warsaw had been warned of the planned operation by partner intelligence services, and Polish intelligence analysts had also identified signs of the threat. "We had information about the specific sites that were to be attacked. The Russian plan envisaged mass casualties," one of the newspaper's sources said. Drawing parallels with the Gleiwitz incident, a German false-flag operation carried out on 31 August 1939, another source said: "It was supposed to be something similar to Gleiwitz. Of course, those who crossed the border would most likely have been shot, or evidence that they had come from Ukraine would have been found on them. The aim was to stop aid to Ukraine." Polish intelligence services took action after Russian intelligence officers responsible for coordinating sabotage operations appeared on the Russian side of the border. Such operations are mainly planned and coordinated by Russia's military intelligence agency, the GRU. Advertisement Advertisement Police forces in areas bordering Russia were reinforced by officers from other parts of Poland in late October for this reason. Border Guard posts also received reinforcements, and additional Internal Security Agency officers were deployed to the area. Special forces held exercises in the Warmian-Masurian region, where Poland's Territorial Defence Forces had also held exercises earlier. "The aim was deterrence, but also to ensure the ability to take pre-emptive action," a source familiar with the details said. Rzeczpospolita asked Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland's Minister-Coordinator of Special Services, whether the Russians had planned to carry out a terrorist attack in Poland at a location where large numbers of people might have been present. "I don't know the answer to that question – you'd have to ask the Russians, and they don't usually admit to planning such actions. Even if we have such information, we don't share it," he replied. Advertisement Advertisement Siemoniak added, however: "If we took certain measures, it was because we considered the threat to be real. In my opinion, all the measures taken in this case were appropriate. The available evidence indicated that the threat had been assessed as real," the minister said.
