title: Frame – 31.5" color ePaper display
body_text: Introducing Frame | TRMNL About Blog Developers Integrations For Business Discover Login Sign up About Blog Developers Integrations For Business Discover Case Studies Login Sign up ← Back to all posts Introducing Frame November 16, 2026 image-lightbox#open keydown.enter->image-lightbox#open turbo:before-cache@document->image-lightbox#close"> tl;dr our 3rd release, a full color 31.5" ePaper display in a handmade wooden frame, is now available for pre-order. watch the short film: the 1st batch is just ~470 units and i intend to ship at least a few by the end of 2026. most deliveries will happen early 2027. see logistics for more details or pre-order here . background in 2013 i founded ArtSpot. our vision was to give New Yorkers a bit of joy by exposing them to local art. we did this through informal agreements with dozens of cafes, small galleries, and restaurants. " let us curate art on your walls, get paid if someone buys it. " and it worked. sort of. finding artists was easy, building the platform was easy. getting permission from venues was slow but straightforward. the problem was nobody actually bought the art. i remember the admin email notification that first time a piece was sold. it was a small painting of Janelle Monáe. the buyer was my friend, a gift to me. here it is, still in my possession. anyway ArtSpot failed. five years later i paid back my investors (+ 13% interest). but the vision never went away. i love making and consuming art. opinionated platform i probably say " the most popular feature request since launch is ______ " too often. after saying no (and yes) to so many requests, it's tough to keep count. but with certainty, one of our strongest convictions was about color. TRMNL is not a television. it is not a clock. we avoid trying to do too much. then grayscale happened . photos look great. art is possible. community member Clark debuted Jaws (yes the movie), 1 frame at a time . 1-bit Jaws on TRMNL which got us thinking... maybe we were wrong about color. maybe it aligns with our vision and just maybe, it makes it even bigger. introducing Frame today i'm thrilled to bury the lede and announce Frame . it's a 31.5 inch full color ePaper display, enclosed in a hand made wooden body that we manufacture ourselves. yes, we opened our own woodworking shop a few miles from HQ. a closer look at the workshop is coming soon. Schedule + Weather + Art in 1 screen Frame gets all the same features as other TRMNL devices, with a few additional perks spanning both the web platform and the hardware itself. watch the short film or read along below. Clock Sync often requested, always ignored, until now. Frame will update at specified moments of the day versus a relative "every N minutes" cadence. this reduces screen flicker while also extending the battery life and adding continuity to your schedule. Offline Mode the best interface is no interface the internet is cool but totally unnecessary. Frame's microSD port lets you run devices completely offline with zero personal information reaching our servers. Dedicated Power (optional) 1st port is available on the side panel like all TRMNL devices, a rechargeable battery is included (10-20k mAh available). but with Frame we added an extra USB-C port on the rear of the device, accessible with a small hole through the back panel for always-on connectivity. Color Expertise Lazarus workbench some of my colleagues are snobs about ePaper dithering algorithms and LUTs (look-up tables). this is now your gain. over the past few months we've been developing Lazarus, a color conversion engine that we think provides Frame the best color matching on the market for any Spectra 6 display. it's also coming soon to our 4-color device , and yes it will be open source for your own tuning pleasure. Three Orientations Frame at Cafe Brûlée in LaGrange, Georgia Hang Frame in portrait or landscape orientation without additional hardware, both are built-in and flush mounted. You can optionally buy or build your own kickstand. And More we're negotiating with some of our favorite community developers to build more Frame-centric features. paying homage to ArtSpot , we just created a Local Art plugin where anyone can submit their work and even sell it through the TRMNL platform. transparent supply chain before TRMNL i spent 10 years in b2b software and knew nothing about making physical products for everyday people. nobody ever blasted me on reddit about injection mold flow lines or damaged UPS packages. at best i'd get a G2 review every 3 months. this all changed in July 2024 and after shipping 60,000 devices to 79 countries we've gotten pickier about operational design. chief among these new requirements is doing as much production as possible in-house. here are Frame's components and where they're sourced: Component Location Lead Times Inventory EPD (31.5" screen) Overseas 2-3 months 300 in warehouse, 200 en route Packaging Alabama, USA 1-2 months samples received, design tweaks sent for larger batch Wooden body TRMNL shop, Pine Mountain, Georgia 1 week made-to-order pending wood species chosen at checkout USB-C Charging Cable and Block Overseas 3-4 weeks 500 in warehouse, includes American + European style adapters Plastic parts TRMNL HQ, LaGrange, Georgia 1-2 days made daily from a growing fleet of 3D printers PCBA Overseas 2-3 weeks 1,000 full assemblies (raw components) in warehouse, bulk pick & place order TBD Fasteners Overseas + USA 2-3 weeks 500 full assemblies ordered, en route next week Rigid foam Overseas + USA 1 week 50 in warehouse, 450 en route Batteries Overseas 2-3 weeks Samples in warehouse, 800 ordered, en route next week by reducing complexity, learning from past releases, and having everything we need either in stock or on order, i expect this to be our smoothest fulfillment cycle yet. as with other devices, all Frames are assembled by our own team and never outsourced. logistics Batch #1 is available to customers in locations our USA warehouse already ships to: USA, Canada, Mexico, Australia. pre-order here . we're open to shipping elsewhere, but Duty / Import fees could be quite high given the product's Customs value. to participate in On Call Supercomputing REG AD saas Microsoft blames monster email outage on software defect introduced in July fix Summer code change caused a Fall fail – frantic engineers had to patch the patch instead of rolling back Richard Speed Richard Speed MICROSOFT ECOSYSTEM REPORTER Published mon 16 Nov 2026 // 11:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google READ MORE Microsoft's official Python agent framework hijacked to distribute malware 7 hours ago PowerShell 7 heading into Windows as 5.1 hits the end of the road 9 hours ago Time for frustrated M365 customers to stage a 'distributed denial of satisfaction' action 16 hours ago Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal 1 day ago Satya sorry for SaaS-y SNAFU - look over there, more AI! 1 day ago Microsoft has blamed last week's epic outage on a change it made in July that lurked in the network gateway servers until a surge in load and a drop in capacity triggered the defect, giving the Microsoft 365 world a day off from email. According to a preliminary post incident report published by Microsoft on November 15, the defect was introduced in July 2026. The update looked fine at the time, Microsoft says, having passed load testing and been deployed without any impact. However, the testing wasn't good enough. Microsoft's report states: "Our load testing tended to focus on weaker hardware with fewer cores." The defect caused "lock contention inside an internal Windows process which caused the machine's resources (CPU & memory) to be exhausted." REG AD "The contention issue is worsened on machines with more cores and newer hardware." REG AD The fix containing the defect was prepared specifically for Microsoft 365 network gateway servers. Then two things happened at once. Teams failed over to the "primary" gateway that supports Exchange Online, creating a surge in load that was not, in itself, particularly unusual. At the same time, almost 14 percent of server capacity for the networking gateway was out of service, which wasn't a problem by itself either: it was on its way to being restored and, according to Microsoft, "the service had sufficient capacity headroom." Together, they pushed the gateway into the defect and chaos ensued.  It was a classic cascading failure scenario. When a server loses connectivity, traffic gets routed to the next healthy endpoint. Which encountered the same problem. So traffic was rerouted again and… you can see where this was going. Within two hours, the defect was encountered across Microsoft's fleet. "At its lowest," the report states, "more than 80 percent of servers were unresponsive." So, what to do? Bringing servers back to service didn't help – they were immediately overwhelmed and fell over again. "Our normally automated recovery processes were not designed to restore service from this broad unresponsive state." A straightforward rollback was also not possible because the defect was months old. Instead, engineers developed patch for the patch or, in Microsoft's words, "an update that returned the code path to the previously known good state in Windows." The patch was applied to groups of servers and service was gradually restored. The timings show the pain customers experienced and the floundering in Redmond as Microsoft tried to work out why Exchange Online and other cloud services were so poorly. The Teams failover, which turned out to be a factor in the outage, happened at 0107 UTC on November 12. During the day, the load began to ramp up until, at 1603 UTC, Microsoft's connectivity anomaly detection monitor identified an increase in connectivity issues. At 1633 UTC, the first support case came in. It is not difficult to imagine the stress engineers felt as, over the next 15 hours, nothing they tried resolved the issue. All ongoing and planned deployments and configuration changes were paused while the team attempted to resurrect the service. Extra capacity was added. Traffic was rerouted. Yet servers kept falling over. REG AD "Those services that were able – like Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint, and Office apps – failed out of the faulty network gateway infrastructure," the report says. "But not all services, like Exchange Online, can fail out of this network gateway for scale reasons." Hence the length of time for which Exchange Online (or, from the perspective of many users, Outlook) was out of action. By 0030 UTC on November 13, Microsoft had identified connection negotiation as the main culprit for the access failures and concluded that competing processes were preventing connections from being handled. However, it took until 0720 UTC before "We identified a mitigation and applied the mitigation –  an update that reverted the defective change." At 1610 UTC, Microsoft confirmed that things were once again looking healthy and, at 0415 on November 14, issued its final customer update. A final post incident report is due on November 20. However, the preliminary report will do little to calm jangling nerves. An update applied three months ago managed to cause Exchange Online (and other services) disruption on a global scale? With load testing that didn't reflect scenarios under Microsoft's control? The engineers who worked feverishly to restore services deserve commendation and will hopefully never have to buy their own beverages in Redmond again (or at least escape the next round of firings). However, the processes that led to an update with a latent defect reaching production deserve a long, hard look. ® outlook microsoft saas outage Make us preferred on Google REG AD South Korea tries to out exam cheats with Extreme Emergency smartphone alert At least it’s less disruptive than an internet shutdown Chinese web giant Tencent says new US GPU ban ‘sets everyone back in China’ Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because company president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover PARTNER CONTENT: As carriers tighten underwriting, a backup job marked green is no longer enough. title: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch
body_text: Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch | Cornell Chronicle Skip to main content Toggle navigation Search Cornell University Cornell.edu Media Relations Search Cornell University Cornell Chronicle Topics Architecture & Design Artificial Intelligence Arts & Humanities Business, Economics & Entrepreneurship Computing & Information Sciences Energy, Environment & Sustainability Food & Agriculture Global Reach Health, Nutrition & Medicine Law, Government & Public Policy Life Sciences & Veterinary Medicine Physical Sciences & Engineering Social & Behavioral Sciences Research Matters Campus & Community News & Events Local Impact NYS Impact New York City Public Engagement Features Photos of the Week Student Life Staff News Big Red Sports Inclusion and Belonging University Statements In Memory Around Cornell All Stories Podcast Media Relations Cornellians Pause Video Researchers track whole body movement with just a smartwatch By Patricia Waldron Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science November 11, 2026 For the first time, researchers can track the movement of a person’s entire body with ultrasonic sound waves, using just an off-the-shelf smartwatch and a lightweight artificial intelligence model – all while ensuring privacy and efficiency. The new technology, called EchoMotion, was developed by Cornell’s  Smart Computer Interfaces for Future Interactions (SciFi) Lab , directed by Cheng Zhang , associate professor of information science in the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. It uses the built-in speaker and microphone on a commercial smartwatch to determine a person’s body position using a sonar-like sensing system. Once EchoMotion is integrated into commercial wearables or virtual reality (VR) systems, it could be used for tracking workouts, daily activities and progress on physical rehabilitation. EchoMotion represents a scalable approach that can use AI to understand human behaviors in the real world, Zheng said. He presented the paper, “ EchoMotion: Towards Full-Body Pose Tracking with a Single Smartwatch Using Active Acoustic Sensing ,” at the Association for Computing Machinery international joint conference on Pervasive and Ubiquitous Computing and International Symposium on Wearable Computing (UbiComp/IWSC), Oct. 13 in Shanghai. Credit: Provided Saif Mahmud, a Ph.D. candidate in the field of information science, demonstrates EchoMotion, a system for tracking body movements using an off-the-shelf smartwatch. “This is a very important jump for body tracking,” said Saif Mahmud, doctoral student in the field of information science and lead author of the new research. Existing wearable devices use sensors such as accelerometers and gyroscopes that determine the movement of the device alone, he said. As a result, whole body tracking traditionally has required more complicated setups that may also include smartphones, earbuds or VR headsets. Some tracking systems also integrate cameras, but EchoMotion’s use of sound waves offers multiple advantages. Acoustic signals preserve privacy for the wearer and the people around them – no need to set up a camera at the gym – and generate smaller amounts of data for easier and cheaper processing. “While large language models, like ChatGPT, have been in the news, EchoMotion shows how very small models running on wearables have also revolutionized sensing in human-computer interaction,” said co-author  François Guimbretière , professor of information science in Cornell Bowers. The technology also saves on battery power and works with existing off-the-shelf watches. In the prototype, sensing drew about 12 milliwatts, roughly 40 times less than a wearable camera, and a 30-minute session on a Galaxy Watch 6 used only 5% to 6% of the battery. “We have made significant efforts in making EchoMotion work on commercial devices, so that the adoption can be very easy,” Mahmud said. To develop the technology, the researchers initially created their own 3D-printed watch replica, which included a microphone and speaker pair on each side. The two speakers emit ultrasonic signals that surround a person in a sphere of inaudible sound waves. Then the two microphones pick up the echoes that bounce off the person’s limbs as they move. The researchers collected echo patterns from 10 volunteers who wore the watch on their nondominant hand as they performed 18 exercises. Using that data, the researchers developed a deep learning model to translate those patterns into body movements. They measured accuracy by comparing the predicted positions of 12 joints, from head to ankles, with the body poses captured by cameras. Off-the-shelf smartwatches have only a single microphone and speaker pair, however, so they tested the EchoMotion system on an unmodified Samsung Galaxy Watch 6 with 15 new volunteers. When used by people new to the system, the average error for predicting the location of each joint was under four inches. A one-time, 12-minute calibration cut that error by more than one third, to about 2.4 inches. The same AI model, without any retraining, also worked on a Samsung Galaxy Watch 7 and a Google Pixel Watch 3. To see how EchoMotion performed beyond the lab, the researchers asked 10 new participants to wear a smartwatch as they did the 18 exercises in a small room, in a narrow hallway and next to a noisy road. Furniture and ambient noise did not interfere, but the system’s performance suffered slightly in the hallway, due to echoes coming off of other people. Mahmud expects, however, that with more data – from thousands of users instead of dozens – their model will get better at interpreting a wearer’s movements even in crowded environments, like the subway. Currently, the team is developing the technology for use in fitness tracking, so a personal fitness agent will be able to count a user’s reps and even correct their form, for example, in a Bulgarian split squat. They are also exploring the use of EchoMotion in combination with first-person vision on smartglasses to efficiently track the objects that a person handles. “In the very near future, with wearables like smartwatches or smartglasses, a personal agent will write a description of your whole day – what you did, what you ate,” Mahmud said. “This project enables the body tracking part of that vision.” Co-authors on the study include Jiwan Kim of KAIST; Tianhong Catherine Yu, a doctoral student in the field of information science; Kenny Liang ’24 and Vineet Parikh ’20, M.S. ’24. The research was supported by the National Science Foundation. Patricia Waldron is a writer for the Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science. title: Many of Amazon’s Black Friday and Cyber Monday “deals” offered no savings
body_text: Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive - Groundwork Collaborative Menu Who We Are What We Do In The News Our Team Join Us Contact Us Gouged Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive November 16, 2026 Amazon’s Decoy Deals: Groundwork Investigation Reveals Nearly 1 in 3 Black Friday and Cyber Monday “Deals” Advertised by Amazon Offered No Savings to Shoppers, Nearly 1 in 10 Were Actually More Expensive A blockbuster new investigation from Groundwork Collaborative exposes how Amazon shoppers may be getting hosed during the retail giant’s much-touted Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events . The report, Deal or Decoy? Amazon’s Deceptive Discounts , examines products the retailer showcased as some the “best” discounts of the year to shoppers hunting for bargains during these sale events. A closer look at hundreds of these “deals” finds that Amazon frequently offered shoppers the same price, or in some cases a higher price, during recent holiday sale events than they could have paid just weeks earlier. The report’s authors, Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens, find that nearly 1 in 3 of these Amazon “deals” offered no real savings – the exact same products were sold for the same price or less in the month before the sale. During Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales in the past two years, prices for nearly 1 in 10 products advertised as “deals” were higher than what customers could have paid for the products in the month leading up to the sales. Groundwork’s analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products included on Amazon’s own deal pages for the Black Friday and Cyber Monday sale events in 2024 and 2025. These pages promote these deals as some of the “best” deals available. Amazon’s Black Friday 2025 deals page says, “With so many deals to explore, we’ve handpicked some of the best ones you’ll find.” Groundwork Collaborative President and CEO and report co-author Lindsay Owens , shared the following reaction: “Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Shoppers trust that the deals advertised to them deliver real savings because Amazon promotes them that way. But it turns out that these major sales aren’t all they’re cracked up to be. Instead, our investigation reveals that shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette. “Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars. With the holiday shopping season upon us and prices continuing to rise, shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. If Amazon can’t deliver that basic promise, lawmakers should hold them accountable.” Owens is the author of the recent book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet , which exposes how corporations are sophisticated pricing schemes to overcharge consumers. The report’s key findings include: The price of nearly 1 in 3 products that Amazon described as “deals” was the same – or higher – during sale events than what customers could have purchased them for in the month leading up to the sale. Some Amazon “deals” offered shoppers higher prices than they could have paid before the sale. On Black Friday 2025, a pair of yellow Hunter Women’s Short Rain Boots “on sale” for $126.99 had been $79.97 nine days before the sale event started, meaning customers looking for a deal could’ve paid 59% more if they waited for the sale. On Cyber Monday 2025, a pair of men’s UGG Butte boots “on sale” for $179.98 had been $98.40 roughly four weeks before the start of the sale event, meaning the “deal” cost 83% more than the recent low. Among these “worse” deals, the median sale-event price was 19% higher than what shoppers could have paid for the products in the weeks leading up to the sale. Since learning of our study, Amazon has removed the aforementioned deal pages our study drew from, but archived versions of these pages can be found at the following links: Black Friday 2024 , Cyber Monday 2024 , Black Friday 2025 , Cyber Monday 2025 . Amidst the ongoing affordability crisis, millions of Americans count on holiday sale events, like Black Friday, to deliver real savings. In 2025, a record 203 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, and this year, 70% of U.S. customers plan to take advantage of holiday promotions. Deal or Decoy calls on federal and state regulators to crack down on misleading discounts and require retailers to show the lowest price a product sold for in the previous 30 days when advertising a sale. ADDITIONAL BACKGROUND The new report builds on Groundwork’s work exposing corporate pricing abuses and delivering results for American consumers. In December 2025, Groundwork teamed up with Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union to expose how Instacart was charging shoppers different prices for the exact same groceries at the same store and time. The findings made national headlines , triggered investigations by the Federal Trade Commission and New York Attorney General , and prompted Instacart to end the practice just weeks later. Following the publication of Groundwork’s Owens’ book Gouged: The End of a Fair Price—And What That Means for Your Wallet , the Federal Trade Commission launched an investigation into major retailers’ use of customers’ personal data to set prices, adding to growing scrutiny of corporate pricing practices and their impact on Americans’ wallets in response to Groundwork and Owens’ research. In October 2026, Groundwork exposed Walmart’s creepy patent filings and pricing playbook. The report digs into patent filings, privacy disclosures, and technology investments to reveal how the retailer is building the infrastructure that could allow it to deploy personalized pricing at scale.
